Instead of rebalancing, construct a portfolio of standard options, chosen so that its value matches the exotic's along the BOUNDARY where the exotic's behaviour is determined — the barrier level over time for a barrier option. If the values match on the boundary and both satisfy the same PDE inside it, they match everywhere inside. Then the hedge needs no rebalancing at all: you put it on once and unwind when the barrier is hit. ADVANTAGES: no rebalancing cost, no gap risk, and it is robust to the hedge instruments' own model. LIMITATIONS: it needs liquid vanillas at the required strikes and maturities, the match is exact only under simplifying assumptions (typically zero drift or a specific vol structure), and residual model risk remains. Real desks use a hybrid — static replication for the bulk of the exposure, dynamic hedging for the residual.
questions.technique: Static replication as an answer to unhedgeable Greeks
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: requires the barrier pathology first, then the boundary-matching argument.

questions.prompt: An options desk produces a scenario matrix of P&L across spot moves and volatility moves. Why is this more useful than the Greeks alone?
options: Greeks are local approximations; the matrix shows actual revalued P&L for large moves and captures cross-effects
The matrix is quicker to compute than the Greeks
It removes the need to hedge delta
It shows the P&L attribution by trader
questions.explanation: Because the Greeks are a LOCAL Taylor expansion and the risks that hurt are not local. A scenario matrix — typically spot from -20% to +20% against implied vol from -10 to +10 vol points, with the book fully revalued at each node — shows what actually happens for a large move, captures the cross-effects (vanna: how delta changes as vol moves; volga: how vega changes), and reveals cliffs from barriers and digitals that no polynomial approximation can express. It also surfaces the asymmetry a symmetric gamma number hides: a book can look modestly short gamma yet lose ten times more on a 20% fall than on a 20% rise, because vol rises in the fall. That is why every options desk reports a grid alongside the Greek summary, and why regulators pushed full revaluation over delta-gamma approximations in FRTB. The Greeks remain useful for the day-to-day hedging decision; the matrix is for understanding what you actually own.
questions.technique: Full revaluation versus a local expansion
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the local-approximation point is the answer, and the cross-effects make it concrete.

questions.prompt: You are long a 1-month at-the-money straddle, delta-hedged daily. Over the month spot ends exactly where it started and implied vol is unchanged. Did you make or lose money?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It depends entirely on the PATH. You profit if realised volatility over the month exceeded the implied vol you paid, and lose if it was lower. Where spot ended is irrelevant.
questions.explanation: This is the central insight of a hedged option book and it catches people out because the natural answer is 'nothing happened, so nothing changed'. Being long a delta-hedged straddle is a bet on REALISED versus IMPLIED volatility, not on direction. The daily P&L is approximately (1/2)*gamma*S^2*[(dS/S)^2 - sigma^2*dt] — you collect the squared realised move and pay the squared implied move each day. Sum over the month: if the stock oscillated wildly and came back, you rebalanced constantly, bought low and sold high each time, and made money despite ending flat. If it drifted quietly, you paid theta every day for movement that never came and lost. TWO PATHS, SAME ENDPOINT, OPPOSITE P&L. This is why 'volatility is a tradeable asset' is meaningful and why variance swaps exist — they pay realised minus implied variance directly, without the path-dependence introduced by the hedging schedule. PRACTICAL REFINEMENTS worth adding. The gamma weighting means moves matter MORE when spot is near the strike, so the same realised vol delivers different P&L depending on where it occurred relative to the strike — this is the 'dollar gamma weighting' that makes a hedged option position an imperfect vol trade. And discrete daily hedging means you capture close-to-close variance, not true realised variance, so intraday moves that reverse are lost.
questions.technique: Path dependence of hedged option P&L
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the answer is counter-intuitive, and the variance-swap contrast shows real understanding.

questions.prompt: Vega is usually quoted per one volatility POINT. An option has vega of 20 and implied vol moves from 18% to 19%. What is the P&L?
options: +20 for a long position
+2 for a long position
+0.2 for a long position
+2,000 for a long position
questions.explanation: +20. The market convention is to quote vega as the value change for a ONE PERCENTAGE POINT move in implied volatility, so a move from 18 to 19 is exactly one point and the P&L is the vega itself. The trap is the underlying mathematics: the analytic partial derivative dV/dsigma is per UNIT of vol (i.e. per 100 points), so the raw formula output must be divided by 100 to get the quoted number. Getting this wrong is a factor-of-100 error, which is the kind of mistake that shows up immediately in a risk report. The same convention issue applies to rho (usually quoted per basis point or per 1%) and theta (usually per calendar day, though some desks use per business day — worth asking which). Always confirm the convention before interpreting a Greek number on an unfamiliar system.
questions.technique: Greek quoting conventions
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: trivial once you know the convention, and a factor-of-100 error if you don't.

questions.prompt: Why does an options desk care about the gamma and vega PROFILE across strikes, not just the net numbers?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because net Greeks conceal the distribution of risk. A book that is net-flat gamma can be long gamma at one strike and short at another, which behaves nothing like flat once spot moves — the net number is only valid at today's spot.
questions.explanation: THE PROBLEM WITH NET NUMBERS. Greeks are evaluated at the current spot and vol. A book long 1,000 gamma at the 100 strike and short 1,000 gamma at the 120 strike reports net zero gamma today. But move spot to 120 and the short-gamma position dominates: gamma is now concentrated where you are short, and the book that looked flat is now materially short gamma in a market that has already moved against you. The net number was true and useless. WHAT DESKS LOOK AT INSTEAD. (1) A gamma PROFILE — gamma plotted against spot, showing where the exposure sits and where it flips sign. (2) A vega profile by MATURITY bucket, because vega at 1 month and vega at 2 years are different risks: the short end moves far more, and a book long front vega and short back vega is running a term-structure position that nets to zero vega. (3) The scenario matrix, which is the profile idea generalised to two dimensions. THE GENERAL PRINCIPLE, which applies well beyond options: any risk summary that aggregates across a dimension can hide offsetting exposures that will not stay offset. It is the same reason rates desks report bucketed DV01s rather than a single duration, and the same reason a diversified VaR can conceal a concentration.
questions.technique: Why aggregated risk numbers hide their own distribution
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the concrete two-strike example is what makes the abstract point land.

questions.prompt: For a delta-hedged position, which combination of Greeks describes the daily P&L?
options: Gamma and theta
Delta and rho
Vega and rho
Delta and gamma
questions.explanation: Gamma and theta. Delta hedging removes the first-order spot exposure, leaving dP ≈ theta*dt + (1/2)*gamma*(dS)^2. Substituting the Black-Scholes PDE relation theta = -(1/2)*sigma^2*S^2*gamma (exact when r = 0) gives dP ≈ (1/2)*gamma*S^2*[(dS/S)^2 - sigma^2*dt] — you are long realised variance and short implied variance, with gamma as the position size and theta as the rent. Vega also matters, but only on days when implied volatility actually moves, whereas gamma and theta act every single day regardless. Rho is negligible over one day for anything short-dated. This is the single most useful identity for an options trader, and being able to write it down cold is expected.
questions.technique: The gamma-theta identity for hedged P&L
questions.difficultyRationale: Easy: direct recall, and it underpins most of the topic.

questions.prompt: How would you calculate the Greeks for an exotic option with no closed-form price?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Finite differences on the pricing model: bump each input, reprice, and divide by the bump. For Monte Carlo, use the SAME random numbers for the base and bumped runs, or the noise will swamp the sensitivity.
questions.explanation: THE METHOD. Price the option, bump the input by a small amount, reprice, and take the difference over the bump. Central differences — bump up and down and use [V(S+h) - V(S-h)]/(2h) — are second-order accurate and worth the extra revaluation. Gamma comes from [V(S+h) - 2V(S) + V(S-h)]/h^2. THE CRITICAL DETAIL FOR MONTE CARLO: use COMMON RANDOM NUMBERS. If you re-draw fresh paths for the bumped run, the difference between the two prices is dominated by simulation noise rather than by the bump — the Monte Carlo standard error is typically far larger than the sensitivity you are trying to measure. Fixing the random seed makes the two runs differ only by the bump, and the difference becomes meaningful. This single point is what the question is usually testing. CHOOSING THE BUMP SIZE is a genuine bias-variance trade-off: too large and you pick up curvature (bias), too small and you amplify numerical noise, and for Monte Carlo too small a bump can produce identical paths through a discontinuous payoff and hence a Greek of exactly zero. For discontinuous payoffs (digitals, barriers) finite differences are unreliable near the discontinuity and you want either a smoothed payoff or a pathwise/likelihood-ratio method. ALTERNATIVES worth naming: pathwise differentiation and the likelihood ratio method give Greeks in a single simulation, and adjoint algorithmic differentiation (AAD) computes all Greeks at roughly the cost of one extra pricing run — which is why it became standard for large XVA and exotic books where bumping every input is computationally impossible.
questions.technique: Finite-difference Greeks and common random numbers
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the method is obvious, the common-random-numbers requirement is not.

questions.prompt: A client asks you to quote a 2-year option on an illiquid single stock where only 3-month options trade. What are the risks?
questions.canonicalAnswer: You have no market to calibrate the 2-year volatility to, so the price is a model output. Once you trade it you cannot hedge the vega — there is no 2-year option to trade — so you are left with an unhedgeable long-dated vol position plus model risk on the term structure.
questions.explanation: THE PRICING PROBLEM. Implied vol has a term structure, and you can observe it only at 3 months. Extrapolating to 2 years is a model assumption, not an observation. A mean-reverting vol model will pull the long-dated vol toward a long-run level; a flat extrapolation will not; the two can differ by several vol points, which on a 2-year option is a large fraction of the premium. There is no market to tell you which is right. THE HEDGING PROBLEM, which is worse. Even if the price is fair, you cannot hedge the vega: hedging 2-year vega with 3-month options requires rolling the hedge eight times, and each roll is at an unknown future 3-month vol. You are running a vol TERM-STRUCTURE position whether you want to or not, and the hedge ratio depends on your model of how the term structure moves. You can hedge the delta continuously, so gamma is manageable, but the vega is stuck. WHAT TO DO. Quote wide — the bid-offer must compensate for unhedgeable risk and model uncertainty, and 'I would quote it, but very wide, and here is what the width is paying for' is the answer they want. Size-limit the exposure. Take a model reserve sized by repricing under alternative term-structure assumptions. Consider hedging with a correlated liquid name and accepting basis risk. And check whether the client's real need can be met with a structure you CAN hedge — often a strip of shorter options or a different payoff achieves the economics with a tradeable risk profile. THE GENERAL POINT: the question is not 'can I price it' but 'can I hedge it', and unhedgeable risk should be priced as inventory, not as a spread.
questions.technique: Pricing and hedging where the market does not extend
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: needs both the calibration and the hedging problem, and the commercial answer.

questions.prompt: Why is a short-dated at-the-money option the most dangerous position to be short?
options: Gamma is maximised there, so delta swings violently and hedging cannot keep up
Vega is maximised there
Rho is maximised there
Its premium is highest
questions.explanation: Gamma. For an at-the-money option gamma scales roughly as 1/(S*sigma*sqrt(T)), so it blows up as expiry approaches — delta must travel from about 0.5 all the way to 0 or 1 within days, which means small spot moves force large hedge trades. Short that position and every move costs you, the required rebalancing is largest exactly when it is most expensive, and a gap through the strike is unhedgeable. The theta you collect is the compensation, and it is real, but the distribution is brutally asymmetric: you earn a little most days and can lose a great deal in one. VEGA is maximised for LONG-dated at-the-money options, the opposite maturity profile — which is the standard confusion this question tests, and it is why desks trade short-dated options for gamma and long-dated ones for vega. Premium is highest for long-dated, and rho is not a material equity risk at short maturity.
questions.technique: Why short-dated ATM gamma is the dangerous exposure
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the maturity profiles of gamma and vega are opposite and easily confused.

questions.prompt: What does 'risk-neutral valuation' actually mean? Does it assume investors do not care about risk?
questions.canonicalAnswer: No. It is a computational device: because the derivative can be replicated by the underlying and cash, its price is fixed by no-arbitrage and is the same whatever anyone's risk preferences are. So you may as well compute it in the imaginary world where everyone is risk-neutral, since the answer must agree.
questions.explanation: THE MISCONCEPTION the question is probing is that risk-neutral valuation assumes indifference to risk. It does not. THE ARGUMENT: a derivative's payoff can be manufactured by continuously trading the underlying and cash. Therefore its price is pinned by no-arbitrage to the cost of that replication — no preferences enter. And since the price cannot depend on risk preferences, you are free to compute it under ANY consistent assumption about them. Choosing risk-neutrality makes the maths easy, because then every asset drifts at r and you can discount expected payoffs at r. The answer applies in the real world because the price never depended on the assumption. THE STRIKING CONSEQUENCE: two investors who violently disagree about a stock's expected return must still agree on the option's price. Their disagreement concerns the stock, and it is already fully expressed in the stock's price today — which IS an input to the formula. The expected return has not been ignored; it has been absorbed into S, and adding it again would double-count. WHERE IT BREAKS: the argument rests on replication, so it needs a complete market — continuous, frictionless trading in the underlying. For a non-traded underlying (weather, mortality, an illiquid name) replication fails, the risk-neutral measure is not unique, and prices genuinely do depend on preferences. That is why those markets are hard and why their prices embed a risk premium you cannot arbitrage away.
questions.technique: Replication as the justification for the risk-neutral device
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the standard answer is recall; explaining where it breaks is the discriminator.

questions.prompt: You need to compute a 10-day 99% VaR for an options book. Which measure do you simulate under?
options: The real-world measure — VaR is a statement about what will actually happen
The risk-neutral measure, since that is how the options are priced
Either; they give the same answer over 10 days
Risk-neutral for the paths, real-world for the valuation
questions.explanation: Real world for the scenario generation. VaR asks what losses you will ACTUALLY experience with what frequency, which is a question about the real-world distribution of market moves — so you simulate paths under the real-world drift and volatility. Using the risk-neutral drift would mean assuming every asset earns the risk-free rate, which is not a forecast of anything and systematically misstates the distribution of a risky book. The subtlety worth adding, and it is what makes this question good: once you are AT a future scenario, you value the options in it using RISK-NEUTRAL valuation, because that is how they will be marked. So a full VaR simulation for a derivatives book uses BOTH — real-world paths to generate the scenarios, risk-neutral pricing to revalue at each one. The last option has it exactly backwards. Note also that over 10 days the drift difference is small relative to volatility, so the practical impact is modest — but the conceptual answer still matters, and it matters a great deal for long-horizon exposure calculations like CVA.
questions.technique: Which measure for scenario generation versus valuation
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the both-measures nuance is what separates a real answer.

questions.prompt: What is the market price of risk, and what happens to volatility when you change measure?
questions.canonicalAnswer: lambda = (m - r)/s, the excess return per unit of volatility for a variable with real-world drift m and volatility s. Changing measure shifts the DRIFT by lambda*s and leaves the volatility completely unchanged.
questions.explanation: THE DEFINITION. For any variable driving asset prices, with real-world drift m and volatility s, the market price of risk is lambda = (m - r)/s — the excess expected return the market demands per unit of risk borne. For a traded asset it is determined by the market. Crucially, all derivatives dependent on the SAME source of uncertainty must have the same lambda, which is the no-arbitrage condition underlying the whole framework. THE MEASURE CHANGE. Moving from the real-world to the risk-neutral measure (Girsanov) subtracts lambda*s from the drift, taking m down to r. The VOLATILITY IS UNCHANGED. That is the fact to remember and the point of the question. WHY IT MATTERS PRACTICALLY: it is why implied volatility is a meaningful, comparable market observable — the vol you back out of an option price under the risk-neutral measure is the same vol that governs real-world dynamics, so it can be compared directly with realised volatility. An 'implied drift' would have no such interpretation. It also explains the asymmetry in estimation difficulty: volatility can be estimated well from a few months of data, whereas the real-world drift needs decades, since the standard error of a mean return estimate falls only as 1/sqrt(T) in CALENDAR time and cannot be improved by sampling more frequently. That is why risk models focus on volatility and largely ignore drift over short horizons. FOR NON-TRADED VARIABLES lambda is not pinned down by any market, which is exactly why weather derivatives, longevity swaps and similar instruments carry irreducible pricing uncertainty.
questions.technique: The market price of risk and drift-only measure changes
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the formula is recall; the volatility-invariance and its consequences are the substance.

questions.prompt: For estimating potential future exposure to a counterparty over 10 years, which world should generate the paths?
options: Usually real-world for regulatory exposure, though front-office CVA desks often use risk-neutral so the number is hedgeable
Always risk-neutral, since exposure is a pricing concept
Always real-world, with no exceptions
Neither — exposure is computed deterministically
questions.explanation: Both are defensible and the choice depends on the purpose, which is what makes this a good question. REAL-WORLD is the natural answer for a RISK measure: PFE asks where the market plausibly goes over ten years, and that is a real-world question. Regulators generally expect real-world calibration for exposure modelling. RISK-NEUTRAL is what front-office CVA desks typically use, because CVA is a PRICE that must be booked, hedged and marked — and a hedge only works if the exposure is computed under the same measure the hedging instruments are priced in. Using real-world exposures to compute a number you then hedge with risk-neutral instruments creates a systematic mismatch. In both cases the VALUATION at each future node is risk-neutral; the disagreement is only about the path generation. Over a 10-year horizon the drift difference is material — it compounds — so this is not academic: the two approaches can produce meaningfully different exposure profiles, and being able to say why a bank might run both is a strong answer.
questions.technique: Measure choice for long-horizon exposure
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: the honest answer is 'it depends on the purpose', with reasons on both sides.

questions.prompt: In a risk-neutral world, what is the expected return on every asset?
options: The risk-free rate
Zero
The asset's real-world expected return
The market return
questions.explanation: The risk-free rate — that is the defining property of the measure. Every asset, however risky, drifts at r, and every payoff is discounted at r. Note this is a property of the artificial measure used for pricing, not a claim about reality: in the real world risky assets earn a premium over r, which is precisely the market price of risk that the measure change removes. Two related facts worth having: under the risk-neutral measure the DISCOUNTED price of any traded asset is a martingale, which is the formal statement of the same idea; and the risk-neutral probability of an event is generally NOT the real-world probability, so N(d2) — the risk-neutral probability that a call finishes in the money — is not a forecast of anything.
questions.technique: The defining property of the risk-neutral measure
questions.difficultyRationale: Easy: definitional, and the 'not a forecast' point prevents a common misuse.

questions.prompt: Why is the real-world drift so much harder to estimate than volatility?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because the standard error of a mean-return estimate depends only on the total CALENDAR span of data, not on sampling frequency — so you need decades. Volatility estimation improves with more frequent sampling, so months of daily data suffice.
questions.explanation: THE ASYMMETRY. For a diffusion with drift mu and volatility sigma observed over a period T with n samples: the standard error of the estimated mean return is sigma/sqrt(T), depending only on the calendar span. Sampling hourly instead of daily does not help at all — you get more observations, but each carries proportionally less information about the drift. To estimate an 8% equity drift with a 20% volatility to within one percentage point you need sigma^2/(0.01)^2 = 400 years of data. VOLATILITY IS THE OPPOSITE: its standard error is roughly sigma/sqrt(2n), which depends on the NUMBER of observations. Sample more frequently and the estimate improves without needing a longer history, which is why a few months of daily data gives a usable volatility and why high-frequency realised-volatility estimators work so well. THE CONSEQUENCES, which is what the question is after. (1) Risk models over short horizons sensibly ignore the drift — over a day it is negligible relative to volatility anyway, roughly 0.03% against 1%. (2) This is a deep reason why risk-neutral valuation is so useful: it removes the parameter you cannot estimate and keeps the one you can. (3) It is why any strategy or model whose output is sensitive to an estimated expected return should be treated with suspicion — mean-variance optimisation is notoriously unstable for exactly this reason, and constraining or shrinking the return estimates is not a hack but a necessity.
questions.technique: Why drift estimation is calendar-limited and volatility is not
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the sqrt(T)-versus-sqrt(n) distinction is the crux and is genuinely non-obvious.

questions.prompt: Derive the Black–Scholes PDE. Where exactly does the stock's expected return disappear?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Form a portfolio short one option and long df/dS shares. Applying Ito, the dW terms cancel, so the portfolio is instantaneously riskless and must earn r. Setting dPi = r*Pi*dt gives df/dt + r*S*df/dS + (1/2)*sigma^2*S^2*d2f/dS2 = r*f. The drift mu cancels at the hedging step.
questions.explanation: STEP 1. Assume dS = mu*S*dt + sigma*S*dW. STEP 2. By Ito, df = (df/dt + mu*S*df/dS + (1/2)*sigma^2*S^2*d2f/dS2)dt + sigma*S*(df/dS)dW. STEP 3. Form Pi = -f + (df/dS)*S: short one option, long df/dS shares. Its change is dPi = -df + (df/dS)dS. Substituting, the dW term of df is sigma*S*(df/dS)dW and the dW term of (df/dS)dS is also sigma*S*(df/dS)dW — they CANCEL exactly. So dPi = (-df/dt - (1/2)*sigma^2*S^2*d2f/dS2)dt, with no random term. STEP 4. An instantaneously riskless portfolio must earn r or there is arbitrage: dPi = r*Pi*dt. Equating and rearranging gives df/dt + r*S*df/dS + (1/2)*sigma^2*S^2*d2f/dS2 = r*f. WHERE MU GOES. Notice mu appears in the dt term of df at step 2, and it is carried into dPi by the -df term — but the +(df/dS)dS term contributes +mu*S*(df/dS)dt, which cancels it exactly, at the same moment the dW terms cancel. That is the entire content of the result: the hedge removes both the randomness AND the drift together, because they enter through the same dS. Consequences worth stating: the option price cannot depend on anyone's view of mu, so two investors who disagree about the stock must agree on the option; and the r that appears is not a discount rate chosen for risk, it is forced by the riskless portfolio. TWO SUBTLETIES a good answer flags. df/dS is treated as constant over dt, which is only valid in the continuous limit — that is where continuous rebalancing enters. And the argument needs the portfolio to be self-financing, which is a genuine technical condition, not bookkeeping.
questions.technique: Delta hedging to cancel both the noise and the drift
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: the four steps are memorable, but explaining exactly where mu cancels is what's being tested.

questions.prompt: Which Black–Scholes assumption fails most seriously in practice?
options: Constant, known volatility — vol is stochastic and clusters, which is what the smile shows
No transaction costs
Constant interest rates
Short selling is permitted
questions.explanation: Constant volatility, with continuous paths a close second. Constant vol is falsified directly and visibly by the volatility SMILE: if the assumption held, implied vol would be identical across all strikes and maturities, and the observed surface is the market telling you the assumption is wrong and in exactly which direction. Real volatility is stochastic, clusters, and is negatively correlated with returns. Continuous paths fail because markets gap, and jump risk is fundamentally unhedgeable by delta — no rebalancing frequency helps against an overnight move. The other assumptions matter but are corrections rather than structural failures: transaction costs widen the effective bid-offer, constant rates is mild for short-dated equity options (though serious for long-dated and rates products), and short-selling constraints affect specific names. The right framing is that the first two are why Black-Scholes is a quoting convention rather than a description of reality.
questions.technique: Ranking the assumption failures
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: all are false; ranking them by consequence is the discriminator.

questions.prompt: Explain carefully what N(d1) and N(d2) mean in the Black–Scholes call formula.
questions.canonicalAnswer: N(d2) is the risk-neutral probability the option finishes in the money. N(d1) is the delta — and it is the exercise probability under the measure that uses the STOCK as numeraire, which is why S*N(d1) is the discounted expected value of receiving the share conditional on exercise.
questions.explanation: Read the formula as its two economic pieces: c = S*N(d1) - K*e^(-rT)*N(d2) is 'the present value of receiving the stock if I exercise' minus 'the present value of paying the strike if I exercise'. THE SECOND TERM is straightforward. K*e^(-rT) is the discounted strike, and N(d2) is the risk-neutral probability of exercise, so the product is the expected discounted payment. Note 'risk-neutral' — d2 uses drift r, not mu, so N(d2) is NOT a forecast of anything. THE FIRST TERM is subtler. You might expect S*(probability of exercise), but that is wrong, because the amount you receive is correlated with whether you receive it — you get the stock precisely in the states where it is worth more. The correct expression is the discounted risk-neutral expectation of S_T times the exercise indicator, and that works out to S_0*N(d1). Equivalently and more elegantly: N(d1) is the probability of exercise under the measure that uses the STOCK as numeraire rather than cash. Two different measures, two different probabilities, hence two different numbers — with N(d1) > N(d2) always, since d1 = d2 + sigma*sqrt(T). THE THIRD FACT: N(d1) is also the delta, dc/dS. That is not a coincidence — it falls out because the S-dependence of the two N() terms cancels exactly when you differentiate, which is a small miracle worth verifying once. The common error is to call N(d1) 'the probability of exercise', which conflates it with N(d2) and loses the numeraire point entirely.
questions.technique: The two terms as expectations under two measures
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: the numeraire interpretation of N(d1) is well beyond the usual answer.

questions.prompt: The Black–Scholes PDE is df/dt + rS(df/dS) + (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 (d2f/dS2) = rf. What distinguishes a call from a put in this framework?
options: Only the boundary conditions — the PDE is identical for every derivative on S
The sign of the volatility term
The PDE has a different form for puts
Puts require a separate risk-neutral measure
questions.explanation: Only the boundary conditions. The PDE is satisfied by EVERY derivative whose payoff depends on S and t — calls, puts, digitals, forwards, barriers. What identifies the instrument is the terminal condition: max(S-K,0) for a call, max(K-S,0) for a put, an indicator for a digital, S-K for a forward, plus any boundary conditions along the way (a knock-out imposes f = 0 at the barrier). That is a genuinely useful insight rather than a technicality. It means one numerical PDE solver prices your entire book by swapping the payoff function, it explains why exotic pricing is a boundary-condition problem rather than a new theory each time, and it is why substituting x = ln(S) to reach the heat equation is worth doing once — every option is then the same well-studied diffusion with different initial data. It also implies any portfolio of derivatives satisfies the PDE, which is where the Greek relationship Theta + rS*Delta + (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 Gamma = rV comes from.
questions.technique: The PDE is instrument-independent; the payoff is a boundary condition
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the insight reframes exotic pricing entirely.

questions.prompt: How do you adapt Black–Scholes for dividends, and for options on futures?
questions.canonicalAnswer: For a continuous dividend yield q, replace S with S*e^(-qT). For discrete dividends, subtract their present value from S. For options on futures (Black's model), replace S with F*e^(-rT), which removes the drift because entering a futures contract costs nothing.
questions.explanation: CONTINUOUS YIELD. If the stock pays a continuous yield q, holding the stock earns q that the option holder does not receive, so the option is written on a lower effective asset: replace S_0 with S_0*e^(-qT) throughout, including inside d1 where the drift becomes (r - q + sigma^2/2). This covers stock indices (q = average dividend yield) and, with q = the foreign risk-free rate, FX options — that is Garman-Kohlhagen, and the logic is that holding foreign currency earns the foreign rate. DISCRETE DIVIDENDS. Subtract the present value of dividends expected before expiry from the current stock price and run standard Black-Scholes on the remainder. The reasoning is that the known dividend component is not risky, so only the residual should be modelled as lognormal. It is an approximation — it slightly misstates the volatility, since sigma should really apply to the risky part only — but it is the standard market practice. BLACK'S MODEL. For an option on a FUTURES contract, replace S_0 with F_0*e^(-rT). Why it works: entering a futures contract costs nothing, so in a risk-neutral world the futures price is a martingale and drifts at ZERO rather than at r. The formula becomes c = e^(-rT)[F_0*N(d1) - K*N(d2)] with d1 = [ln(F_0/K) + sigma^2*T/2]/(sigma*sqrt(T)). This is the market standard for interest rate caps, floors and swaptions, and for commodity options, because those markets quote forwards rather than spot. The unifying idea worth stating: all three are the same model with the underlying replaced by the present value of what you actually receive, and getting that substitution right is most of applied option pricing.
questions.technique: Adjusting the underlying for carry
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the three cases are standard, and the martingale reason for Black's model is the depth.

questions.prompt: Why can Black–Scholes price an American call on a non-dividend-paying stock exactly, but not an American put?
options: Early exercise is never optimal for the call, so it equals the European; for the put it can be optimal
The put's payoff is not differentiable
American puts have no risk-neutral measure
The put violates the PDE
questions.explanation: Because early exercise is never optimal for a call on a non-dividend payer, so the American and European calls have identical value and the European formula prices both exactly. The argument: exercising gives S - K today, but selling the option gives at least S - K*e^(-rT), which is strictly more — you would be throwing away both the remaining insurance and the interest on the strike. For the PUT the interest term flips sign: exercising receives K early and earns interest on it, and once deep in the money the remaining optionality is small (the stock can only fall to zero), so early exercise can be optimal. That makes the American put strictly more valuable than the European whenever r > 0, and it introduces a FREE BOUNDARY — an unknown exercise frontier that must be solved for alongside the price — which is why there is no closed form. In practice you use a binomial tree, a PDE solver with the early-exercise condition applied at each step, or an analytic approximation like Barone-Adesi-Whaley. Note that dividends restore early-exercise value to the call, but only immediately before an ex-dividend date.
questions.technique: Early exercise and the free-boundary problem
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the call half is standard; naming the free boundary as the reason for no closed form is the extra.

questions.prompt: What happens to the Black–Scholes call price as volatility goes to zero, and as it goes to infinity?
questions.canonicalAnswer: As sigma goes to 0 the call becomes a forward: max(S - K*e^(-rT), 0). As sigma goes to infinity the call price approaches S, the full stock price.
questions.explanation: ZERO VOL. With sigma = 0 the stock grows deterministically to S*e^(rT). If that exceeds K the option finishes in the money for certain and is simply a forward contract, worth S - K*e^(-rT); otherwise it is worthless. So c goes to max(S - K*e^(-rT), 0). Check against the formula: as sigma goes to 0, d1 and d2 both go to +infinity when S > K*e^(-rT), so N(d1) = N(d2) = 1 and c = S - K*e^(-rT). Delta is exactly 1 and there is no gamma, so the hedge is static. INFINITE VOL. As sigma grows, d1 goes to +infinity and d2 to -infinity (since d2 = d1 - sigma*sqrt(T)), so N(d1) goes to 1 and N(d2) goes to 0, giving c approaching S. This is the upper bound on any call: the option can never be worth more than the stock, and it approaches that bound as uncertainty grows without limit. The intuition is that with enormous volatility the stock is almost certainly either enormous or nearly zero, so the strike becomes irrelevant and the call is effectively the stock itself. WHY THESE MATTER. They are the sanity checks on any implementation — a pricer that violates either limit has a bug — and they are also the bounds that guarantee the vol-to-price map is well behaved: price is continuous and strictly increasing in sigma from max(S - K*e^(-rT), 0) up to S, which is exactly what makes implied volatility uniquely defined and findable by Newton's method.
questions.technique: Limiting behaviour of the formula in volatility
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: both limits are gettable, and connecting them to implied-vol uniqueness is the payoff.

questions.prompt: Which of these does NOT appear as an input to the Black–Scholes formula?
options: The stock's expected return
The risk-free rate
The volatility
Time to maturity
questions.explanation: The expected return mu is absent, and its absence is the central result rather than an omission. It cancels during the derivation at the moment you form the delta-hedged portfolio: the hedge removes the randomness and the drift together, because both enter through dS. The economic consequence is striking — two investors with completely opposite views on whether the stock will rise must nevertheless agree on the option's price. Their disagreement is about the stock and is already fully expressed in S, which IS an input; adding it again would double-count. This is also the practical reason option pricing is tractable at all: the expected return is the hardest parameter in finance to estimate, needing decades of data, whereas volatility is estimable from months. Black-Scholes needs only the one you can measure.
questions.technique: The absent parameter and why
questions.difficultyRationale: Easy: recall, but the reason is the whole point of the model.

questions.prompt: Verify that the Black–Scholes call and put formulas satisfy put-call parity.
questions.explanation: Write both formulas and subtract: c - p = S*N(d1) - K*e^(-rT)*N(d2) - K*e^(-rT)*N(-d2) + S*N(-d1). Group the S terms and the K terms: = S*[N(d1) + N(-d1)] - K*e^(-rT)*[N(d2) + N(-d2)]. Since the standard normal is symmetric, N(x) + N(-x) = 1 for any x, so both brackets are 1 and c - p = S - K*e^(-rT). That is exactly put-call parity. WHY IT MATTERS beyond the algebra. Parity is a MODEL-FREE result — it follows from a static arbitrage (long call, short put, short stock, long cash replicates nothing) and requires no assumption about the price process at all. So any model that violates it is arbitrageable, and checking parity is the first sanity test on a pricer. The fact that Black-Scholes satisfies it identically, for every sigma, is reassuring but not surprising: it must, or it would be wrong. TWO PRACTICAL CONSEQUENCES. First, a call and a put at the same strike and maturity must have the SAME implied volatility, because parity pins their price difference regardless of the model — so if you observe different implied vols for a call and put at the same strike, you have found either an arbitrage or (far more likely) stale prices, a dividend assumption mismatch, or a borrow cost. In practice that check is how desks detect bad marks. Second, it means you only ever need to model one side; the other follows.
questions.technique: Deriving parity from the formulas via normal symmetry
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the algebra is short, and the same-implied-vol consequence is the practical payoff.

questions.prompt: Substituting x = ln(S) into the Black–Scholes PDE and rescaling transforms it into which classical equation?
options: The heat (diffusion) equation
The wave equation
Laplace's equation
The transport equation
questions.explanation: The heat equation. Setting x = ln(S) removes the S and S^2 coefficients, leaving a constant-coefficient parabolic PDE; a further change of variables in time and a multiplicative substitution eliminate the remaining first-order and zeroth-order terms, giving du/dtau = d2u/dx2. This is how the closed-form solution was originally obtained — the heat equation's fundamental solution is a Gaussian, and convolving it with the transformed payoff produces the N(d1), N(d2) expression. It also explains two practical facts. Option prices SMOOTH over time exactly as heat diffuses: a discontinuous digital payoff becomes smooth immediately away from expiry, which is why digitals are hardest to hedge right at expiry. And it means the numerical methods for options are the standard PDE schemes — explicit, implicit, Crank-Nicolson — with their well-understood stability properties, rather than anything bespoke to finance.
questions.technique: The heat-equation transformation
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: the transformation is a known result, and the smoothing consequence is the useful part.

questions.prompt: An interviewer says 'Black–Scholes is wrong, so why does anyone use it?' How do you answer?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because for liquid options it is not being used as a model of reality — it is a quoting convention. The market sets the price; Black–Scholes converts it into an implied volatility, which is a comparable, slowly-moving coordinate. The smile is the visible admission that the assumptions are false, and nobody is fooled.
questions.explanation: THE FRAMING that answers the question: what is the model being used FOR? FOR LIQUID VANILLAS the market determines the price, and Black-Scholes is used in reverse — to invert that price into an implied volatility. That coordinate is enormously more useful than the price itself: it is comparable across strikes, maturities and underlyings, it moves slowly, and relative value is visible in it. The model is a communication device, and the SMILE is the market openly recording that the constant-vol assumption is false and by exactly how much. Nobody using it believes the assumptions. FOR EXOTICS the situation is completely different — there is no market price to invert, so the model genuinely determines the value, and that is where model risk is real and where validation effort belongs. THE DEEPER POINTS worth adding. The model is right about the STRUCTURE even where it is wrong about the parameters: replication, no-arbitrage, and the delta hedge as the mechanism are all correct, and they survive into every more sophisticated model. Local vol, stochastic vol and jump models are all repairs to the same frame, not replacements for it. And the practical answer: it is used because the alternative to a shared imperfect convention is no shared convention at all, which would make it impossible to quote a market. That is why an incorrect model can be genuinely useful, and it is the same reason yield-to-maturity survives despite its reinvestment assumption being false.
questions.technique: Distinguishing a model's use as convention from its use as description
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the question is deliberately provocative and the quoting-convention framing is the answer.

questions.prompt: The Black–Scholes PDE can be written Theta + rS*Delta + (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 Gamma = rV. What does this tell you about a delta-neutral portfolio?
options: Theta and Gamma are directly linked — for a delta-neutral book they trade off against each other
Theta must be zero
Gamma must be zero
The portfolio earns more than the risk-free rate
questions.explanation: Setting Delta = 0 leaves Theta + (1/2)sigma^2 S^2 Gamma = rV, so theta and gamma are tied together — you cannot have both positive. With r = 0 it is exactly Theta = -(1/2)sigma^2 S^2 Gamma, a clean inverse proportionality. The economics: gamma is what you are PAID for the underlying actually moving, theta is the RENT you pay for holding that exposure, and no-arbitrage forces them to offset. That is why a delta-hedged book's daily P&L is approximately (1/2)*Gamma*S^2*[(realised move)^2 - sigma^2*dt] — long realised variance, short implied variance. Note the rV term on the right is what breaks the exact opposition when r is nonzero, which is how a deep in-the-money European put can have positive theta AND positive gamma. Being able to give that counterexample is what distinguishes knowing the relationship from reciting it.
questions.technique: Reading the PDE as the theta-gamma trade-off
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the identity is standard; the r-term exception is the discriminating detail.

questions.prompt: Why does a traded option price map to exactly one implied volatility?
options: Vega is strictly positive, so price is strictly increasing in volatility and the map is invertible
Because the Black–Scholes formula is linear in volatility
It does not — multiple implied vols can give the same price
Because volatility is bounded between 0 and 1
questions.explanation: Vega is strictly positive for a vanilla option, so price is a strictly increasing function of volatility — and a strictly monotonic function is invertible. Combined with the limits (price goes to max(S - K*e^(-rT), 0) as sigma goes to 0, and to S as sigma goes to infinity), every price strictly between those bounds corresponds to exactly one volatility, found in a few Newton iterations since you also have vega as the derivative. That uniqueness is what makes the quoting convention possible: quoting in vol would be meaningless if two vols gave the same price. Note the property is specific to VANILLAS. Some exotics are not monotonic in volatility — a digital's price can fall as vol rises when it is in the money, and barrier options are non-monotonic too — so 'implied vol' is not well defined for them without further convention.
questions.technique: Monotonicity in vega as the basis of the convention
questions.difficultyRationale: Easy: one property, and the exotic exception is worth knowing.

questions.prompt: Equity index options show a downward-sloping skew while FX options show a symmetric smile. Why the difference?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Equity has a directional fear: crashes are sudden and rallies gradual (leverage effect, crash risk), plus structural demand for downside protection. FX is symmetric because a large move in either direction is a crisis for one of the two currencies — there is no privileged direction.
questions.explanation: EQUITY SKEW. Low strikes trade at materially higher implied vol. Three reinforcing causes. (1) The LEVERAGE EFFECT: as equity value falls, the firm's debt-to-equity ratio rises, making the equity riskier — so volatility is negatively correlated with returns, and the left tail is genuinely fatter. (2) CRASH RISK: equity markets fall suddenly and rise gradually, so the return distribution is negatively skewed, not merely fat-tailed. (3) FLOW: institutions are structurally long equities and buy puts as insurance, while call overwriting supplies upside — a persistent demand imbalance at low strikes. Historically the skew was near-flat before 1987 and has been pronounced ever since, which tells you how much of it is learned rather than structural. FX SMILE. For a currency pair there is no privileged direction — a large move up is a crisis for one currency and a large move down for the other — so demand for protection is roughly symmetric and the smile is too. What FX has instead of skew is a symmetric excess over the at-the-money vol, reflecting fat tails in both directions. Where FX DOES skew is when the two currencies are asymmetric in character, such as an emerging-market currency against the dollar, where devaluation risk is one-sided. A THIRD CASE worth adding: single stocks have FLATTER skew than the index. The extra index skew comes from correlation risk — in a crash correlations rise toward 1, so index volatility rises more than the constituents' do, and that correlation exposure is priced into index puts specifically. Trading that gap is the dispersion trade.
questions.technique: Reading skew shape from the underlying's economics
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the equity causes are standard; the FX contrast and the index-vs-single-stock point add depth.

questions.prompt: Spot falls 5%. Under 'sticky delta', what happens to the implied vol of the option struck at the original at-the-money level?
options: It rises, because that strike is now out-of-the-money on the downside and the smile has slid with spot
It stays the same, by definition of sticky delta
It falls, because the whole surface shifts down
It is unchanged for calls but rises for puts
questions.explanation: Under sticky DELTA the smile is a function of moneyness, so the whole curve slides sideways with spot. The original at-the-money strike is now 5% above spot in relative terms — wait, spot FELL, so a strike at the old spot is now ABOVE spot, i.e. out-of-the-money for a call and in-the-money for a put. Since the equity skew is downward-sloping in strike, moving the reference point down means the fixed strike now sits at a HIGHER moneyness where implied vol is LOWER... The cleaner way to see it: under sticky delta, the vol at a fixed MONEYNESS is constant, so the vol at a fixed STRIKE changes as that strike's moneyness changes. This is why the distinction matters for hedging: under sticky delta your effective delta differs from the Black-Scholes delta, because a spot move mechanically changes the vol you are marked at, and you are long or short vega at that strike. Under sticky STRIKE the vol attached to each strike stays put and Black-Scholes delta is correct. Empirically equity markets look closer to sticky-strike in quiet periods and sticky-delta in trending ones, and choosing wrong produces a systematic, persistent hedging error rather than random noise.
questions.technique: How the surface's dynamics change the effective delta
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: the mechanics are easy to get backwards, and the hedging consequence is the real content.

questions.prompt: What no-arbitrage constraints must a volatility surface satisfy, and why can't you just spline-interpolate?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Butterfly: the second derivative of call price with respect to strike must be non-negative, since it IS the risk-neutral density. Calendar: total variance sigma^2*T must be non-decreasing in maturity for fixed moneyness. A naive interpolation can produce a smooth surface that violates both.
questions.explanation: BUTTERFLY (strike direction). Breeden and Litzenberger showed that d2C/dK2 equals the risk-neutral probability density at K, discounted. Densities cannot be negative, so d2C/dK2 >= 0 for all strikes. Violate it and there is a literal arbitrage: a butterfly spread (long one call at K-h, short two at K, long one at K+h) would have negative cost and a non-negative payoff. Equivalently, call prices must be convex and decreasing in strike. CALENDAR (maturity direction). For a fixed moneyness, total implied variance sigma^2*T must be non-decreasing in T. Otherwise a calendar spread — long the longer option, short the shorter — has negative cost with non-negative value, since more time cannot make an option less valuable in variance terms. WHY SPLINES FAIL. A cubic spline through observed vol quotes is smooth in VOL, but the constraints bind on the implied DENSITY, which involves second derivatives of PRICE with respect to strike. Small wiggles in the vol interpolation, entirely invisible to the eye, can produce a negative density in the wings — and if you then price an exotic or run a Monte Carlo off that surface, you get nonsense with no obvious symptom. Extrapolating beyond the quoted strikes is worse still, since the wings are exactly where the density is most fragile. THE FIX is to use a parameterisation that enforces the constraints by construction. Gatheral's SVI is the standard for the strike slice, with SSVI extending it across maturities; alternatively fit a model (local vol, stochastic vol) that is arbitrage-free by construction and read the surface off it. The general lesson is that smoothness in the quoted coordinate is not the same as validity in the priced object.
questions.technique: Static arbitrage constraints on the surface
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: the density interpretation is the key, and the spline failure mode is a real production issue.

questions.prompt: Implied volatility exceeds subsequently realised volatility on average. What is that called and why does it persist?
options: The variance risk premium — buyers pay up for protection and sellers demand compensation for a negatively skewed payoff
The volatility smile, caused by fat tails
A market inefficiency that arbitrageurs have failed to eliminate
Measurement error in realised volatility
questions.explanation: The variance risk premium. It persists because it is COMPENSATION, not a mispricing: option buyers are hedging, and are willing to pay more than the actuarially fair price for protection that pays off precisely when the rest of their portfolio is losing. Sellers, correspondingly, require a premium for taking a payoff with severe negative skew — small steady gains punctuated by large losses, exactly when their own funding is tightest. The consequence for forecasting is a useful nuance: implied vol is the best available predictor of the DIRECTION and TIMING of volatility changes, while being systematically biased HIGH in level. So use it as a forecast after correcting the bias, not raw. Selling the premium (short straddles, short variance swaps) is a real and persistent strategy — and also the canonical picking-up-nickels-in-front-of-a-steamroller payoff, with the 2018 'Volmageddon' unwind of short-VIX products as the standard cautionary tale.
questions.technique: The variance risk premium as compensation
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: naming it is easy; explaining why it survives arbitrage is the substance.

questions.prompt: What does VIX actually measure, and how is it constructed?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The 30-day risk-neutral expected VARIANCE of the S&P 500, quoted as an annualised volatility. It is computed model-free from a strip of out-of-the-money option prices weighted by 1/K^2 — it is the fair strike of a 30-day variance swap, not a Black–Scholes implied vol.
questions.explanation: WHAT IT IS. VIX is the square root of the 30-day risk-neutral expected variance of the S&P 500, annualised and quoted in percentage points. Crucially it is MODEL-FREE: it does not invert Black-Scholes on any single option. THE CONSTRUCTION. Take a strip of out-of-the-money puts below the forward and out-of-the-money calls above it, across all listed strikes for the two maturities bracketing 30 days, and weight each option's price by 1/K^2. That weighting is not arbitrary — it is exactly the replication of a log contract, and hence of a variance swap, which is the result that makes the whole thing work. Interpolate between the two maturities to a constant 30 days. WHY 1/K^2. A variance swap's payoff can be statically replicated by a portfolio of options weighted 1/K^2 plus a dynamic futures position. So the strip's cost IS the fair strike of a variance swap, and that is what VIX quotes. THINGS WORTH KNOWING. VIX is a risk-neutral expectation, so it includes the variance risk premium and runs above subsequent realised vol on average — it is not a forecast. It is often called the 'fear gauge', which is loose but captures that it rises sharply in selloffs, partly because realised vol rises and partly because demand for puts spikes. And because the deep out-of-the-money puts carry meaningful weight, VIX is sensitive to the SKEW, not just at-the-money vol — an index can be quiet while VIX rises if crash protection is bid. You cannot trade VIX directly; you trade VIX futures and options, and the persistent contango in that curve is why long-VIX ETPs bleed.
questions.technique: VIX as a model-free variance swap rate
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: 'implied vol of the S&P' is the common wrong answer; the variance-swap construction is right.

questions.prompt: You want a clean bet on realised volatility with no dependence on where the underlying moves. What do you trade?
options: A variance swap
A delta-hedged straddle
An at-the-money call
A risk reversal
questions.explanation: A variance swap. It pays realised variance minus a fixed strike, with no path dependence beyond the realised variance itself — exactly the exposure you asked for. A delta-hedged straddle is the natural first thought and is a much worse instrument for the purpose: its P&L is weighted by DOLLAR GAMMA, so the same realised volatility produces different P&L depending on where the moves occurred relative to the strike. Move a long way from the strike and gamma collapses, so you stop earning from movement even though volatility is high. The variance swap fixes this precisely because it is replicated by a strip of options across ALL strikes weighted 1/K^2, so there is gamma everywhere and the weighting is uniform in variance terms. Practical caveats worth adding: variance swaps pay VARIANCE not volatility, so the payoff is convex in vol and a large spike pays disproportionately — which is why most are capped, usually at 2.5x the strike, after 2008. Volatility swaps pay vol directly but have no clean static replication.
questions.technique: Why a variance swap beats a hedged straddle as a vol trade
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the dollar-gamma weighting is the reason, and it is easy to miss.

questions.prompt: What are vanna and volga, and why does an FX options desk care about them more than an equity desk might?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Vanna is d(delta)/d(vol) — equivalently d(vega)/d(spot). Volga is d(vega)/d(vol). They describe how a book responds to the SURFACE moving rather than to spot alone, and FX desks care because the smile is quoted and traded directly as risk reversal (vanna) and butterfly (volga).
questions.explanation: DEFINITIONS. Vanna is the cross-derivative d2V/(dS d(sigma)), readable two ways: how your delta changes when vol moves, or how your vega changes when spot moves. Volga (vol gamma) is d2V/d(sigma)^2, the convexity of value in volatility. Both vanish for an at-the-money option and are largest in the wings, which is the first clue as to who cares. WHY THEY MATTER. First-order Greeks assume the other variables hold still. In reality spot and vol move together — the equity skew exists precisely because they are negatively correlated — so a book that is delta- and vega-neutral can still lose when spot and vol move jointly. Vanna captures exactly that co-movement, and volga captures the fact that vega itself changes as vol moves, which matters when you are short options in the wings. WHY FX ESPECIALLY. The FX options market quotes the smile directly in three instruments per maturity: at-the-money vol, the 25-delta RISK REVERSAL (the call vol minus put vol, which is a vanna exposure), and the 25-delta BUTTERFLY (the wings relative to the middle, which is a volga exposure). So an FX desk's risk is naturally expressed in vanna and volga because those ARE the traded instruments — the 'Vanna-Volga' pricing method for exotics is built directly on this. Equity desks think in skew and term structure instead, and often manage the same risks through scenario matrices rather than named second-order Greeks. The underlying exposure is identical; the vocabulary follows the market convention.
questions.technique: Second-order cross-Greeks and market quoting conventions
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: the definitions are recall, and connecting them to FX's risk-reversal/butterfly quoting is the depth.

questions.prompt: The implied vol term structure is normally upward-sloping but inverts in a crisis. Why?
options: Short-dated vol reacts most to a shock while long-dated vol is anchored by mean reversion
Long-dated options become illiquid and stop trading
Interest rates fall in a crisis, lowering long-dated vol
It does not invert; the term structure is always upward-sloping
questions.explanation: Because volatility mean-reverts. A shock raises the expected volatility over the next few weeks enormously, but expected volatility over the next two years far less — the market expects conditions to normalise. Since implied vol at maturity T reflects the average expected variance over that horizon, the short end spikes and the long end barely moves, inverting the curve. In calm periods the reverse holds: current vol is below its long-run level, so the curve slopes upward as the market prices reversion back toward normal. This is exactly the GARCH forecast structure — E[variance at n+k] = V_L + (alpha+beta)^k*(current - V_L) — expressed in traded prices, and it is why fitting GARCH gives you a term structure that can be compared against the implied one for relative value. Practical consequence: after a spike, a short-dated long-vol position is expensive and decays fast, so the trade is usually expressed further out the curve or as a calendar spread.
questions.technique: Mean reversion in the volatility term structure
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the mechanism is the answer, and the GARCH link makes it concrete.

questions.prompt: Artzner et al. proposed four properties a risk measure should have to be 'coherent'. Name them, and say which one VaR fails.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Monotonicity, translation invariance, homogeneity, and subadditivity. VaR satisfies the first three but fails SUBADDITIVITY.
questions.explanation: THE FOUR AXIOMS. (1) MONOTONICITY: if portfolio A does worse than B in every state of the world, A's risk measure must be greater. (2) TRANSLATION INVARIANCE: adding cash K to a portfolio reduces its risk measure by exactly K — cash is riskless and directly offsets required capital. (3) HOMOGENEITY: scaling a portfolio by lambda while keeping its composition fixed scales the risk measure by lambda. Note this deliberately ignores liquidity: doubling every position really does more than double your risk if you cannot exit, which is a recognised limitation of the axiom rather than of VaR. (4) SUBADDITIVITY: merging two portfolios cannot increase total measured risk, risk(A+B) <= risk(A) + risk(B). WHICH VaR FAILS. Only subadditivity. VaR is monotonic, translation-invariant and homogeneous, so it fails exactly one axiom — but it is the one that matters most for a capital measure, because it means merging portfolios can INCREASE measured risk, so diversification can be penalised and desk-level limits can all be met while the aggregate breaches. Expected Shortfall satisfies all four and is therefore coherent. THE FRAMING WORTH ADDING: the axioms were derived by asking what properties a measure must have if it is to equal the capital an institution should hold. Under that reading, translation invariance says capital and cash are interchangeable, and subadditivity says a merged firm should never need more capital than its parts — which is why the failure is a governance problem, not just a mathematical curiosity.
questions.technique: The coherence axioms and VaR's single failure
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: naming all four is the recall test; identifying exactly one failure is the precision test.

questions.prompt: The loss on a portfolio over 10 days is normal with mean zero and standard deviation $20m. Compute the 10-day 99% VaR and the 10-day 97.5% Expected Shortfall.
questions.explanation: VaR. Under normality with mean mu and standard deviation sigma, VaR = mu + sigma*N^-1(X). With mu = 0 and X = 0.99: 20 * 2.326 = $46.5m. ES. The closed form is ES = mu + sigma * exp(-Y^2/2)/(sqrt(2*pi)*(1-X)) where Y = N^-1(X). At X = 0.975, Y = 1.960, so Y^2/2 = 1.921 and exp(-1.921) = 0.1464. Divide by sqrt(2*pi) = 2.5066 to get 0.0584, then by (1-X) = 0.025 to get 2.336. Times sigma = 20 gives $46.7m. THE POINT OF DOING BOTH. The two numbers are almost identical — $46.5m against $46.7m — and that is not a coincidence. It is why FRTB chose 97.5% for ES: under normality, 97.5% ES matches 99% VaR very closely, so the switch changed the measure's PROPERTIES (coherent, tail-sensitive) without a discontinuous jump in capital. The corollary is the important one: for a FAT-TAILED distribution the two diverge, with 97.5% ES exceeding 99% VaR — which is exactly the intended bite, since books with genuine tail risk now attract more capital while near-normal books see little change. Also note the ES formula's numerator is just the normal density at Y, so ES = mu + sigma*phi(Y)/(1-X), which is easier to remember.
questions.technique: Closed forms for VaR and ES under normality
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: two formula applications, and the near-equality is the insight.

questions.prompt: Basel's original market risk framework used a 10-day horizon at 99% confidence. Why 10 days rather than 1?
options: It approximates the time needed to unwind or hedge a troubled position
Because 10 days is two trading weeks, which matches reporting cycles
To make the sqrt-of-time scaling exact
Because daily data is too noisy to use
questions.explanation: The horizon should reflect how long you would be exposed before you could act — the time to liquidate or hedge a position in an orderly way. Ten days was the regulators' judgement of a plausible unwind period for a trading book. The CONFIDENCE level is chosen for a different reason: it reflects how conservative the capital requirement should be, i.e. how rarely you are prepared to be wrong. In practice banks compute a ONE-day VaR from daily data (there are far more independent daily observations, so the estimate is far better) and then scale by sqrt(10), which is where the accuracy problem enters rather than being solved. Note that FRTB abandoned the blanket 10 days precisely because the liquidation assumption was shown to be wrong for illiquid positions, replacing it with risk-factor-specific liquidity horizons of 10 to 120 days. That progression — a single assumed horizon, then evidence it was wrong, then differentiated horizons — is the useful thing to be able to narrate.
questions.technique: The economic meaning of the VaR horizon
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the liquidation rationale is the answer, and the FRTB follow-on shows depth.

questions.prompt: Daily P&L has first-order autocorrelation of 0.1. By what factor should you scale a one-day VaR to get a 10-day VaR, and how does that compare with the sqrt(t) rule?
questions.canonicalAnswer: About 3.46, against sqrt(10) = 3.16 — roughly 10% higher. The variance of the T-day sum is sigma^2*[T + 2(T-1)rho + 2(T-2)rho^2 + ... + 2*rho^(T-1)], so positive autocorrelation makes the true multiple exceed sqrt(T).
questions.explanation: THE FORMULA. If daily changes each have variance sigma^2 and the correlation between changes j days apart is rho^j, then the standard deviation of the T-day sum is sigma*sqrt(T + 2(T-1)rho + 2(T-2)rho^2 + 2(T-3)rho^3 + ... + 2rho^(T-1)). Every cross-covariance term contributes, weighted by how many pairs are separated by that lag. With rho = 0 all cross terms vanish and you recover sigma*sqrt(T) — the familiar rule is the special case of zero autocorrelation. NUMBERS. Hull tabulates the multiples: at T = 10, the factor is 3.16 for rho = 0, 3.31 for rho = 0.05, 3.46 for rho = 0.1, and 3.79 for rho = 0.2. So a 0.1 autocorrelation understates 10-day VaR by about 10% if you use sqrt(10), and at rho = 0.2 the error is 20%. Over T = 250 the gap widens further, from 15.81 to 19.35. WHY IT MATTERS AND WHICH DIRECTION. Positive autocorrelation means trends persist, so losses compound rather than partially offsetting — the true multi-day risk is HIGHER than sqrt(t) implies. That is the dangerous direction to be wrong in, and it is the empirically relevant one: illiquid assets, credit and hedge fund returns commonly show positive autocorrelation, sometimes substantially, partly from genuine momentum and partly from stale marking. Note the multiple does not depend on sigma or on the confidence level — it is a pure scaling property — which is why a single table of factors suffices. A useful sanity habit: if someone quotes a 10-day VaR scaled from daily, ask what autocorrelation they assumed, because the default assumption is zero and it is rarely true.
questions.technique: Autocorrelation-adjusted multi-period scaling
questions.difficultyRationale: Hard: the general variance formula is not widely known and the direction of the error is what matters.

questions.prompt: Two business units have one-day 99% VaRs of $30m and $40m. What is the firm-wide VaR, and what assumption are you making?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Under the assumption that both loss distributions are normal with zero mean and correlation rho, the combined VaR is sqrt(30^2 + 40^2 + 2*rho*30*40). At rho = 0 that is $50m; at rho = 1 it is $70m; at rho = 0.5 it is about $60.8m.
questions.explanation: THE FORMULA. If each unit's loss is normal with mean zero, VaR is proportional to the standard deviation, so VaRs aggregate exactly like standard deviations: VaR_total = sqrt(VaR_1^2 + VaR_2^2 + 2*rho*VaR_1*VaR_2). At rho = 0: sqrt(900 + 1600) = $50m. At rho = 1: sqrt(900+1600+2400) = $70m, the simple sum. At rho = 0.5: sqrt(2500 + 1200) = $60.8m. THE ASSUMPTIONS, which are the substance of the answer. (1) NORMALITY with zero mean — this is what makes VaR proportional to sigma and therefore additive in quadrature. For fat-tailed or skewed distributions the relationship fails and the formula has no justification. (2) A SINGLE correlation summarising the dependence, which ignores tail dependence entirely: two units can have modest correlation in normal markets and lose together in a crisis. (3) That the units' positions are static and there is no netting benefit or offsetting exposure being missed. WHAT THIS BUYS YOU. The gap between $50m and $70m is the DIVERSIFICATION BENEFIT, and allocating it back to the units is a genuine governance problem — Euler allocation via component VaR is the principled answer, since the components sum exactly to the total. WHAT TO WATCH: aggregating this way credits diversification that may not survive stress, so regulators generally require a conservative correlation or simple summation across risk TYPES (market, credit, operational), where the dependence is least well understood.
questions.technique: Aggregating VaR across units, and the assumptions it rests on
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the formula is easy; the assumption list and the allocation problem are the content.

questions.prompt: Why is Expected Shortfall harder to backtest than VaR?
options: ES is a conditional expectation over rare events, so you need the SIZE of tail losses, not just a count of exceptions
ES cannot be computed from historical data
ES has no closed form
Because ES is not a coherent risk measure
questions.explanation: Backtesting VaR is simple because VaR makes a frequency claim: losses should exceed it X% of the time, so you count exceptions and compare with a binomial. ES makes a claim about the AVERAGE SIZE of losses beyond the threshold, so testing it needs the magnitudes of the exceedances — and by construction there are very few of them. At 97.5% over 250 days you expect about 6 exceedances, and estimating a conditional mean from 6 observations has enormous standard error. That difficulty was the principal argument AGAINST moving to ES, and it is why FRTB still backtests VaR at the desk level while capitalising on ES: you use the easily-testable measure for model validation and the better-behaved measure for capital. Practical approaches to ES backtesting do exist — Acerbi-Szekely tests, or testing the whole predicted distribution rather than just the tail — but none has VaR's simplicity. Note ES IS coherent; that is the reason for adopting it, not an obstacle.
questions.technique: Why testing a conditional expectation is harder than counting exceptions
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the count-versus-magnitude distinction is the answer.

questions.prompt: Your desk's VaR limit is $10m and you are at $9.8m. A trader proposes a new position with a standalone VaR of $3m. Can you take it?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Possibly — it depends on the position's INCREMENTAL VaR, not its standalone VaR. If it is negatively correlated with the existing book its incremental VaR can be small or even negative, reducing total VaR.
questions.explanation: THE ERROR to avoid is adding standalone VaRs. VaR is not additive: what matters is the position's contribution to the PORTFOLIO's VaR, which depends on its covariance with what you already hold. THE RIGHT CALCULATION is INCREMENTAL VaR — recompute portfolio VaR with the position included and take the difference. A $3m standalone position that hedges existing exposure might raise total VaR by $0.5m, or lower it. Conversely, a $3m position highly correlated with the book could add nearly the full $3m and breach the limit. The relevant quantity under the variance-covariance approach is the position's covariance with the portfolio, which is what marginal VaR measures. PRACTICAL POINTS. (1) Use INCREMENTAL for a discrete decision like this (the position is large relative to the book) and MARGINAL for small adjustments — marginal VaR times position size is only a first-order approximation and understates the effect for a large addition. (2) Watch the perverse incentive: because incremental VaR can be negative, a limit framework based purely on VaR can encourage taking large offsetting positions that look risk-reducing but increase gross exposure, liquidity risk and operational complexity. That is why desks carry gross notional and stressed-loss limits alongside VaR. (3) Check the position under the STRESS scenarios too — a hedge that works under estimated correlations may fail when correlations converge, and the whole benefit you just credited disappears.
questions.technique: Incremental versus standalone VaR for a limit decision
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the non-additivity is the core, and the perverse-incentive point is the depth.

questions.prompt: A risk measure satisfies translation invariance. What does that mean?
options: Adding K of cash to the portfolio reduces the risk measure by exactly K
The measure is unchanged if all positions are scaled
The measure does not depend on the currency of reporting
The measure is unchanged by a shift in the mean return
questions.explanation: Translation invariance says risk(portfolio + K cash) = risk(portfolio) - K. Cash is riskless, so it directly offsets the capital you need to hold. Read as a capital requirement the axiom is almost a definition: if the measure is meant to say how much capital you need, then holding K more cash must reduce that requirement by exactly K, no more and no less. Both VaR and ES satisfy it. The second option describes HOMOGENEITY, which is a different axiom (and also satisfied by both). The axiom that VaR fails is subadditivity — merging portfolios can raise measured risk — and that is the single reason VaR is not coherent.
questions.technique: Translation invariance read as a capital statement
questions.difficultyRationale: Easy: definitional, and the capital reading makes it memorable.

questions.prompt: What is economic capital, and how does it differ from regulatory capital?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Economic capital is the firm's OWN estimate of the capital needed to absorb losses at a chosen confidence level over a chosen horizon, aggregated across all risk types. Regulatory capital is what the rules require. They differ in confidence level, in aggregation method, and in which risks are counted.
questions.explanation: ECONOMIC CAPITAL is an internal number: pick a horizon (usually one year) and a confidence level, estimate the loss distribution for each risk type, aggregate, and the resulting quantile is the capital you believe you need. The confidence level is typically chosen to match a TARGET CREDIT RATING — a firm wanting a AA rating, whose historical one-year default rate is around 0.03%, would use 99.97% confidence. That link is the elegant part and worth stating: economic capital translates 'what rating do we want' into a number. HOW IT DIFFERS FROM REGULATORY CAPITAL. (1) CONFIDENCE and horizon are chosen by the firm rather than the rules, and are usually far more stringent than the market-risk 99%/10-day standard. (2) AGGREGATION: internally you can credit diversification across market, credit and operational risk; regulators typically require simple addition across risk types because the cross-dependence is poorly understood and conservatism is preferred. So economic capital is often LOWER than regulatory in total even while being more stringent per risk type. (3) SCOPE: economic capital covers risks the rules may not capture well — business risk, strategic risk, reputational risk. (4) The loss distributions have very different SHAPES by risk type: market risk is roughly symmetric, credit risk is heavily right-skewed, operational risk is extremely fat-tailed with rare enormous losses. That shape difference is why aggregating them by a single correlation is dubious. WHAT IT IS FOR: allocating capital between businesses and computing RAROC — return divided by economic capital — so that a business's profit is judged against the risk it consumes rather than its notional size. That is the mechanism by which risk measurement actually affects decisions.
questions.technique: Economic capital, the rating link, and RAROC
questions.difficultyRationale: Medium: the target-rating link and the aggregation contrast are what make it more than a definition.

questions.prompt: Under a normal assumption, the ratio of T-day VaR to one-day VaR does not depend on which two quantities?
options: The daily standard deviation and the confidence level
The horizon and the autocorrelation
The mean and the standard deviation
The portfolio composition and the confidence level
questions.explanation: Neither sigma nor the confidence level enters the scaling ratio. Under normality with zero mean, VaR = sigma*N^-1(X), so the T-day VaR is sigma_T * N^-1(X) and the ratio to the one-day figure is sigma_T/sigma_1 — the N^-1(X) factor cancels, and so does sigma_1. The ratio depends only on T and on the autocorrelation structure. That is why a single table of scaling factors serves for every portfolio and every confidence level, which is a genuinely convenient property and the reason the sqrt(t) rule is quoted so freely.
