questions.prompt: A $50m position trades with a bid-ask spread of 10 basis points. Under the standard cost-of-liquidation measure, what does it cost to unwind?
questions.canonicalAnswer: $25,000 — half the spread on the full notional: 0.5 * 0.0010 * 50,000,000.
questions.explanation: Mid-price is the fair mark, so selling at the bid costs you half the spread. The standard formula is cost = 0.5 * s * V, giving 0.0005 * 50m = $25,000. Two caveats that matter more than the arithmetic. This assumes you can hit the quoted spread for the whole size, which is exactly what fails when the position is large relative to normal volume — real unwind cost includes market impact on top. And spreads widen in stress, so the right input for a liquidity-adjusted VaR is a stressed spread, often the 99th percentile of the observed spread distribution rather than today's.
questions.technique: Cost-of-liquidation from the bid-ask spread
questions.difficultyRationale: One multiplication, with the halving as the only trap.

questions.prompt: A standard deck is shuffled. What is the probability the BOTTOM card is an ace?
questions.canonicalAnswer: 1/13 — the same as for any other position.
questions.explanation: There are 4 aces in 52 cards, so 4/52 = 1/13. No conditioning, no working through the other 51 cards. The reason is symmetry: a shuffle makes all 52! orderings equally likely, so every position is exchangeable with every other, and the bottom card is as likely to be an ace as the top one. Recognising exchangeability is what turns a page of casework into a single line, and it is the whole point of this topic.
questions.technique: Exchangeability of positions after a shuffle
questions.difficultyRationale: One symmetry observation; the arithmetic is 4/52.

questions.prompt: An urn holds 10 balls, 3 of them red. Balls are drawn one at a time without replacement. What is the probability the THIRD ball drawn is red?
questions.explanation: Same as the first. You could condition on how many reds appeared in the first two draws and sum three cases, and you would get 3/10 after some work — but the symmetry argument gets there immediately. Since the balls are drawn in a uniformly random order, each of the 10 balls is equally likely to occupy position 3, and 3 of them are red. The habit to build: when a question asks about the k-th draw without replacement, check whether position even matters before computing anything.
questions.technique: Symmetry over draw order
questions.difficultyRationale: Direct application of the shortcut the topic is named for.

questions.prompt: How many rolls of a fair six-sided die do you expect to need before you have seen all six faces?
questions.explanation: Break the wait into stages. Once you hold k distinct faces, the chance the next roll is new is (6-k)/6, so the expected wait for the next new face is 6/(6-k) — a geometric. Summing over k = 0..5 gives 6/6 + 6/5 + 6/4 + 6/3 + 6/2 + 6/1 = 6 * H_6. The general answer is n * H_n ~= n ln n. Note the shape: the first five faces take about 8.7 rolls between them and the LAST one alone takes 6, which is the whole intuition for why collecting the final coupon dominates.
questions.technique: Sum of geometric waiting times
questions.difficultyRationale: One standard decomposition and a six-term harmonic sum.

questions.prompt: For a coupon collector problem with n equally likely coupon types, the expected number of draws to collect them all grows like:
options: n log n
n
questions.explanation: The exact answer is n * H_n where H_n is the n-th harmonic number, and H_n ~= ln n + 0.577, so the growth is n log n. The intuition for the extra log factor is that the final few coupons are individually very slow — the last one alone takes n draws in expectation. For n = 100 that is about 519 draws, comfortably more than the 100 a linear guess would suggest but nowhere near quadratic.
questions.technique: Asymptotic growth of the collector time
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of one asymptotic result.

questions.prompt: What does a === b (mod n) mean, and what is 17 mod 5?
questions.canonicalAnswer: a === b (mod n) means n divides a - b, equivalently a and b leave the same remainder on division by n. 17 mod 5 = 2.
questions.explanation: Congruence partitions the integers into n residue classes, and the useful fact is that addition and multiplication respect the classes: you may reduce mod n at any point in a calculation without changing the final answer. That is what keeps numbers small — to find 17 * 23 mod 5 you can reduce first to 2 * 3 = 6 === 1, rather than multiplying out to 391. Division is the operation that does NOT carry over cleanly, which is why modular inverses need separate treatment.
questions.technique: Definition of congruence
questions.difficultyRationale: Definition plus one remainder.

questions.prompt: X is uniform on [0, 10]. What are E[X] and P(X > 7)?
questions.explanation: For a uniform on [a,b], the mean is the midpoint (a+b)/2 = 5, and probabilities are proportional to length: the interval (7,10] has length 3 out of 10, so 0.3. Also worth carrying: Var = (b-a)^2/12 = 100/12 = 8.33, so the standard deviation is about 2.89. Note that P(X > 7) and P(X >= 7) are identical here — for any continuous distribution a single point has probability zero, which is not true for discrete ones.
questions.technique: Uniform distribution facts
questions.difficultyRationale: Two direct reads from the definition.

questions.prompt: For a normal distribution, roughly what fraction of the probability lies within one standard deviation of the mean?
questions.explanation: The 68-95-99.7 rule: about 68% within one standard deviation, 95% within two, 99.7% within three. The numbers worth memorising alongside it are the two-tailed quantiles used in risk work — 1.96 for 95% and 2.576 for 99% — and their one-tailed counterparts, 1.645 and 2.326, which are the ones VaR actually uses. Confusing the one- and two-tailed values is a common and expensive slip.
questions.technique: Normal distribution rules of thumb
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of a standard rule.

questions.prompt: How many ways can a committee of 3 be chosen from 10 people?
questions.explanation: Order does not matter on a committee, so this is a combination. Compute it as the falling product 10*9*8 divided by 3! to remove the double-counting of the 6 orderings of each committee. If order DID matter — say the three roles were chair, secretary and treasurer — you would stop at 720, the permutation count P(10,3). Deciding whether order matters before you pick a formula is the entire skill.
questions.technique: Combinations vs permutations
questions.difficultyRationale: One binomial coefficient computed directly.

questions.prompt: How many distinct 3-letter arrangements can be made from the 5 letters A, B, C, D, E, using each at most once?
questions.canonicalAnswer: 60. There are 5 choices for the first letter, 4 for the second, 3 for the third: 5*4*3 = 60.
questions.explanation: Order matters here, so this is a permutation: P(5,3) = 5!/(5-3)! = 120/2 = 60. Compare with the committee version, C(5,3) = 10 — exactly 60/3! , since each set of three letters can be arranged in 3! = 6 ways. That factor of 3! IS the difference between the two formulas, and seeing it explicitly once is more useful than memorising both.
questions.technique: Permutations via the multiplication principle
questions.difficultyRationale: Three factors multiplied.

questions.prompt: You are flipping a fair coin until you get heads. You have flipped 5 tails in a row. How many MORE flips do you expect to need?
questions.canonicalAnswer: 2 — exactly the same as at the start.
questions.explanation: The geometric distribution is memoryless: P(X > m + n | X > m) = P(X > n). The coin has no record of the five tails, so your expected remaining wait is unchanged at 1/p = 2. This is the formal refutation of the gambler's fallacy, and it is worth stating clearly because the intuition that a head is 'due' is very persistent. Among discrete distributions the geometric is the ONLY memoryless one (the exponential is its continuous counterpart).
questions.technique: Memorylessness
questions.difficultyRationale: One property applied; the answer is the unconditional mean.

questions.prompt: Roughly how many comparisons does binary search need to find an item in a sorted list of one million entries?
questions.canonicalAnswer: About 20, since log2(1,000,000) is about 20.
questions.explanation: Each comparison halves the remaining range, so the count is log2(n). The number to anchor on is 2^10 = 1024 ~= 10^3, so a thousand items takes about 10 steps and a million takes about 20. That anchor also handles a billion (30) instantly. The contrast with linear search — 500,000 comparisons on average — is the reason logarithmic complexity is worth caring about, and the same halving logic underlies bisection root-finding in numerical work.
questions.technique: Logarithmic complexity, anchored on 2^10 ~= 10^3
questions.difficultyRationale: One log evaluated from a memorised anchor.

questions.prompt: List the five inputs to the Black-Scholes formula for a European call, and say which one is not directly observable.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Spot price S, strike K, time to expiry T, risk-free rate r, and volatility sigma. Volatility is the only one not directly observable.
questions.explanation: Four of the five are contractual or quoted; sigma is the future volatility of the underlying over the option's life, which nobody can observe. That asymmetry is the reason the market works backwards — take the traded price, invert the formula, and quote the sigma that reproduces it. That is implied volatility, and it is why options are quoted in vol terms rather than in currency. (Dividend yield q is a sixth input for dividend-paying underlyings, entering as a downward adjustment to the drift on S.)
questions.technique: Black-Scholes inputs
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of five inputs plus one observation about which is special.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped four times. What is the probability that all four flips give the same result?
questions.canonicalAnswer: 1/8. Two favourable sequences (HHHH, TTTT) out of 2^4 = 16.
questions.explanation: The sample space has 2^4 = 16 equally likely sequences and exactly two of them are constant, so 2/16 = 1/8. An alternative that scales better: the first flip can be anything, and each of the remaining three must match it, giving (1/2)^3 = 1/8 with no enumeration at all. Fixing an arbitrary first outcome and only counting the constrained rest is a habit worth building — it turns exponential enumeration into a short product.
questions.technique: Enumerate sequences, or fix the first outcome and constrain the rest
questions.difficultyRationale: Sixteen outcomes with two favourable; the shortcut is one product.

questions.prompt: Three people each independently pick a day of the week at random. What is the probability they all pick different days?
questions.explanation: Total outcomes 7^3 = 343. For all-different, the first person has 7 choices, the second must avoid one day so has 6, the third must avoid two so has 5: 210. Hence 210/343 = 30/49 ~= 0.61. Written the other way, the probability is 1 * (6/7) * (5/7), which is the same calculation with the denominators distributed — and that form is the one that generalises straight into the birthday problem.
questions.technique: Sequential counting with shrinking choices
questions.difficultyRationale: Three factors over a three-factor total.

questions.prompt: A factory has two machines. Machine A makes 70% of output with a 1% defect rate; machine B makes 30% with a 4% defect rate. A defective item is found. What is the probability it came from machine B?
questions.explanation: Numerator is the joint probability of the hypothesis and the evidence; denominator is the total probability of the evidence across all hypotheses. Thinking in counts is often faster: out of 10,000 items, machine A makes 7,000 with 70 defects and machine B makes 3,000 with 120 defects, so 120 of the 190 defects are B's — 63%. Note the flip: B makes a MINORITY of the output but a MAJORITY of the defects, because a four-times-higher defect rate more than offsets a smaller share.
questions.technique: Bayes with two sources, via joint counts
questions.difficultyRationale: Two products, one sum, one division.

questions.prompt: What is the odds form of Bayes' theorem, and why is it convenient?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Posterior odds = prior odds x likelihood ratio. It is convenient because the denominator P(evidence) cancels, so you never have to compute it.
questions.explanation: Divide Bayes' theorem for hypothesis H by the same expression for not-H: the P(evidence) terms cancel, leaving P(H|E)/P(notH|E) = [P(H)/P(notH)] x [P(E|H)/P(E|notH)]. Evidence enters only through the likelihood ratio, so updates just multiply — and independent pieces of evidence multiply their ratios together. Worked example: prior odds 1:1, evidence three times more likely under H, so posterior odds 3:1, i.e. probability 3/4. Converting back is odds/(1+odds).
questions.technique: Odds form / likelihood ratio
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of a rearrangement plus one two-step example.

questions.prompt: You start with $20 and bet $1 at a time on a fair coin, stopping when you reach $50 or $0. What is the probability you reach $50?
questions.canonicalAnswer: 2/5. In the fair case the probability of hitting N before 0 from k is k/N = 20/50.
questions.explanation: For a fair game the answer is simply the fraction of the way you already are. The quickest justification is a martingale one: your wealth has constant expectation, so 20 = 50p + 0(1-p) and p = 0.4. The point most people miss is that expected final wealth being $20 does not make the outcome benign — you go broke 60% of the time. Fair in expectation is not the same as safe.
questions.technique: Gambler's ruin, fair case (k/N)
questions.difficultyRationale: One substitution into the fair-game formula.

questions.prompt: A gambler plays a FAIR game against a casino with unlimited money, betting $1 a time and never voluntarily stopping. What happens to them eventually, and why?
questions.canonicalAnswer: They go broke with probability 1. The target N is effectively infinite, so the survival probability k/N tends to 0.
questions.explanation: Take the fair-game result P(reach N before 0) = k/N and let N grow without bound: it goes to zero for any finite starting bankroll k. The asymmetry is entirely about the barriers, not the odds — the gambler has an absorbing barrier at 0 and the casino effectively does not. A symmetric random walk is recurrent, so it visits every level eventually, including zero, and zero is the one level you cannot leave. This is the cleanest statement of why unlimited play with limited capital is fatal even with no house edge, and it generalises directly to leverage and margin calls.
questions.technique: Limiting behaviour of the ruin probability
questions.difficultyRationale: One limit of a formula, stated conceptually.

questions.prompt: London has about 8 million residents and a human head carries at most about 150,000 hairs. Show that two Londoners have exactly the same number of head hairs.
questions.canonicalAnswer: The possible hair counts are 0 to 150,000 — at most 150,001 pigeonholes — and there are 8,000,000 people. Since 8,000,000 > 150,001, some count is shared by at least two people.
questions.explanation: The pigeonholes are the possible VALUES, not the people, which is the step that takes a moment to see. Note how much slack there is: 8,000,000 / 150,001 is about 53, so the generalised pigeonhole principle actually guarantees some hair count shared by at least 53 Londoners. The argument needs no data about how hair counts are distributed — it is a proof, not an estimate.
questions.technique: Pigeonhole with values as the holes
questions.difficultyRationale: One comparison of two counts once the holes are identified.

questions.prompt: The generalised pigeonhole principle says that if n items are placed into k boxes, then some box contains at least:
options: The ceiling of n/k items
Exactly n/k items
n - k items
Two items, whenever n > 1
questions.explanation: If every box held fewer than the ceiling of n/k, the total would fall short of n. The ceiling matters: 10 items in 3 boxes guarantees some box with at least 4, not 3.33. 'Exactly n/k' is wrong because the principle bounds the MAXIMUM box from below and says nothing about any particular box — an even split is possible but not guaranteed. The basic principle is just the case k = n - 1.
questions.technique: Generalised pigeonhole
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of one bound, with rounding as the only subtlety.

questions.prompt: A $25m equity position has an annualised volatility of 16%. Assuming 250 trading days and zero mean, what is its 1-day 95% VaR?
questions.explanation: Two steps, and the first is where the errors happen. Converting annual to daily volatility divides by sqrt(250) ~= 15.8, NOT by 250 — variance scales with time, so volatility scales with its square root. That gives 1.012% a day. Then apply the 95% one-tailed normal quantile 1.645: 1.66% of $25m, about $416k. A useful sanity anchor is that 16% annual vol is almost exactly 1% a day, which makes this kind of estimate fast in an interview.
questions.technique: Annual-to-daily volatility conversion, then delta-normal VaR
questions.difficultyRationale: Two steps, each one operation, with the sqrt conversion as the trap.

questions.prompt: In a historical stress test of the 2008 crisis, why do you apply the 2008 factor MOVES to today's portfolio rather than simply looking up what the firm lost in 2008?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because the question is what TODAY'S book would lose. The 2008 P&L reflects the positions held then, which may bear no resemblance to current exposures.
questions.explanation: A stress test is a statement about the current portfolio, so the historical episode supplies only the scenario — the set of factor moves — and today's positions supply the sensitivity. This is the same revaluation logic as historical simulation VaR, just with a hand-picked episode instead of a rolling window. It also explains a common practical headache: risk factors that did not exist in 2008 have no historical move to apply, so they have to be proxied, and how you proxy them can dominate the answer.
questions.technique: Scenario applied to current positions
questions.difficultyRationale: Conceptual, one distinction, no computation.

questions.prompt: A single-factor sensitivity stress test — shock one risk factor and hold the others fixed — has which main weakness?
options: Real stress episodes move many factors together, so it misses the joint effect
It is too computationally expensive to run daily
It cannot be applied to non-linear positions
It requires a full historical dataset for every factor
questions.explanation: Single-factor shocks are cheap, easy to interpret and good for limit-setting, but they say nothing about combinations — and the losses that hurt come from equities falling while credit widens, correlations go to one and liquidity disappears, all at once. That is what multi-factor historical and hypothetical scenarios are for. The method's virtues are the opposite of the distractors: it is cheap, handles non-linearity fine because it revalues the book, and needs no history at all.
questions.technique: Single-factor vs multi-factor scenarios
questions.difficultyRationale: One weakness identified among plausible alternatives.

questions.prompt: What is the remainder when 2^10 is divided by 7? Do it without computing 1024.
questions.explanation: Find a small power that reduces to 1 and the rest collapses. Here 2^3 = 8 leaves remainder 1 mod 7, so powers of 2 cycle with period 3 and you only need the exponent mod 3: 10 = 3*3 + 1, so 2^10 behaves like 2^1, giving 2. Checking directly, 1024 = 7*146 + 2. The general strategy for any 'a^n mod m' question is the same — find the cycle length of a modulo m, then reduce the exponent by it.
questions.technique: Reduce the exponent using the cycle of powers
questions.difficultyRationale: One small power found, one exponent reduced.

questions.prompt: Two fair dice are rolled. What is the probability the first die shows a strictly higher number than the second?
questions.explanation: Split the 36 outcomes into three groups: first higher, second higher, and equal. The first two are mirror images of each other, so they have the same probability. Ties are the 6 doubles, probability 6/36 = 1/6. That leaves 1 - 1/6 = 5/6 to be shared equally, so each side gets 5/12. Enumerating the 15 favourable pairs gives the same answer with five times the work — spotting the mirror symmetry and subtracting the tie case is the technique.
questions.technique: Symmetry between mirrored events, minus the tie case
questions.difficultyRationale: One symmetry observation plus the probability of a tie.

questions.prompt: A fair coin is flipped 5 times. What is the probability of getting at least one head?
questions.explanation: 'At least one' has many favourable cases (exactly one head, exactly two, and so on) but its complement has exactly one: all tails, probability (1/2)^5 = 1/32. Subtract from 1 to get 31/32. The rule of thumb is to check the complement whenever a question says 'at least one' — the complement of 'at least one X' is always the single clean event 'no X at all', regardless of how many trials there are.
questions.technique: Complementary counting on 'at least one'
questions.difficultyRationale: One complement and one fifth power.

questions.prompt: What is close-out netting, and why does it reduce counterparty exposure?
questions.canonicalAnswer: On a counterparty's default, all trades under the master agreement are terminated and collapsed into a single net amount owed one way. Exposure becomes the net mark-to-market rather than the sum of the positive-value trades.
questions.explanation: Without netting, a defaulted counterparty's administrator could enforce the trades that are in their favour while leaving you to claim on the rest as an unsecured creditor — 'cherry-picking'. An ISDA master agreement prevents that by making every trade a single contract. Concretely, if you are up $100m on one swap and down $90m on another with the same counterparty, exposure is $10m rather than $100m. This is also why netting sets, not individual trades, are the unit for CVA and for regulatory exposure calculations — and why netting enforceability in the counterparty's jurisdiction is a legal question with a direct capital consequence.
questions.technique: Netting sets and exposure measurement
questions.difficultyRationale: One definition plus a two-trade example.

questions.prompt: Write the general risk-neutral pricing formula for a derivative paying X at time T, and say what each part does.
questions.canonicalAnswer: V_0 = e^{-rT} E^Q[X], where E^Q is the expectation under the risk-neutral measure Q and e^{-rT} discounts at the risk-free rate.
questions.explanation: Two ingredients: take the expected payoff under Q, then discount it at r. What makes it work is that the same rate r appears in both places — assets drift at r under Q, and discounting is also at r, so the discounted price process is a martingale. That martingale property IS the no-arbitrage condition, which is the content of the fundamental theorem of asset pricing. Everything else is machinery for evaluating that expectation: Black-Scholes does it in closed form for a lognormal underlying, binomial trees do it by backward induction, and Monte Carlo does it by averaging simulated payoffs.
questions.technique: Risk-neutral pricing formula
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of one formula plus what each factor is doing.

questions.prompt: Five cards are dealt from a shuffled standard deck. What is the expected number of aces among them?
questions.canonicalAnswer: 5/13, about 0.385. Each card has probability 4/52 = 1/13 of being an ace, and 5 * (1/13) = 5/13.
questions.explanation: Let X_i indicate that the i-th card dealt is an ace. By symmetry each has E[X_i] = 4/52, so the total is 5 * 4/52 = 5/13. The important part is what you did NOT need: the cards are dealt WITHOUT replacement, so the indicators are dependent — knowing card 1 is an ace lowers the chance for card 2. Linearity does not care. Trying to do this by summing k * P(exactly k aces) over k = 0..4 with hypergeometric probabilities gets the same answer after a great deal more work.
questions.technique: Indicator variables with dependent trials
questions.difficultyRationale: One product; the point is recognising dependence is irrelevant.

questions.prompt: Your risk report says "1-day 99% VaR: £5m". State precisely what that claims — and three things it does not.
questions.canonicalAnswer: It claims that on 99% of days the loss will be less than £5m, i.e. you expect to lose more than £5m about 1 day in 100. It does not say how much more you lose on those days, that £5m is the worst case, or that the losses will be spread evenly.
questions.explanation: The claim is about a frequency, not a bound. Over 250 trading days you should expect roughly 2 to 3 breaches — zero breaches is evidence the model is too conservative, not evidence of safety. What it is silent on: the SIZE of the tail beyond the quantile (that is expected shortfall's job), the possibility that breaches cluster in one bad week rather than arriving evenly, and anything about a holding period longer than a day. Being able to state the claim this tightly is what separates someone who uses the number from someone who just reports it.
questions.technique: Interpreting a VaR figure
questions.difficultyRationale: Definitional, but requires stating the negative space precisely.

questions.prompt: Two positions have standalone 1-day VaRs of £4m and £3m, with returns uncorrelated. What is the portfolio VaR?
questions.canonicalAnswer: £5m. VaR combines like standard deviations: sqrt(4^2 + 3^2) = sqrt(25) = 5.
questions.explanation: With normal returns and zero correlation the cross term drops out, leaving VaR_p = sqrt(V1^2 + V2^2). The 3-4-5 triangle makes the arithmetic instant. Note the diversification benefit: the standalone VaRs sum to £7m, so £2m of risk vanished purely from imperfect correlation. And note the shape — combining EQUAL risks at zero correlation gives sqrt(2) times one of them, not twice, which is the same sqrt(n) scaling that governs everything else in this topic.
questions.technique: Portfolio VaR at zero correlation
questions.difficultyRationale: One Pythagorean sum.

questions.prompt: Define component VaR, and explain why the components sum exactly to the portfolio VaR when marginal VaRs do not.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Component VaR for position i is its marginal VaR multiplied by its position size: C_i = (dVaR/dx_i) * x_i. They sum to total VaR because VaR is homogeneous of degree one in position sizes, so Euler's theorem gives sum of (dVaR/dx_i)*x_i = VaR.
questions.explanation: Marginal VaR is a derivative — a per-unit sensitivity — so adding derivatives across positions of different sizes is meaningless. Multiplying each by its own position size converts sensitivities into contributions, and Euler's theorem for homogeneous functions guarantees they add up. Under the variance-covariance model this works out to C_i = VaR * w_i * beta_i, where beta_i is the position's beta to the portfolio. The practical value is that component VaR tells you where your risk actually IS, and a negative component identifies a genuine hedge — a position whose removal would INCREASE portfolio VaR.
questions.technique: Euler decomposition of VaR
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing why homogeneity is what makes the decomposition additive, not just the formula.

questions.prompt: Distinguish marginal VaR, incremental VaR and component VaR. Which would you quote to a trader asking "what does this new trade cost me in risk?"
questions.canonicalAnswer: Marginal VaR is the derivative of VaR with respect to a small change in the position. Incremental VaR is the actual change in VaR from adding or removing the whole position. Component VaR is marginal VaR times position size, and the components sum to total VaR. For a new trade of material size, quote INCREMENTAL VaR.
questions.explanation: Marginal is a local first-order sensitivity — accurate only for small changes, but cheap and additive. Incremental requires revaluing VaR twice, with and without the trade, and is the honest answer for a large ticket because it captures the non-linearity that marginal VaR's linearisation misses. Component is a decomposition of the EXISTING book, useful for attribution and limit-setting rather than for pricing a new trade. Quoting marginal VaR for a trade that doubles a concentration is the standard error here, and it understates the cost.
questions.technique: Choosing the right VaR sensitivity measure
questions.difficultyRationale: Three similar measures that are routinely confused; the discriminating question is the size of the change.

questions.prompt: A book holds £60m of asset A (daily vol 1%) and £40m of asset B (daily vol 2%), uncorrelated. Compute the 99% VaR and each position's component VaR.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Portfolio VaR = £2.33m. Component VaR is £0.84m for A and £1.49m for B.
questions.explanation: Cash standard deviations: A gives 60(0.01) = £0.6m, B gives 40(0.02) = £0.8m. With zero correlation, sigma_p = sqrt(0.36 + 0.64) = £1.0m, so VaR = 2.326(1.0) = £2.33m. At zero correlation each component's share of variance is (sigma_i V_i)^2 / sigma_p^2, giving 0.36 and 0.64. So C_A = 2.326(0.36) = £0.84m and C_B = 2.326(0.64) = £1.49m, which sum to the total. The lesson: B is 40% of the notional but 64% of the risk. Notional tells you almost nothing; the risk contribution scales with the SQUARE of the volatility-weighted exposure.
questions.technique: Component VaR from variance shares
questions.difficultyRationale: Two-step computation plus the interpretation that notional and risk share diverge.

questions.prompt: Your loss distribution has skewness +0.5 rather than zero. Use the Cornish-Fisher expansion to adjust a 99% VaR built on a normal quantile, and comment on the size of the effect.
questions.canonicalAnswer: z_CF = z + (1/6)(z^2 - 1) * S = 2.326 + (1/6)(4.410)(0.5) = 2.69. VaR rises by about 16% relative to the normal figure.
questions.explanation: Cornish-Fisher corrects a normal quantile for the higher moments of the actual distribution, the leading term being (1/6)(z^2 - 1)S for skewness. Here 2.326^2 - 1 = 4.410, so the adjustment is +0.367 and the quantile moves from 2.326 to 2.693 — a 16% larger VaR from a modest skew. Watch the sign convention: this is the LOSS distribution, where positive skew means a long right tail of large losses. There is a further kurtosis term, (1/24)(z^3 - 3z)(K-3), which for fat-tailed returns pushes the quantile up again. Cornish-Fisher is cheap and adds real accuracy for mildly non-normal books, but it breaks down for strongly non-normal ones — at that point you simulate.
questions.technique: Cornish-Fisher quantile adjustment
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the expansion, correct sign convention on the loss distribution, and judgement about its validity range.

questions.prompt: Walk through the steps of a Monte Carlo VaR calculation, and say when you would choose it over historical simulation.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Estimate the risk factor distribution and covariance matrix; decompose the covariance matrix (Cholesky) to generate correlated draws; simulate many joint factor scenarios; fully revalue the portfolio under each; sort the resulting P&Ls and read off the quantile. Choose it when you need more scenarios than history provides, or want to impose a distribution history does not contain.
questions.explanation: The distinguishing feature versus historical simulation is that the scenarios are GENERATED rather than observed, which is both the strength and the weakness. Strength: you can produce 100,000 scenarios instead of 500, you can stress the correlation structure directly, and you can price path-dependent instruments properly. Weakness: everything now depends on the distributional assumption you imposed, so you have swapped sampling error for model error. In practice it is the default for books full of exotics where full revaluation matters and the analytic route is hopeless.
questions.technique: Monte Carlo VaR procedure
questions.difficultyRationale: Multi-step procedure plus a judgement about when it is the right tool.

questions.prompt: Why does a Monte Carlo VaR need a Cholesky decomposition of the covariance matrix, and what goes wrong if the matrix is not positive definite?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Cholesky writes Sigma = LL', so multiplying a vector of independent standard normals by L produces draws with exactly the target covariance. If Sigma is not positive definite the decomposition fails — there is no real matrix square root, because some portfolio would have negative variance.
questions.explanation: You can only simulate independent normals directly; L is what imprints the correlation structure on them. The failure mode is common in practice: correlations estimated pairwise from different sample windows, or overridden by a risk manager's judgement, routinely produce a matrix that is not a valid covariance matrix of anything. The symptom is a Cholesky routine hitting a negative number under a square root. The standard repairs are eigenvalue flooring — decompose, set negative eigenvalues to a small positive number, rebuild and renormalise — or fitting the nearest valid correlation matrix. Silently patching it without telling anyone is how a risk system starts reporting numbers nobody can reproduce.
questions.technique: Simulating correlated risk factors
questions.difficultyRationale: Links a linear-algebra property to a concrete production failure.

questions.prompt: You run 10,000 Monte Carlo trials and want to halve the standard error of your VaR estimate. What do you do, and what does that tell you about Monte Carlo as a method?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Run 40,000 trials — four times as many. Monte Carlo error falls as 1/sqrt(N), so accuracy is expensive: each extra decimal place costs a hundredfold increase in trials.
questions.explanation: The 1/sqrt(N) rate is the central limit theorem applied to the simulation average, and crucially it does NOT depend on the dimension of the problem — which is exactly why Monte Carlo beats grid methods for high-dimensional portfolios, where a lattice would need points exponential in the number of factors. The rate is the reason variance-reduction techniques exist: antithetic variates, control variates and importance sampling all attack the constant in front of the 1/sqrt(N) rather than the rate itself. For tail quantiles specifically, importance sampling matters most, because plain sampling wastes almost all its effort on scenarios that never approach the 99th percentile.
questions.technique: Monte Carlo convergence rate
questions.difficultyRationale: One rate, but the implications (dimension-independence, variance reduction) are the substance.

questions.prompt: Your covariance matrix is estimated from 250 equally weighted days. A single extreme day drops out of the window and VaR falls sharply with no change in positions. What is this called, and how do you avoid it?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The ghost feature (or echo effect). It happens because equal weighting gives a day full weight for 250 days and zero thereafter. Avoid it by using exponentially weighted estimates (EWMA or GARCH), where a shock's influence decays smoothly.
questions.explanation: With equal weights an observation's influence is a step function, so the estimate jumps twice for one event — once when the shock arrives and once, in reverse, when it leaves the window. Risk limits get breached and released for reasons that have nothing to do with the book. EWMA replaces the step with a geometric decay, so the shock's influence fades continuously and the estimate is smooth. The same reasoning explains why a naive VaR often falls to its lowest just as a crisis window rolls off, which is precisely the wrong time to be reporting a comfortable number.
questions.technique: Weighting schemes in covariance estimation
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires recognising an artefact of the estimator rather than a change in risk, and naming the fix.

questions.prompt: RiskMetrics uses lambda = 0.94 for daily EWMA volatility. Where does that number come from, and what would using 0.97 instead do?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It was chosen empirically to minimise forecast error across a wide range of series. A higher lambda like 0.97 puts more weight on older data, giving a smoother estimate that reacts more slowly to new shocks.
questions.explanation: Lambda controls the memory of the estimator. The effective window is roughly 1/(1-lambda) days, so 0.94 corresponds to about 17 days of meaningful history and 0.97 to about 33. Lower lambda means faster reaction and a noisier, more volatile VaR series; higher lambda means a stable number that is slow to recognise a regime change. RiskMetrics landed on 0.94 for daily data and 0.97 for monthly. It is a smoothing choice, not a law of nature, and a bank that picks lambda to make its VaR look calm is making a model-risk decision it should be documenting.
questions.technique: EWMA decay parameter
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires understanding lambda as a memory-length choice with a trade-off, not a constant to memorise.

questions.prompt: Model-building VaR assumes a zero mean return over one day. Why is that acceptable at a one-day horizon but not at a one-year horizon?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because the mean scales with time while the standard deviation scales with its square root. Over one day the drift is negligible next to the volatility; over a year it is comparable and cannot be dropped.
questions.explanation: Put numbers on it. An equity with 8% expected annual return and 20% annual volatility has a daily drift of about 0.03% against a daily volatility of about 1.26% — the drift is 2.5% of the noise, immaterial to a quantile. Over a year the drift is 8% against 20%, or 40% of the noise, and ignoring it would overstate the loss quantile substantially. The general point is that the signal-to-noise ratio of a drift grows like sqrt(T), which is also why estimating expected returns is so much harder than estimating volatility: you need decades of data to pin down a mean that volatility reveals in months.
questions.technique: Scaling of drift versus diffusion
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the sqrt(T) argument and the ability to put rough numbers on when the drift starts to matter.

questions.prompt: Daily returns are positively autocorrelated with first-order coefficient rho = 0.2. Does square-root-of-time scaling from 1-day to 10-day VaR overstate or understate the risk, and by how much?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It understates it. The variance of the 10-day sum exceeds 10 times the daily variance when returns are positively autocorrelated; the correct multiplier is about sqrt(14.5)/sqrt(10) = 1.20 times the naive figure.
questions.explanation: Var(sum of T returns) = T*sigma^2 + 2*sigma^2*sum over lags of (T-k)*rho_k. With only first-order autocorrelation rho = 0.2 and T = 10, the correction is 2(0.2)(9) = 3.6 extra units, plus higher-lag terms if the autocorrelation decays geometrically — taking the total to roughly 14.5 sigma^2 rather than 10. The scaling factor is therefore sqrt(14.5) = 3.81 instead of sqrt(10) = 3.16, about 20% higher. Positive autocorrelation means trends persist, so multi-day losses compound; negative autocorrelation (mean reversion) would go the other way. Since the square-root rule assumes independent returns, any serial dependence makes it wrong in a direction you can at least sign.
questions.technique: Time scaling with autocorrelated returns
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the variance-of-a-sum formula with covariance terms, not just the iid shortcut.

questions.prompt: How do you map a single-stock equity position into a model-building VaR system that only carries index risk factors, and what does the mapping throw away?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Map it to a beta-weighted index exposure: a position of value V with beta b to the index is treated as b*V of index exposure. It throws away idiosyncratic risk — everything in the stock's return not explained by the index.
questions.explanation: The decomposition is r_stock = b*r_index + e, so total variance is b^2 * var(index) + var(e). Beta mapping keeps the first term and discards the second. For a well-diversified book that is defensible, because the idiosyncratic terms are largely independent and wash out. For a concentrated position it is a serious understatement — a single stock's variance is typically dominated by its idiosyncratic component, often 60-70% of it. The fix is to keep a specific-risk term alongside the mapped exposure, which is exactly what the regulatory specific-risk charge is for.
questions.technique: Risk-factor mapping and specific risk
questions.difficultyRationale: Standard technique, but the discriminating part is quantifying what the mapping loses.

questions.prompt: Decompose a forward contract to buy USD 10m for GBP in six months into the risk factors a VaR system would use.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Three: a long USD 10m spot FX exposure, a long position in a six-month USD zero-coupon bond, and a short position in a six-month GBP zero-coupon bond. Equivalently it is spot FX risk plus the two interest rate exposures implied by the forward points.
questions.explanation: A forward is a spot position plus two funding legs, which is exactly what covered interest parity says: F = S * (1 + r_USD*t)/(1 + r_GBP*t). Decomposing it this way means the VaR system needs no separate 'forward FX' factor — it reuses the spot rate and the two yield curves it already carries. That is the whole point of risk-factor mapping: express every instrument in terms of a small common set of factors so the covariance matrix stays tractable. It also explains why a forward's risk is not purely FX: a parallel move in either rate curve changes its value even with spot unchanged.
questions.technique: Risk-factor decomposition of a forward
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires seeing the instrument as a portfolio of primitives rather than as one thing.

questions.prompt: A long straddle is delta-neutral and has large positive gamma. Does the delta-gamma VaR approximation overstate or understate its risk, and why?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It overstates the LOSS, because positive gamma means the quadratic term is positive for a move in either direction — the position profits from large moves. The real risk is the reverse: theta decay and a fall in implied volatility, neither of which the delta-gamma approximation contains.
questions.explanation: With delta zero, dP = (1/2)*gamma*(dS)^2, which is positive whatever the sign of dS, so a pure delta-gamma model reports the straddle as having essentially no downside from spot moves. That is directionally right — a long straddle really does want movement — but it means the model is measuring the wrong risk entirely. The actual losses come from time passing with nothing happening (theta) and from implied volatility falling (vega). This is the clearest illustration of why an options book needs a vega risk factor and why FRTB treats volatility as a risk factor in its own right rather than a parameter.
questions.technique: Limits of delta-gamma for volatility positions
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires recognising that the approximation is not merely inaccurate but is measuring the wrong exposure.

questions.prompt: A desk starts trading a new product with no price history. How do you get it into a model-building VaR, and what are the risks of each approach?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Either proxy it with a related instrument that does have history, or decompose it into existing risk factors and price it from those. Proxying risks a basis that only shows up in stress; decomposition risks missing a factor the product is genuinely exposed to.
questions.explanation: Decomposition is preferred where possible, because it reuses factors already in the covariance matrix and keeps the product consistent with the rest of the book. Proxying is the fallback, and its danger is that the proxy and the real instrument track closely in normal conditions and decouple exactly when it matters — proxying a peripheral sovereign with a core one worked fine until 2011. Either way the treatment should be documented as a model limitation with a proxy-basis reserve or an add-on, and FRTB addresses this directly through the non-modellable risk factor regime, which forces a separate stress-based capital charge for factors without sufficient real price observations.
questions.technique: Proxying and non-modellable risk factors
questions.difficultyRationale: Open-ended judgement question; a good answer names both routes and their distinct failure modes.

questions.prompt: In cash-flow mapping, a £100 cash flow at 4 years is split between the 3-year and 5-year standard tenors. The split is chosen to preserve:
options: The present value and the variance of the cash flow
The nominal amount and the maturity
The nominal amount only
The duration only
questions.explanation: The mapping must not change what the position is worth, so present value is preserved by construction; and it must not change how risky it is, so the weights are chosen so the mapped pair has the same variance as the original flow — which requires knowing the correlation between the 3-year and 5-year rates. Preserving nominal amount is wrong because a nearer cash flow is worth more, and preserving duration alone would leave the variance unmatched whenever the two tenors are less than perfectly correlated.
questions.technique: Cash-flow mapping constraints
questions.difficultyRationale: Tests the two constraints together; the common error is remembering only present value.

questions.prompt: Your book has a large position in a currency pegged to the dollar. Historical volatility is near zero, so model-building VaR reports almost nothing. What is wrong with that number?
questions.canonicalAnswer: A peg suppresses observed volatility without removing the risk — it converts continuous small moves into a rare, large jump if the peg breaks. A model calibrated to the pegged period is measuring the peg's success, not the exposure.
questions.explanation: This is the sharpest example of history being the wrong guide. Under the peg the sample variance is genuinely tiny and every statistical test agrees the risk is small, right up until the devaluation, which is a move of 20-30% in a day. The distribution is bimodal and no Gaussian fitted to the quiet regime describes it. The treatment is not to adjust the volatility input but to handle it outside VaR entirely: a stress scenario for a break of the peg, sized on comparable historical breaks, plus a concentration limit. The same reasoning applies to any managed rate, credit position with no defaults in sample, or short-deep-out-of-the-money option book — all show low variance because the loss has not happened yet.
questions.technique: Peso problems and regime-dependent volatility
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires recognising that a low sample variance can be evidence of hidden risk rather than its absence.

questions.prompt: Under the variance-covariance model, when is a position's component VaR negative, and what does that tell you?
questions.canonicalAnswer: When the position's beta to the portfolio is negative — its returns are negatively correlated with the rest of the book. It means the position is a genuine hedge: increasing it would REDUCE total VaR.
questions.explanation: Component VaR is VaR * w_i * beta_i, so its sign is the sign of beta_i. A negative component identifies a position that pays when the rest of the book suffers, and it is one of the few outputs of a VaR system that gives a trader something directly actionable — it says where to add rather than where to cut. Two cautions. The beta is estimated from a sample correlation, so a marginally negative component may be noise. And correlations that hold on average often go to one in a crisis, which means the hedge you are being credited for may not be there when it is needed. Component VaR describes the book under normal conditions, and it should be read alongside a stress test, not instead of one.
questions.technique: Sign of the risk contribution
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires linking the sign of a formula to a portfolio interpretation, plus the caveats on estimated correlation.

questions.prompt: How many days of history would you use for a 1-day 99% historical simulation VaR, and what is the trade-off?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Typically 250 to 750 days (one to three years). More data gives a more stable tail estimate but assumes the market regime has not changed; less data reacts faster but leaves too few observations in the tail.
questions.explanation: At 99% only 1% of the sample sits beyond the quantile, so 250 days gives you 2 or 3 observations to estimate from — statistically almost nothing. Going to 750 days gives 7 or 8, which is better, but you are now asserting that market conditions from three years ago are relevant to tomorrow. Basel's requirement is at least one year of daily data. The tension is real and unavoidable, which is why the usual answer is to use a longer window with age weighting or volatility scaling, so old data contributes without being treated as equally informative.
questions.technique: Sample window choice
questions.difficultyRationale: One trade-off, with the numbers making the point.

questions.prompt: In historical simulation, what exactly is applied to the current portfolio?
options: The historical percentage changes in each risk factor
The historical P&L the desk actually made
The historical levels of each risk factor
A random sample drawn from the fitted distribution of each risk factor
questions.explanation: Each historical day supplies a set of factor MOVES, which are applied to today's factor levels to produce a hypothetical revalued portfolio. Option 2 is the past P&L of a past portfolio and answers a different question. Option 3 would price today's book at prices from years ago, which is meaningless. Option 4 describes Monte Carlo — the defining feature of historical simulation is that no distribution is fitted at all.
questions.technique: Historical simulation mechanics
questions.difficultyRationale: One mechanic, with the three standard confusions as distractors.

questions.prompt: Explain age-weighted historical simulation (the Boudoukh-Richardson-Whitelaw approach) and how the VaR is read off.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Each historical scenario gets a weight decaying geometrically with age — weight proportional to lambda^(i-1) for the i-th most recent day, normalised to sum to one. Sort the losses from worst to best, accumulate weights, and take the loss at which the cumulative weight first reaches 1%.
questions.explanation: Plain historical simulation gives a day from three years ago exactly the same weight as yesterday, which contradicts everything known about volatility clustering. Age weighting fixes that without discarding the old data entirely — the tail estimate keeps its observations but they count for less. Reading the quantile changes from 'the 5th worst of 500' to a weighted cumulative sum, which is the only fiddly part. A useful side effect is that the ghost feature disappears: a shock's influence decays smoothly instead of dropping out of the window in one step. The cost is a shorter effective sample, so the tail is estimated from fewer effective observations.
questions.technique: Age-weighted historical simulation
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires both the weighting scheme and the modified quantile-reading procedure.

questions.prompt: Explain filtered historical simulation: what gets filtered, and what is the filter for?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Standardise each historical return by the volatility estimate for that day, sample from the standardised residuals, then rescale by TODAY'S volatility. It solves the problem that a return drawn from a calm period understates risk in a turbulent one, and vice versa.
questions.explanation: The procedure is: fit a volatility model (usually GARCH or EWMA), divide each historical return by its contemporaneous volatility to get residuals that are approximately identically distributed, then multiply the sampled residual by the current volatility forecast. The shape of the tail comes from history; the SCALE comes from today. Plain historical simulation implicitly assumes the distribution is unconditional and unchanging, so after a quiet six months it reports a comfortable VaR just as a regime is turning. Filtering is also what makes EVT usable in practice, since the theory assumes identically distributed observations and raw returns plainly are not.
questions.technique: Volatility filtering of historical scenarios
questions.difficultyRationale: Three-step procedure whose justification (restoring the iid assumption) is the substance.

questions.prompt: Distinguish the block maxima and peaks-over-threshold approaches in EVT. Which is normally used in market risk, and why?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Block maxima takes the single largest loss from each block (say each month) and fits a generalised extreme value distribution. Peaks-over-threshold keeps every loss above a high threshold and fits a generalised Pareto. Market risk normally uses peaks-over-threshold, because it uses the data far more efficiently.
questions.explanation: Block maxima throws away information: if a month contains three catastrophic days it keeps one and discards two, and if a month is quiet it keeps a maximum that is not extreme at all. Peaks-over-threshold keeps exactly the observations that carry tail information and no others. Given how little data there is in a financial tail to begin with, that efficiency matters. Block maxima survives mainly in hydrology and insurance, where the natural blocking (annual maxima) is meaningful and the record is long.
questions.technique: Block maxima vs POT
questions.difficultyRationale: Two methods to contrast, with data efficiency as the discriminating argument.

questions.prompt: Name the three extreme value distributions and say which describes financial returns.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Gumbel (xi = 0, thin tail, e.g. normal), Frechet (xi > 0, heavy power-law tail) and Weibull (xi < 0, bounded tail). Financial returns are Frechet.
questions.explanation: The Fisher-Tippett theorem says a normalised block maximum can only converge to one of these three, and the generalised extreme value distribution unifies them through the single shape parameter xi. The sign of xi is the whole story: xi = 0 for distributions whose tails decay exponentially, xi > 0 for power-law tails where extreme events are far more likely than a normal would suggest, and xi < 0 where the variable has a hard upper bound. Equity returns consistently fit xi in the range 0.1 to 0.4, which is squarely Frechet, and that is the formal statement of 'financial returns have fat tails'.
questions.technique: Fisher-Tippett and the GEV family
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of a classification, with the sign of xi carrying the meaning.

questions.prompt: A GPD fit to losses above a £5m threshold gives xi = 0.2 and beta = 2 (£m), with 25 exceedances in 500 days. The 99.9% VaR from this fit is £16.9m. What is the corresponding expected shortfall?
questions.explanation: The generalised Pareto has a closed form for expected shortfall, which is one of the reasons it is convenient. Substituting: 16.9/0.8 = 21.13, and (2 - 0.2*5)/0.8 = 1/0.8 = 1.25, summing to £22.4m. The ratio ES/VaR is 1.32 here, against about 1.15 under normality at the same confidence — that gap is precisely the extra tail severity a fat-tailed fit reveals and a Gaussian model hides. Note the formula requires xi < 1; if xi >= 1 the mean of the tail is infinite and expected shortfall does not exist, which is a genuine possibility for some operational-loss datasets though not for market returns.
questions.technique: Expected shortfall from a fitted GPD
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the closed form, correct substitution, and awareness of the xi < 1 condition.

questions.prompt: A fitted GPD gives xi = 0.5. What does that imply about the moments of the loss distribution, and why should it worry you?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Moments of order 1/xi = 2 and above do not exist, so the variance is infinite. Any risk measure or statistical procedure that relies on a finite variance is invalid for that tail.
questions.explanation: For a generalised Pareto tail, the k-th moment is finite only when k < 1/xi. At xi = 0.5 the mean exists but the variance does not, so a sample standard deviation computed from the data is not estimating anything — it will simply grow as you add observations. That invalidates volatility-based risk measures, any normal approximation, and the central limit theorem in its usual form. Expected shortfall still exists (it needs only xi < 1), which is one argument for preferring it. Values that high are more typical of operational and insurance losses than of daily equity returns, where xi is usually 0.1 to 0.4 — so a market-risk fit returning 0.5 is more likely a sign of too low a threshold or too little data than a real finding.
questions.technique: Moment existence and the tail index
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the moment condition and the judgement to treat an extreme estimate as a possible fitting artefact.

questions.prompt: What is a mean excess plot, and how do you use it to choose the GPD threshold?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Plot the mean of (loss - u) over all losses exceeding u, against u. For a generalised Pareto tail this is linear in u, so you choose the lowest threshold above which the plot is approximately straight.
questions.explanation: The GPD has the property that its mean excess function is linear with slope xi/(1-xi), so linearity in the plot is direct evidence the asymptotic approximation has taken hold. Below that point the plot curves, meaning the threshold is in the body of the distribution where the theory does not apply. Choosing the LOWEST such threshold matters, because you want as many exceedances as possible for the fit. The plot gets noisy at the right-hand end simply because few observations remain, so the last stretch should be ignored rather than interpreted. It is a judgement call dressed up as a diagnostic, and different analysts will pick different thresholds from the same plot — which is itself a model risk worth disclosing.
questions.technique: Threshold selection diagnostics
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing why linearity is the signal, and the practical caveats on reading the plot.

questions.prompt: You compute a 99% VaR by historical simulation from 500 days and want a confidence interval around it. How do you get one?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Bootstrap: resample 500 days with replacement many times, compute the VaR for each resample, and take the 2.5th and 97.5th percentiles of the resulting distribution. Alternatively use the analytic standard error of an order statistic.
questions.explanation: The bootstrap is the practical route because it makes no distributional assumption and reuses the machinery you already have. The analytic version uses the fact that a sample quantile is asymptotically normal with standard error sqrt(q(1-q)/n)/f(x_q), where f is the density at the quantile — which exposes the problem directly: at q = 0.99 the density in the denominator is tiny, so the standard error is large. Expect intervals of plus or minus 10-20% around a 99% VaR from 500 days. Quoting a VaR to three significant figures without that context implies a precision the estimate does not have.
questions.technique: Bootstrapping a quantile estimate
questions.difficultyRationale: Two routes to the same answer, and the point is the size of the resulting uncertainty.

questions.prompt: Would you use EVT to estimate a 95% VaR? Explain.
questions.canonicalAnswer: No. At 95% roughly 5% of the sample sits beyond the quantile, so historical simulation already has plenty of observations and the empirical estimate is reliable. EVT earns its place at 99% and beyond, where data runs out.
questions.explanation: EVT is an extrapolation tool, and extrapolation costs you a distributional assumption. Where the empirical distribution has adequate data there is no reason to pay that cost. Worse, applying EVT at 95% means setting a threshold low enough that it sits in the BODY of the distribution, where the Pickands-Balkema-de Haan convergence result does not apply, so the GPD fit is simply misspecified. The rule of thumb is that EVT is for the region where you have single-digit numbers of observations — 99%, 99.9%, and the economic capital quantiles beyond.
questions.technique: When extrapolation is warranted
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing the theory's domain of validity rather than treating it as universally better.

questions.prompt: Two risk managers compute a 99% historical simulation VaR in March 2020, one with a 500-day window and one with a 1,000-day window. Whose number is higher, and which is more useful?
questions.canonicalAnswer: In March 2020 the 500-day window gives the HIGHER number, because the crash days are a larger fraction of a smaller sample. The shorter window is more useful at that moment because it reflects the current regime.
questions.explanation: A given set of extreme days carries twice the weight in a 500-day sample as in a 1,000-day one, so the shorter window responds faster to a regime change — in both directions. The corollary is uncomfortable: run the same comparison in January 2020 and the 500-day window gives the LOWER number, because it has already dropped the 2018 selloff. Window length is not a question with a right answer, it is a choice about how quickly you want the measure to react, and a firm that shortens its window in a crisis and lengthens it afterwards is managing its reported number rather than its risk. This is the main argument for age weighting or volatility filtering, which get the responsiveness without the arbitrary cliff.
questions.technique: Window length and regime sensitivity
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires reasoning about the same choice in two opposite regimes, not just naming the trade-off.

questions.prompt: In the peaks-over-threshold method, doubling the threshold u will typically:
options: Reduce estimation error from model misspecification but increase it from having fewer observations
Reduce both sources of estimation error
Increase both sources of estimation error
Leave the fitted shape parameter unchanged
questions.explanation: This is the bias-variance trade-off in its purest form. A higher threshold means the GPD approximation is closer to exact, since the asymptotic result holds as u tends to infinity — that reduces bias. But it also discards observations, so the parameters are fitted on less data — that increases variance. Threshold choice is the whole art of applying EVT, and neither extreme works: too low and you are fitting a Pareto to the body of the distribution, too high and you are fitting two parameters to five points.
questions.technique: Bias-variance trade-off in threshold choice
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires seeing both error sources moving in opposite directions.

questions.prompt: Historical simulation gives every scenario equal probability. What does that imply about the correlations embedded in the resulting VaR?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The correlations are whatever actually occurred in the sample period, jointly and simultaneously, and are never specified anywhere. Each scenario preserves the exact combination of factor moves observed on that day.
questions.explanation: This is historical simulation's quiet strength. Because a scenario is a whole day's set of moves applied together, the method automatically captures the real joint behaviour — including non-linear dependence and the tendency of correlations to rise in crashes — without anyone estimating a correlation matrix, checking it is positive semi-definite, or choosing a copula. The corresponding weakness is that it can only reproduce dependence structures that appeared in the window. If equities and gold never sold off together in your sample, the method assigns that scenario probability zero, and no amount of extra data makes an unobserved combination appear. That gap is the argument for pairing it with hypothetical stress scenarios.
questions.technique: Implicit dependence structure
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires articulating what the method assumes by NOT assuming anything, plus the corresponding blind spot.

questions.prompt: Your 99% historical simulation VaR has been flat for eight months, then jumps 40% in a single day with no material change in positions. Give two explanations and say how you would tell them apart.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Either a new extreme day entered the sample and displaced the quantile, or the portfolio's sensitivity to an existing scenario changed. Distinguish them by re-running yesterday's VaR with today's positions, and today's VaR with yesterday's positions.
questions.explanation: The two-way re-run is the standard attribution: holding positions fixed isolates the scenario effect, and holding scenarios fixed isolates the position effect. The 'flat for eight months' detail is itself the tell — a quantile read off an unweighted sample only moves when the identity of the 5th-worst scenario changes, so it sits still and then steps, rather than drifting. That step behaviour is not a bug in the calculation but it is a bad property for a limit-monitoring measure, and it is another argument for age weighting or volatility scaling, which produce a number that moves continuously with market conditions.
questions.technique: VaR attribution between scenario and position effects
questions.difficultyRationale: Diagnostic question requiring a concrete decomposition procedure, not just a list of possible causes.

questions.prompt: Set up the maximum likelihood estimation of the generalised Pareto parameters from a set of threshold exceedances.
questions.canonicalAnswer: For exceedances y_i = x_i - u, the GPD density is f(y) = (1/beta)(1 + xi*y/beta)^(-1/xi - 1). The log-likelihood is L = -n*ln(beta) - (1/xi + 1) * sum of ln(1 + xi*y_i/beta), maximised numerically over xi and beta.
questions.explanation: There is no closed-form solution, so it is a two-parameter numerical optimisation — trivial computationally, but with two things worth knowing. The support condition 1 + xi*y/beta > 0 must hold for every observation, which constrains the search when xi is negative. And for xi < -0.5 the maximum likelihood estimator loses its usual asymptotic properties, so standard errors from the Hessian are unreliable there; in market risk xi comes out positive so this rarely bites. Alternatives worth naming are probability-weighted moments, which are more stable in small samples, and the Hill estimator, which estimates the tail index directly but assumes xi > 0.
questions.technique: Maximum likelihood for the GPD
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires writing the likelihood correctly and knowing the conditions under which the estimator misbehaves.

questions.prompt: Economic capital is often set at a 99.9% one-year confidence level. Why is that quantile essentially impossible to estimate from data, and what is done instead?
questions.canonicalAnswer: A 99.9% one-year event is a once-in-a-thousand-years loss, and no institution has anything like that history — even a century of annual data gives 100 observations and zero at the quantile. Instead the tail is modelled parametrically, usually with EVT or a structural model, and cross-checked with stress scenarios.
questions.explanation: The honest position is that the number is a model output, not a measurement, and its confidence interval is enormous. That is why supervisors pair it with things that do not depend on extrapolation: stress tests with named scenarios, a leverage ratio that ignores risk weights entirely, and floors on modelled outputs. It also explains a genuine tension in the framework — the same regulators who require a 99.9% figure also constrain how much a bank may rely on it. Being able to say 'here is the number, and here is why I do not trust it to better than a factor of two' is the answer that lands in an interview.
questions.technique: Limits of extrapolation at extreme quantiles
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires quantifying why the estimate is unreliable and naming the compensating controls.

questions.prompt: What is the Hill estimator, and when would you reach for it rather than fitting a full generalised Pareto?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It estimates the tail index directly from the k largest order statistics: the Hill estimate of xi is the average of ln(x_(i)) - ln(x_(k+1)) over the top k observations. Use it when you only need the tail index, believe xi > 0, and want a fast estimate with no numerical optimisation.
questions.explanation: The Hill estimator is a one-line average of log-ratios, so there is no likelihood to maximise and no convergence to worry about. The cost is that it assumes a strictly positive shape parameter — it cannot represent a thin or bounded tail at all — and it is notoriously sensitive to k, the number of upper order statistics used. The standard diagnostic is a Hill plot of the estimate against k, and the standard disappointment is that it rarely shows the clean stable region the textbooks promise. Use it as a quick cross-check on a GPD fit rather than as the primary estimate: if maximum likelihood says xi = 0.25 and Hill says 0.24, you have some comfort that the threshold choice is not driving the answer.
questions.technique: Hill estimator for the tail index
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the estimator's form plus its two known weaknesses, and the judgement to use it as a cross-check.

questions.prompt: Under historical simulation, what is the largest loss your 99% VaR can ever report, and why does that matter?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The worst loss observed in the sample window — the method cannot produce a scenario it has never seen. It matters because it puts a hard ceiling on the measure that has nothing to do with the portfolio's actual risk.
questions.explanation: Every quantile historical simulation reports is one of the observed P&Ls, so the whole measure is bounded above by the worst day in the window. If the window contains no crash, the 99.9% figure is barely distinguishable from the 99% one, and both are understatements. That ceiling is the single clearest argument for EVT, which fits a parametric tail and can extrapolate past the sample maximum, and for stress testing, which drops the sample entirely. It is also why a firm that shortened its lookback window in 2007 was, quite literally, unable to compute a 2008-sized loss.
questions.technique: The sample-maximum ceiling
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires recognising a structural limit of the estimator rather than a tuning problem.

questions.prompt: A 10-year zero-coupon bond yields 5%. What is its Macaulay duration, and what is its modified duration?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Macaulay duration is 10 years — for a zero there is only one cash flow. Modified duration is 10/1.05 = 9.52 (annual compounding).
questions.explanation: Macaulay duration is the present-value-weighted average time to the cash flows, so for a zero-coupon bond it equals maturity exactly. That makes zeros the reference point: any coupon bond of the same maturity has a SHORTER duration, because some value arrives earlier. Modified duration divides by (1 + y/k) for k compounding periods, converting a weighted average time into a price sensitivity: dP/P = -D_mod * dy. Under continuous compounding the two coincide, which is why quant texts often use them interchangeably and practitioners do not.
questions.technique: Macaulay vs modified duration
questions.difficultyRationale: One definition and one division, with the zero-coupon case as the anchor.

questions.prompt: Define convexity and explain why a bondholder values it. When would you be willing to give it up?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Convexity is the second derivative of price with respect to yield, scaled by price: C = (1/P) * d2P/dy2. Positive convexity means you gain more when yields fall than you lose when they rise. You give it up when it is priced too expensively — when the yield give-up for the convex bond exceeds what the expected volatility justifies.
questions.explanation: The second-order price change is +(1/2)*C*(dy)^2, positive for either sign of dy, so convexity is a free option on volatility — which is exactly why it is not free. Convex bonds trade at lower yields, and the yield concession you pay is the market's price for that optionality. The trade-off is therefore a volatility view: if you think rates will stay in a narrow range, sell convexity and collect the yield; if you expect large moves, buy it. Note also that convexity grows with duration and with dispersion of cash flows, so a barbell has more convexity than a bullet of the same duration — the standard way to express the view without changing your rate exposure.
questions.technique: Convexity as an option on rate volatility
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires framing convexity as a priced optionality rather than an unambiguous good.

questions.prompt: A mortgage-backed security has NEGATIVE convexity. Explain what causes it and what it means for the holder when rates fall sharply.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Borrowers hold a prepayment option: when rates fall they refinance, so the security's cash flows shorten exactly when long duration would have been valuable. The holder's price appreciation is capped, and duration falls as rates fall.
questions.explanation: The holder is effectively short a call option on the underlying bond. As rates fall the option moves into the money for the borrower, prepayments accelerate, and the investor is handed principal back to reinvest at the new lower rates. Price rises much less than a comparable non-callable bond, and can plateau entirely. The mirror image is worse: when rates rise, prepayments slow and duration EXTENDS, so the holder is left with more rate exposure precisely when it hurts. That two-way effect is called extension risk, and hedging it requires a dynamic hedge whose size changes with the market — which is why MBS desks are large consumers of swaptions.
questions.technique: Negative convexity from embedded prepayment options
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires identifying the embedded short option and tracing its effect in both rate directions.

questions.prompt: What is key rate duration, and what does it give you that a single duration number does not?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Key rate duration is the sensitivity of a portfolio's value to a shift in one specific point on the yield curve, holding the others fixed. It decomposes total duration into tenor buckets, so you can see and hedge curve shape risk rather than only parallel-shift risk.
questions.explanation: A single duration compresses the whole curve exposure into one number and therefore assumes every rate moves together. Key rate durations at, say, 2y, 5y, 10y and 30y reveal that a duration-neutral book can be long the front end and short the back — a steepener in disguise. In practice the shifts are triangular: bump the 5-year point and let the effect taper linearly to the neighbouring key rates, so the bumps sum to a parallel shift. The alternative decomposition is PCA, which produces fewer, statistically independent factors (level, slope, curvature); key rate durations are less parsimonious but map directly onto tradeable hedging instruments, which is why trading desks prefer them.
questions.technique: Key rate durations vs a single duration
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires contrasting two decompositions and knowing why desks use one over the other.

questions.prompt: A bank's assets have duration 4 and its liabilities duration 1.5, with liabilities equal to 90% of assets. What is the duration gap, and what happens to equity if rates rise 1%?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Duration gap = D_A - (L/A)*D_L = 4 - 0.9(1.5) = 2.65 years. Equity falls by about 2.65% of ASSETS for a 1% rate rise — which, on equity of 10% of assets, is a 26.5% hit to equity.
questions.explanation: The change in equity is -(D_A - (L/A)D_L) * A * dy. With a positive gap the bank is asset-sensitive in duration terms — it borrows short and lends long, the classic banking book position — so rising rates hurt. The arithmetic is the alarming part: a 2.65-year gap looks modest until you express it against a thin equity layer, where a 1% rate move wipes out a quarter of book equity. This is exactly the 2023 US regional bank story, where long-duration securities funded by deposits produced enormous unrealised losses. It is also why supervisors run an economic value of equity test alongside the earnings-based one.
questions.technique: Duration gap analysis
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the gap formula plus the leverage step that turns a small percentage into a large one.

questions.prompt: Distinguish the two standard supervisory measures of banking-book rate risk: economic value of equity and net interest income. Why can they point in opposite directions?
questions.canonicalAnswer: EVE is the present value of all future cash flows — a balance-sheet, long-horizon measure. NII is projected earnings over the next 1-2 years — a short-horizon, accrual measure. They diverge because a position can improve near-term earnings while destroying long-term value, or the reverse.
questions.explanation: Take a bank that shortens asset duration by moving into floating-rate loans. If rates rise, NII improves immediately because assets reprice faster than deposits — good on the earnings measure. But EVE may barely move, because the bank has given up the long-duration assets that were carrying value. Conversely, a bank holding long fixed-rate securities funded by deposits shows stable NII while rates are low and catastrophic EVE deterioration when they rise. Supervisors require both precisely because either one alone is gameable, and the IRRBB framework specifies six prescribed rate scenarios (parallel up and down, steepener, flattener, short up, short down) run against both.
questions.technique: EVE vs NII
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires constructing a case where the two measures disagree, not just defining them.

questions.prompt: What are non-maturity deposits, why are they the hardest part of banking-book rate risk, and how are they modelled?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Deposits with no contractual maturity that can be withdrawn on demand but in practice stay for years. They are hard because their true duration is behavioural, not contractual. They are modelled by splitting them into a stable 'core' portion with an assumed long duration and a volatile portion treated as overnight.
