questions.explanation: Contractually a current account is overnight money, which would give it zero duration and make the bank look enormously exposed to rising rates. Behaviourally, balances persist for years and the rate paid on them moves only partially with market rates — the deposit beta. So the modelled duration comes from two estimated parameters, the beta and the assumed decay of the core balance, and both are calibrated on a history that may not repeat. That is a model risk with a very large capital consequence, which is why supervisors cap the assumed average life (five years under the Basel IRRBB standardised approach) rather than trusting the bank's own estimate. The 2023 deposit flights showed the failure mode directly: balances assumed to be sticky moved in days once depositors could compare rates on a phone.
questions.technique: Behavioural modelling of non-maturity deposits
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires seeing that the key parameters are estimated behavioural assumptions, and naming why supervisors constrain them.

questions.prompt: Your book is long £50m DV01-equivalent in 2-year rates and short the same in 10-year rates. Name the trade and describe its P&L under a bull flattening.
questions.canonicalAnswer: It is a steepener — it profits if the 2s10s spread widens. A bull flattening (yields fall, long end falling more) LOSES money, because the 10-year leg you are short rallies more than the 2-year leg you are long.
questions.explanation: Being long the front and short the back in DV01 terms means you profit when the front outperforms, i.e. when the curve steepens. Naming the four regimes is the standard drill: bull steepening (yields down, front down more) and bear steepening (yields up, back up more) both make money; bull flattening and bear flattening both lose. Since the position is DV01-neutral overall, a parallel shift is roughly a wash — the P&L is almost entirely the SPREAD move. In practice 'roughly' matters: the two legs have different convexity, so a large parallel move leaves a residual, which is why steepeners are sometimes weighted on a beta rather than a straight DV01 basis.
questions.technique: Curve trades and the four curve regimes
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires classifying the trade and then applying one of four named regimes correctly.

questions.prompt: Why does a swap have almost no duration at inception but substantial DV01?
questions.canonicalAnswer: At inception a par swap has zero net present value, so percentage-based duration is undefined or meaningless. DV01 is a cash sensitivity and does not need a non-zero starting value, so it is the natural measure — roughly the DV01 of the fixed leg.
questions.explanation: Duration is defined as a percentage price change per unit yield change, and dividing by a value of zero is not useful. This is the clearest practical reason desks quote rate risk in DV01 rather than duration: DV01 works for swaps, futures, FRAs and any other instrument entered at zero cost, and it adds across instruments without value-weighting. For a receive-fixed swap the DV01 is essentially that of the fixed-rate bond you are long, since the floating leg reprices to par at each reset and carries only the small sensitivity to the current period's fixing.
questions.technique: Why DV01 rather than duration
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires seeing that a zero-value instrument breaks the definition of one measure but not the other.

questions.prompt: You hedge a 10-year bond position with 10-year swaps and the hedge loses money even though rates barely moved. What happened?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The swap spread moved — the difference between the swap rate and the government bond yield. Hedging a bond with a swap leaves you exposed to that spread, which is a separate risk factor from the level of rates.
questions.explanation: A government bond yield and a swap rate are different curves that usually move together and occasionally do not. The spread between them reflects the credit and funding characteristics of the interbank market, collateral scarcity, and demand from asset-liability managers — and it can move sharply on its own, as it did in 2008 and again during the 2020 dash for cash, when US swap spreads went negative. The general lesson is that a hedge constructed from a different instrument transfers your exposure into a BASIS rather than eliminating it. Basis risks are systematically underestimated because they are quiet for long periods and then move violently, which is precisely the pattern that defeats a VaR calibrated on recent history.
questions.technique: Basis risk in cross-instrument hedging
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires identifying a risk factor that was never explicitly in the hedge design.

questions.prompt: What is a bond's dollar duration, and why do practitioners hedge with it rather than with modified duration?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Dollar duration is modified duration multiplied by the position's value: D_mod * P. It is used for hedging because cash sensitivities add directly across positions, whereas modified durations must be value-weighted before they can be combined.
questions.explanation: To hedge, you need the two legs' cash sensitivities to offset, and that is a statement about dollar duration (or equivalently DV01, which is dollar duration times 0.0001). Trying to work in modified duration means carrying the position values around separately and re-weighting at every step, which is error-prone and pointless. The practical rule for sizing a hedge is: notional of hedge = (dollar duration of position) / (dollar duration per unit of hedge instrument). The same logic applies to any risk measure you want to net across instruments — express it in currency, not in percentages.
questions.technique: Cash sensitivities for hedge sizing
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires articulating why additivity, not accuracy, drives the choice of measure.

questions.prompt: In a yield curve PCA, the first three principal components typically explain what share of the variation in yield changes?
options: Around 95-99%
Around 50-60%
Around 75%
Essentially 100%, by construction
questions.explanation: Empirically the level factor alone explains 80-90% of daily yield-curve variation, with slope adding roughly 5-10% and curvature 1-3%, taking the first three to 95-99%. That is what justifies reducing a twenty-tenor curve to three risk numbers. It is not 100% by construction — you would need as many components as tenors for that — and the residual, though small in variance terms, is exactly where butterfly and basis trades live. A desk hedged against all three factors is not hedged against everything; it has hedged the part of the curve that moves in a correlated way and retained the rest.
questions.technique: PCA variance explained
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of an empirical magnitude, with the residual's significance as the substance.

questions.prompt: Explain immunisation: how do you protect a known future liability from rate moves, and what does the protection NOT cover?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Match the duration of your asset portfolio to the duration of the liability and equate their present values. That neutralises a small parallel shift. It does NOT cover non-parallel curve moves, large moves (where convexity mismatch bites), or the need to rebalance as time passes and durations drift.
questions.explanation: The mechanism is that a rate rise reduces the value of the assets and the liability by roughly the same percentage, leaving the surplus unchanged. Three leaks. Duration is a first-order measure, so a large move leaves a convexity residual — and you want asset convexity to EXCEED liability convexity, which is the condition for the surplus to be locally minimised rather than maximised. A twist in the curve moves assets and liability differently unless their cash flows are matched tenor by tenor, not just in aggregate. And durations decay at different rates, so an immunised portfolio drifts out of immunisation within months and needs rebalancing, which costs money. Cash flow matching avoids all three but is usually infeasible or expensive.
questions.technique: Duration immunisation and its residual risks
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the construction plus three distinct failure modes, including the convexity inequality.

questions.prompt: The 2-year rate is 3% and the 4-year rate is 4%, both annually compounded. What is the implied 2-year forward rate starting in 2 years?
questions.explanation: No-arbitrage: investing for four years must give the same result as investing for two and rolling into the forward. Computing (1.04)^4 = 1.16986 and (1.03)^2 = 1.0609, the ratio is 1.10271, whose square root is 1.0501. The quick approximation is worth having for interviews: the forward is roughly 2*(4%) - 1*(3%) = 5% for these tenors, because the longer rate is a weighted average of the shorter one and the forward. If the forward comes out below the spot rates, the curve is inverted — and note that a forward rate is a no-arbitrage construct, not a forecast, though it is often quoted as if it were one.
questions.technique: Forward rates from spot rates
questions.difficultyRationale: One no-arbitrage identity plus careful compounding arithmetic.

questions.prompt: Distinguish spot rates, par rates and forward rates, and say which one a bond's quoted yield to maturity actually is.
questions.canonicalAnswer: A spot (zero) rate discounts a single cash flow at one maturity. A par rate is the coupon that makes a bond of that maturity price at par. A forward rate is the rate contracted today for a future period. A yield to maturity is none of these exactly — it is the single rate that discounts ALL of a bond's cash flows to its price.
questions.explanation: Yield to maturity is a summary statistic, not a rate on the curve: it is an internal rate of return, and it implicitly assumes every coupon is reinvested at that same yield. Two bonds with identical maturities but different coupons have different yields to maturity even when discounted off the identical spot curve, which is exactly why comparing YTMs across coupons is misleading. The zero curve is the primitive object — par rates and forwards are both derived from it, and bootstrapping is the procedure that recovers it from observable par instruments.
questions.technique: The three curve representations
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires seeing that YTM sits outside the trio as a derived summary.

questions.prompt: Why did the market move from LIBOR discounting to OIS (and now SOFR/SONIA) discounting, and what did that change for rate risk?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because collateralised derivatives are funded at the overnight rate paid on collateral, so the risk-free discount rate for a collateralised trade is OIS, not LIBOR. It split the single curve into a discounting curve and separate forecasting curves, adding basis risk between them.
questions.explanation: Before 2008 the LIBOR-OIS spread was a few basis points and one curve served for both discounting and forecasting. When the spread blew out to over 350bp the approximation became untenable, and the industry moved to multi-curve pricing: discount at OIS, forecast each floating index off its own curve. For a rate-risk system this means a swap now has sensitivity to at least two curves, and the SPREAD between them is a risk factor in its own right. The subsequent transition to overnight risk-free rates (SOFR, SONIA, ESTR) reinforced the same structure, and left a residual basis between legacy LIBOR-linked and new RFR-linked instruments that desks still hedge explicitly.
questions.technique: Multi-curve discounting
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the funding argument for the change and the concrete consequence for risk decomposition.

questions.prompt: A pension fund is short duration relative to its liabilities and rates fall sharply. Describe the mechanism by which this can force it to sell assets.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Falling rates raise the present value of the long-duration liabilities more than the assets, widening the deficit. If the fund uses leveraged interest rate swaps or gilt repo to close the duration gap, those hedges lose value as rates RISE, triggering collateral calls — and meeting them forces asset sales into a falling market.
questions.explanation: The two directions are worth keeping separate. Falling rates worsen the funding position of an underhedged scheme, which is the slow problem. The fast problem is the mirror image: a scheme that has hedged with leverage is long duration through derivatives, so a sharp RISE in rates generates immediate variation margin calls on those hedges even though the economic position has improved. The 2022 UK LDI episode was exactly this — gilt yields rose, hedges required collateral, funds sold gilts to raise it, which pushed yields higher still. It is a liquidity spiral driven by a solvency-improving move, and it shows why interest rate risk and liquidity risk cannot be managed in separate silos.
questions.technique: Leveraged liability hedging and margin spirals
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires tracking the opposite signs of the economic and cash-flow effects, which is where most answers go wrong.

questions.prompt: What is gamma risk on a rates book, and where does it typically come from?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Gamma is the rate of change of DV01 as rates move — the second-order exposure. On a rates book it comes from options: swaptions, caps and floors, callable bonds, and the prepayment options embedded in mortgages.
questions.explanation: A linear rates book has constant DV01 and no gamma; the moment options enter, DV01 becomes a function of the rate level and the hedge must be adjusted as the market moves. Short gamma means your DV01 moves against you — you become more exposed as rates go the wrong way, forcing you to hedge at progressively worse levels, which is why short-gamma books amplify rate moves. Convexity on a plain bond is closely related but not identical: bond convexity is positive and passive, whereas option gamma changes sign with the position and is concentrated near the strike. Vega sits alongside it, since an options book loses from a fall in implied volatility even with rates unchanged.
questions.technique: Second-order rate exposure from optionality
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires distinguishing option gamma from bond convexity and naming the hedging consequence.

questions.prompt: A trader claims the yield curve's upward slope predicts that short rates will rise. What is the counterargument?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The slope also reflects a term premium — the extra return investors demand for holding longer-duration bonds. An upward-sloping curve is consistent with expected rates being flat or even falling, if the term premium is large enough.
questions.explanation: The forward rate decomposes into an expectation plus a term premium, and the two are not separately observable, so reading forwards as pure forecasts is a well-documented error — forwards have historically been poor predictors of realised short rates. The expectations hypothesis in its pure form (zero term premium) is rejected empirically. Two competing explanations for the premium are liquidity preference, where investors demand compensation for locking money up, and market segmentation, where supply and demand at particular tenors set rates independently. In practice the premium varies over time and has occasionally been negative, which is why estimating it is its own research literature rather than a settled number.
questions.technique: Term premium vs expectations
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing that two unobservable components are conflated in one observable, and that the pure theory is rejected.

questions.prompt: Two assets have correlation 0.6. What fraction of one asset's variance is explained by the other in a linear regression?
questions.canonicalAnswer: 36%. The R-squared of a simple linear regression is the square of the correlation: 0.6^2 = 0.36.
questions.explanation: Squaring is the step people skip, and it changes the impression considerably — a correlation of 0.6 sounds like a strong relationship but leaves nearly two-thirds of the variation unexplained. Useful anchors: 0.3 explains 9%, 0.7 explains 49%, and you need 0.9 before you are explaining 81%. Note also that correlation is symmetric while the regression framing is not — regressing Y on X and X on Y gives different slopes but the same R-squared.
questions.technique: Correlation and R-squared
questions.difficultyRationale: One squaring, with the interpretive point carrying the weight.

questions.prompt: Define tail dependence, and state the tail dependence of the Gaussian copula.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Tail dependence is the limiting probability that one variable is extreme given the other is extreme: lambda = lim as q tends to 1 of P(X > F_X inverse of q | Y > F_Y inverse of q). For the Gaussian copula it is ZERO for any correlation below 1.
questions.explanation: This is the single most consequential fact about the Gaussian copula. However high you set the correlation — 0.9, 0.99 — the probability of a JOINT extreme event vanishes asymptotically, meaning the model says truly catastrophic co-movements essentially cannot happen. The Student-t copula has strictly positive tail dependence, increasing as its degrees of freedom fall, and so does the Clayton copula in the lower tail. Choosing a Gaussian copula for a portfolio of correlated credits is therefore not a neutral technical choice; it is an assumption that they will not all default together, which is precisely what CDO models assumed before 2008.
questions.technique: Tail dependence coefficients
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the definition as a limit plus the counterintuitive Gaussian result.

questions.prompt: Why would you use Kendall's tau or Spearman's rho instead of Pearson correlation?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because they are rank-based, so they are invariant to any strictly increasing transformation of the marginals and are not distorted by outliers or non-linear relationships. Pearson measures only linear association and depends on the marginal distributions.
questions.explanation: The invariance property is what makes rank correlations the natural partners of copulas: a copula IS the dependence structure stripped of the marginals, and Kendall's tau depends only on the copula, whereas Pearson correlation changes if you take logs of your data. That matters practically, since returns and log returns should not have different dependence. Rank measures are also robust — one extreme joint observation can move a Pearson correlation substantially and barely moves a tau. The cost is that Pearson slots directly into portfolio variance algebra and rank measures do not, so the usual workflow is to estimate dependence with tau and convert to a copula parameter.
questions.technique: Rank correlation measures
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the invariance argument, which is what connects rank measures to copulas.

questions.prompt: Explain the correlation-smile phenomenon in CDO tranche pricing and what it revealed about the Gaussian copula model.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Implied correlations backed out of traded tranche prices differed by tranche — equity and senior tranches implied higher correlation than mezzanine — producing a smile. Since one model should give one correlation for one portfolio, the smile was direct evidence the model was misspecified.
questions.explanation: The logic mirrors the volatility smile in options. If the one-factor Gaussian copula described reality, the same correlation parameter would price every tranche of the same capital structure. It did not, and the shape of the disagreement was informative: the market was pricing more joint-default risk in the senior tranches than a Gaussian copula could generate — which is exactly the zero tail dependence problem showing up in prices. The industry response was base correlation, a quoting convention that made the numbers consistent without fixing the model, which is a fair description of where things stood in 2007. The transferable lesson is that when a model's implied parameter has to vary by instrument to fit the market, the parameter is absorbing the model's error.
questions.technique: Implied correlation and model misspecification
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the parallel with the volatility smile and the diagnosis of what the smile was compensating for.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a correlation matrix to be positive semi-definite, and give two ways an estimated matrix can fail the test.
questions.canonicalAnswer: It means w'Cw >= 0 for every weight vector w, so no portfolio has negative variance. Estimation can break it when correlations are estimated pairwise over different sample periods, or when a risk manager overrides individual entries by hand.
questions.explanation: The mathematical requirement is that all eigenvalues are non-negative. Pairwise estimation over mismatched windows is the commonest cause in production, because each pair is internally consistent but the set is not mutually consistent — correlation is not transitive, but it is constrained: if A and B are 0.9 correlated and B and C are 0.9, then A and C cannot be -0.9. Manual overrides break it for the same reason. The consequences are concrete: Cholesky decomposition fails so Monte Carlo cannot run, and a mean-variance optimiser will find the negative-variance direction and load into it, producing an absurd portfolio. Repairs are eigenvalue flooring or projection onto the nearest valid correlation matrix.
questions.technique: Validity of estimated correlation matrices
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the definition, two realistic causes, and the downstream failures.

questions.prompt: Your equity-bond correlation has been reliably negative for two decades and turns positive. What are the implications for a standard balanced portfolio, and why might the sign have changed?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The diversification a 60/40 portfolio relies on disappears, so its volatility rises sharply and both legs can fall together. The sign typically flips when inflation rather than growth is the dominant shock driving both markets.
questions.explanation: The mechanism is about which shock dominates. When growth shocks drive markets, weak growth hurts equities and helps bonds (rates fall) — negative correlation. When inflation shocks dominate, rising inflation hurts both, because bonds sell off on rate expectations and equities sell off on discount rates and margin pressure — positive correlation. 2022 was the clean demonstration, with a 60/40 portfolio suffering one of its worst years precisely because the hedge stopped working. The risk-management lesson is that a correlation used as a structural assumption should be understood mechanistically, not just estimated: knowing WHY it is negative tells you the conditions under which it will not be.
questions.technique: Regime dependence of correlation
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires a causal account of the sign, not just the observation that correlations are unstable.

questions.prompt: What is a Clayton copula, and when is it the right choice?
questions.canonicalAnswer: An Archimedean copula with strong LOWER tail dependence and weak upper tail dependence — the variables cluster in their joint left tail. It is the right choice when losses coincide but gains do not, which is the empirical pattern for equity returns.
questions.explanation: Its defining feature is asymmetry. A Gaussian copula is symmetric and has no tail dependence at all; a Student-t copula is symmetric with tail dependence in both tails; Clayton is asymmetric, concentrating dependence where the losses are. That matches the well-documented observation that equity markets crash together but rally separately, and it makes Clayton attractive for downside risk measures. The Gumbel copula is its mirror image, with upper tail dependence, useful where the joint extreme of interest is on the upside. Choosing between them is a modelling decision that should be justified by the shape of the risk you are measuring, not by which one fits the middle of the data best.
questions.technique: Archimedean copulas and tail asymmetry
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires placing one copula within a family by its tail behaviour and matching it to an empirical fact.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would simulate correlated defaults for a loan portfolio using a one-factor Gaussian copula.
questions.canonicalAnswer: For each obligor write a latent variable X_i = sqrt(rho)*M + sqrt(1-rho)*Z_i, where M is a common factor and Z_i idiosyncratic, both standard normal. Obligor i defaults when X_i falls below N-inverse of its default probability. Draw M once per scenario and the Z_i independently.
questions.explanation: The construction gives every pair of obligors correlation rho through the single shared factor M, which is what makes it tractable for thousands of names — you draw one common factor instead of a full correlation matrix. Conditional on M the defaults are independent, which is the property that yields the Vasicek closed form for the large-portfolio loss distribution and underpins the Basel IRB capital formula. Two limitations are worth stating alongside it. Because the copula is Gaussian, there is no tail dependence beyond what the single factor produces, so genuinely simultaneous extreme defaults are underweighted. And a single rho for the whole portfolio ignores sector structure, which multi-factor versions restore at the cost of the closed form.
questions.technique: One-factor Gaussian copula simulation
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the latent-variable construction, the default trigger via the inverse normal, and the conditional-independence property.

questions.prompt: A risk report shows the average pairwise correlation across a book rising from 0.3 to 0.7 during a selloff. Give two explanations, only one of which is a real change in dependence.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Either dependence genuinely increased, or you are seeing sample selection: correlations measured conditional on large moves are biased upward even when the true joint distribution is unchanged. The second is a measurement artefact.
questions.explanation: The artefact is well documented and counterintuitive. If you take a bivariate normal with constant correlation and compute the correlation only over observations where both variables are large, the conditional correlation is higher than the unconditional one — conditioning on the tail truncates the sample in a way that inflates the estimate. So a rise from 0.3 to 0.7 measured across a crisis window is partly mechanical. Distinguishing the two requires comparing against what a constant-correlation model would produce under the same conditioning, which is the standard test in the literature. The finding that survives it is that correlations DO rise genuinely in crises, but by less than naive conditional estimates suggest — and getting this right matters, because overstating the effect leads to hedges being abandoned as useless when they are merely weaker.
questions.technique: Conditional correlation bias
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing that conditioning on extremes biases the estimate, which most answers miss entirely.

questions.prompt: Sklar's theorem guarantees that a copula representation of a joint distribution is unique when:
options: The marginal distributions are continuous
The variables are independent
The joint distribution is elliptical
The correlation matrix is positive definite
questions.explanation: Sklar's theorem says every joint distribution can be written as a copula applied to its marginals, and that the copula is unique when the marginals are continuous. With discrete marginals the decomposition still exists but the copula is not uniquely determined, which is a genuine complication for modelling default indicators and other discrete risks — two different copulas can produce the same joint distribution, so 'the' implied correlation is not well defined. The other options are irrelevant to uniqueness: independence is a special case, ellipticality is a property of a particular family, and positive definiteness is a condition on a correlation matrix rather than on the theorem.
questions.technique: Sklar's theorem uniqueness condition
questions.difficultyRationale: Tests the condition rather than the headline statement, and the discrete case is the practically important exception.

questions.prompt: How do you fit a copula to data in practice? Describe the standard two-stage approach.
questions.canonicalAnswer: First transform each variable to uniform margins — either with its fitted parametric CDF or with the empirical CDF (the semi-parametric route). Then fit the copula parameters to the transformed data by maximum likelihood or by matching Kendall's tau.
questions.explanation: The two-stage structure is exactly what Sklar's theorem licenses: marginals and dependence are separable, so you can model them separately. The semi-parametric version, using empirical CDFs for the margins, is popular because it makes no assumption about the marginal shapes and isolates any misspecification in the copula. Two practical cautions. The transformation uses estimated margins, so the second-stage standard errors are understated unless you account for the first-stage estimation. And with only one or two parameters, most copula families are fitted overwhelmingly by the BODY of the data, while the property you usually care about — tail dependence — is determined by the family you chose rather than by the fit. Choosing the family is the real modelling decision.
questions.technique: Two-stage (inference functions for margins) copula estimation
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the procedure plus the observation that the fit does not determine the tail behaviour.

questions.prompt: Which portfolio has the greater exposure to a 1bp parallel shift: £10m of a bond with modified duration 3, or £4m of a bond with modified duration 8?
options: The £4m position, at £3,200 per bp against £3,000
The £10m position, because notional dominates
They are identical
Cannot be determined without the yields
questions.explanation: Work in DV01, not duration or notional. The first position is 10m x 3 x 0.0001 = £3,000 per basis point; the second is 4m x 8 x 0.0001 = £3,200. The £4m position carries MORE rate risk despite being under half the size, because duration more than compensates. This is the whole reason desks quote rate exposure in cash sensitivity — neither notional nor duration alone ranks two positions correctly, and only their product does.
questions.technique: Ranking positions by DV01
questions.difficultyRationale: Two multiplications, with notional size as the intuitive trap.

questions.prompt: A trader says a 5-year bond has "good carry and roll-down" on an upward-sloping curve. Explain both terms and how each earns money.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Carry is the net income from holding the position — coupon received less funding cost — earned simply by time passing. Roll-down is the price gain from the bond ageing into a lower point on the curve: a 5-year bond becomes a 4-year bond, and if the 4-year yield is lower, the price rises even with the curve unchanged.
questions.explanation: Both are returns you earn if NOTHING happens, which is what makes them the baseline for any relative-value rates trade. Carry depends on the slope at the front (the funding rate versus the coupon); roll-down depends on the slope at the position's own tenor, so the steepest part of the curve offers the most. Two cautions worth stating. Carry and roll-down are exactly what you give up when you hedge, so a duration-neutral trade often has near-zero carry by construction. And a steep curve may be steep because the market EXPECTS rates to rise, in which case the carry is compensation for a risk rather than free money — the classic carry-trade failure mode.
questions.technique: Decomposing the return to a rates position when the curve is unchanged
questions.difficultyRationale: Two distinct sources of return that are routinely conflated, plus the reason the free lunch is not free.

questions.prompt: Relate a stock's beta to the market and its correlation with the market. When are they numerically equal?
questions.canonicalAnswer: beta = rho * (sigma_stock / sigma_market). They are equal only when the stock and the market have the same volatility.
questions.explanation: Beta is a regression slope and therefore carries units of relative volatility; correlation is a scale-free measure of association bounded by 1. The distinction matters in practice: a stock can have a beta of 2 with a correlation of only 0.5, if it is four times as volatile as the market — high beta, weak relationship. Or a utility with correlation 0.9 and half the market's volatility has a beta of 0.45 — strong relationship, low beta. Confusing the two leads to the wrong hedge ratio, because hedging uses beta, while diversification reasoning uses correlation.
questions.technique: Beta as a scaled correlation
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing the scaling factor and constructing the case where they diverge.

questions.prompt: Two asset PRICES have a correlation of 0.95 but their RETURNS are uncorrelated. How is that possible, and which number should a risk manager use?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Both price series trend, so their levels move together over time even though day-to-day changes are independent — spurious correlation between non-stationary series. The risk manager must use the return correlation.
questions.explanation: Correlating two random walks produces a large coefficient purely because both drift, and the result is not evidence of any relationship — the classic demonstration correlates two independently simulated random walks and gets |rho| above 0.8 routinely. Levels are non-stationary, so the sample correlation does not converge to anything and standard significance tests are invalid. Differencing to returns restores stationarity and gives an estimate that means something. The same trap appears with any two series sharing a trend, which is why spurious regressions of macro variables on each other are so easy to produce.
questions.technique: Spurious correlation between non-stationary series
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires diagnosing non-stationarity as the cause rather than treating it as a genuine relationship.

questions.prompt: You estimate a 500x500 correlation matrix from 750 daily observations. Why is most of it noise, and what does random matrix theory say about it?
questions.canonicalAnswer: You are estimating about 125,000 parameters from 375,000 numbers, so the ratio N/T is 0.67 and the sampling error is enormous. Random matrix theory says the eigenvalues of a PURE NOISE correlation matrix spread over the Marchenko-Pastur range (1 +/- sqrt(N/T))^2, so any eigenvalue inside that band carries no information.
questions.explanation: With N = 500 and T = 750, the noise band runs from (1 - 0.816)^2 = 0.034 to (1 + 0.816)^2 = 3.30. Typically only a handful of eigenvalues — the market factor and a few sector factors — sit above 3.30; everything else is indistinguishable from noise. This has a direct consequence for portfolio optimisation: the optimiser loads into the SMALLEST eigenvalue directions, believing them to be low-risk combinations, and those are precisely the directions that are pure estimation error. The standard remedies are eigenvalue clipping (replace the in-band eigenvalues with their average), shrinkage towards a structured target such as constant correlation, or imposing a factor model so you estimate a handful of loadings rather than 125,000 pairs.
questions.technique: Marchenko-Pastur noise bounds on estimated correlation matrices
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the parameter count, the noise-band formula, and the reason it breaks optimisers specifically.

questions.prompt: What is shrinkage estimation of a covariance matrix, and why does a deliberately biased estimate outperform the sample one?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Shrinkage takes a weighted average of the noisy sample covariance matrix and a structured, low-variance target such as a constant-correlation or single-factor matrix. The bias it introduces is more than repaid by the reduction in variance, giving lower total estimation error.
questions.explanation: This is the bias-variance trade-off applied to matrix estimation. The sample covariance matrix is unbiased but has enormous variance when N is comparable to T; the structured target is heavily biased but stable. Ledoit and Wolf's contribution was to derive the shrinkage intensity that minimises expected squared error, so the weight is chosen rather than guessed — more shrinkage when N/T is large, less when data is plentiful. The result is a matrix that is guaranteed positive definite (unlike the sample matrix when T < N) and that consistently produces better out-of-sample portfolios. It is the standard illustration that unbiasedness is not the objective; accuracy is.
questions.technique: Ledoit-Wolf shrinkage
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires articulating why accepting bias improves the estimate, which is counterintuitive on first encounter.

questions.prompt: How would you back out an implied correlation from index option prices and single-name option prices, and what trade does a rich implied correlation suggest?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Use the portfolio variance identity: for an index of weights w_i, sigma_index^2 = sum of w_i^2 sigma_i^2 + correlation term. Assuming one common correlation rho and solving gives roughly rho = sigma_index^2 / (sum of w_i sigma_i)^2 for a large index. If implied correlation is rich, sell index volatility and buy single-name volatility — a dispersion trade.
questions.explanation: The approximation comes from noting that for a large, well-diversified index the own-variance terms are negligible, so index variance is essentially rho times the square of the weighted average volatility. Implied correlation is persistently ABOVE realised correlation, because index puts are in structural demand from investors hedging portfolios while single-name options are less bid — so the dispersion trade (short index vol, long constituent vol) has a positive expected return that is really a risk premium for being short correlation. Its risk profile is the important part: it loses precisely in a crash, when correlations converge to one and the index moves more than the sum of the parts. Short correlation is a short tail position dressed as a relative-value trade.
questions.technique: Implied correlation and dispersion trading
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the variance identity, the approximation for large N, and the risk profile of the resulting trade.

questions.prompt: For a Gaussian copula, how do you convert an estimated Kendall's tau into the copula's correlation parameter?
questions.canonicalAnswer: rho = sin(pi * tau / 2), inverting the relationship tau = (2/pi) * arcsin(rho).
questions.explanation: This identity is why the two-stage fitting procedure is so convenient: estimate tau from the ranks, which is robust and needs no distributional assumption, then map it to the parameter the model wants in closed form — no optimisation at all. A worked example: tau = 0.5 gives rho = sin(pi/4) = 0.707. Note the two are not equal, and the gap is largest in the middle of the range. The same identity holds for the Student-t copula, since it depends only on the elliptical structure, which is what makes tau the natural estimator for that whole family. Spearman's rho has its own mapping, rho = 2*sin(pi*rho_S/6).
questions.technique: Rank correlation to copula parameter
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the specific identity and awareness that it holds for the elliptical family generally.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would compute a two-asset VaR using a Student-t copula rather than the variance-covariance approach.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Fit a marginal distribution to each asset separately; fit the t-copula's correlation and degrees of freedom to the rank-transformed data; simulate many correlated draws from the copula; map each uniform draw back through the inverse marginal CDFs to get returns; revalue the portfolio and read off the quantile.
questions.explanation: The point of the exercise is that the marginals and the dependence are chosen independently — you can give each asset a fat-tailed marginal AND give the pair tail dependence, neither of which the variance-covariance approach permits. The degrees of freedom parameter controls how much: low values produce strong joint extremes, and as it grows the t-copula converges to the Gaussian. Expect the resulting VaR to exceed the variance-covariance figure at high confidence and to be similar at low confidence, since the difference lives entirely in the tail. The cost is that there is no closed form, so it is a simulation exercise, and the answer depends on two modelling choices (marginal family and copula family) rather than on a covariance matrix alone.
questions.technique: Copula-based VaR by simulation
questions.difficultyRationale: Multi-step procedure whose value lies in seeing which assumptions have been decoupled.

questions.prompt: What does a DCC-GARCH model add over EWMA for tracking correlations?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It lets each asset have its own GARCH volatility process and models the correlation dynamics separately, with mean reversion towards a long-run correlation matrix — where EWMA imposes a single decay parameter on everything and has no long-run level.
questions.explanation: Dynamic conditional correlation splits the problem in two: fit a univariate GARCH to each series to get conditional volatilities, then model the standardised residuals' correlation with its own persistence and mean-reversion parameters. The advantages over EWMA are that different assets can have genuinely different volatility dynamics, and that correlation forecasts revert to a long-run level instead of extrapolating today's estimate flat forever. It also guarantees a positive definite matrix by construction. The costs are estimation complexity and the fact that DCC still imposes a common correlation dynamic across all pairs — every pair mean-reverts at the same rate, which is a strong assumption in a large book.
questions.technique: Dynamic conditional correlation
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires comparing two estimators on several dimensions, including what DCC still assumes.

questions.prompt: You estimate a correlation matrix for 300 assets from 200 daily observations. What is necessarily true of the result?
options: It is singular — at least 100 eigenvalues are exactly zero
It is positive definite but poorly conditioned
It is not a valid correlation matrix at all
The estimates are unbiased and the only issue is noise
questions.explanation: With T observations you can estimate a matrix of rank at most T-1, so a 300x300 matrix from 200 observations has at least 101 zero eigenvalues by construction. It is positive SEMI-definite and therefore a valid correlation matrix, but it cannot be inverted — which breaks mean-variance optimisation, Mahalanobis distances, and anything else needing the precision matrix. Worse, the zero eigenvalues correspond to portfolios the estimate claims have exactly zero variance, and an unconstrained optimiser will find them and take an enormous position. The fix is to reduce dimension (a factor model) or regularise (shrinkage), not to gather a little more data.
questions.technique: Rank deficiency when T < N
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the rank bound and its concrete consequence, rather than a general statement that the estimate is noisy.

questions.prompt: Name the three pillars of the Basel framework and say in one line what each does.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Pillar 1 sets minimum capital requirements by formula. Pillar 2 is supervisory review, where regulators assess risks Pillar 1 misses and can require more capital. Pillar 3 is market discipline through mandated public disclosure.
questions.explanation: The structure matters because most interesting risks live outside Pillar 1. Interest rate risk in the banking book, concentration risk, business risk and reputational risk have no Pillar 1 formula at all — they are handled through the ICAAP under Pillar 2, where the bank makes its own case and the supervisor sets an add-on. Pillar 3 exists on the theory that comparable disclosure lets counterparties and investors price a bank's risk, which is why the disclosure templates are prescribed in detail rather than left to the bank.
questions.technique: The three-pillar structure
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of a framework, with the point being what falls outside Pillar 1.

questions.prompt: Under FRTB, model approval is granted or withdrawn at the level of:
options: The individual trading desk
The whole bank
The legal entity
The risk factor class
questions.explanation: Desk-level approval is one of FRTB's structural changes. Under the previous regime approval was firm-wide, so a single failing business could jeopardise the whole internal-model permission — and supervisors were correspondingly reluctant to withdraw it. Desk-level granularity makes the sanction usable: a desk that fails its P&L attribution test or its backtest falls back to the standardised approach on its own, without disturbing the rest of the bank. It also forces banks to define desks formally, with a documented business strategy and a single head, which was itself a change in practice.
questions.technique: Desk-level model approval
questions.difficultyRationale: One structural fact, with the reason it matters as the substance.

questions.prompt: Describe the FRTB standardised approach's three components.
questions.canonicalAnswer: A sensitivities-based method (delta, vega and curvature risk aggregated across prescribed risk classes using supervisory risk weights and correlations), a default risk charge, and a residual risk add-on for exotic payoffs the sensitivities method cannot capture.
questions.explanation: The sensitivities-based method is the bulk of it and is risk-sensitive in a way its predecessor was not: banks supply their own delta and vega sensitivities, but the risk weights and correlations are set by the supervisor, so two banks with the same book get the same number. Curvature captures gamma-type risk through a pair of prescribed up and down shocks rather than a second derivative. The default risk charge covers jump-to-default, which a sensitivities framework misses entirely. The residual add-on is a crude notional-based charge for anything genuinely exotic. The whole thing matters even to banks using internal models, because FRTB requires the standardised number to be computed alongside as a floor and a fallback.
questions.technique: Structure of the FRTB standardised approach
questions.difficultyRationale: Three components with distinct purposes; a good answer says why each exists.

questions.prompt: Why does FRTB require the standardised approach to be computed even by banks with internal model approval?
questions.canonicalAnswer: As a floor and a fallback: it provides a comparable benchmark across banks, guards against internal models producing implausibly low capital, and gives an immediately available number if desk-level model approval is withdrawn.
questions.explanation: The pre-crisis problem was that internal-model capital varied enormously across banks holding essentially identical portfolios — supervisory studies found multiples of difference — which destroyed comparability and invited optimisation. The standardised calculation restores a common yardstick and lets supervisors see the ratio of modelled to standardised capital for each bank. It is also operationally necessary: a desk that fails its P&L attribution test moves to standardised capital immediately, and it can only do so if the calculation is already running. The cost is that banks must maintain two full calculation stacks in parallel, which is a large part of FRTB's implementation expense.
questions.technique: Role of the standardised floor
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the comparability motivation plus the operational reason, not just 'as a floor'.

questions.prompt: Explain how the FRTB expected shortfall measure combines different liquidity horizons.
questions.canonicalAnswer: ES is computed for the full set of risk factors at a 10-day horizon, then separately for progressively narrower subsets containing only the factors with longer horizons, and the results are combined as the square root of a sum of squared incremental terms.
questions.explanation: The construction gives every risk factor an ES contribution scaled to its own liquidity horizon without requiring a full joint model at five different horizons. Concretely you compute ES with all factors shocked over 10 days, then with only the 20-day-and-longer factors shocked, then only 40-day-and-longer, and so on, and aggregate the incremental pieces in quadrature. The effect is that an illiquid exposure attracts capital as though it took 120 days to exit while a liquid one is capitalised over 10. It is deliberately conservative — the square-root aggregation assumes no diversification benefit between horizon buckets — and that conservatism was part of why the industry pushed back on the calibration.
questions.technique: Liquidity-horizon-adjusted ES
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the nested-subset construction, which is the part most summaries omit.

questions.prompt: A desk fails its P&L attribution test. Walk through what the test measures and what happens next.
questions.canonicalAnswer: It compares the risk-theoretical P&L produced by the risk model against the hypothetical P&L from the front-office pricing model, using the two metrics of a Spearman correlation and a Kolmogorov-Smirnov test on the distribution of differences. A desk in the amber zone pays a capital surcharge; a desk in the red zone must use the standardised approach until it passes again.
questions.explanation: The test asks whether the risk model actually describes the same portfolio the traders are pricing — a question backtesting cannot answer, because a risk model can miss whole risk factors and still produce roughly the right number of exceptions. The commonest cause of failure is exactly that: the front office prices with factors (a full vol surface, a basis, a specific curve) that the risk system proxies away. So the remediation is usually to enrich the risk model rather than to recalibrate it. Note the incentive this creates: aligning the two models is expensive, and for some desks the cheaper answer is simply to accept standardised capital, which is a rational outcome the framework anticipates.
questions.technique: P&L attribution test mechanics and consequences
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires both metrics, the three-zone outcome, and the diagnosis of the typical root cause.

questions.prompt: Distinguish actual P&L, hypothetical P&L and risk-theoretical P&L, and say which is used for backtesting.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Actual P&L is what the desk really made, including intraday trading, fees and new deals. Hypothetical P&L holds positions fixed at end of day and revalues them with the next day's market data. Risk-theoretical P&L is what the risk model predicts for those same fixed positions. Backtesting uses hypothetical P&L (and, under FRTB, actual P&L as well).
questions.explanation: The distinction exists because VaR is a statement about a STATIC portfolio held for one day, so testing it against actual P&L conflates model error with the desk's intraday trading and fee income — a desk can trade its way out of a breach, or into one, for reasons the model never claimed to predict. Hypothetical P&L isolates the model. FRTB requires backtesting against both: hypothetical to test the model, actual to catch the case where a desk's real results diverge from the static assumption. Risk-theoretical P&L is the third series and belongs to the attribution test rather than the backtest.
questions.technique: The three P&L series
questions.difficultyRationale: Three similar concepts whose differences determine which test each supports.

questions.prompt: What is the FRTB default risk charge, and why is it computed separately from expected shortfall?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It capitalises jump-to-default risk — the loss from an issuer defaulting outright — separately from the ES measure, which is calibrated to continuous market moves. It is computed from default probabilities and loss-given-default with prescribed correlations, over a one-year horizon at 99.9%.
questions.explanation: The two risks have different shapes. ES is built from a distribution of price moves observed over a stressed period, and a continuous-move model cannot represent a name gapping to recovery value overnight — a credit position can look almost riskless on spread volatility right up to the default. Separating them also avoids double counting: FRTB explicitly removes credit spread migration from the default charge and default from the spread charge. The one-year 99.9% calibration deliberately mirrors the banking-book credit framework, so that the same exposure is capitalised comparably whichever book it sits in — which was one of the boundary problems FRTB set out to fix.
questions.technique: Default risk charge versus ES
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the argument that a continuous-move measure cannot represent a jump, plus the double-counting concern.

questions.prompt: Why does FRTB calibrate expected shortfall to a stressed period rather than to recent data?
questions.canonicalAnswer: To remove procyclicality. A measure calibrated on recent data falls in calm markets, releasing capital exactly when risk is building, and spikes in a crisis, forcing deleveraging at the worst moment.
questions.explanation: The 2008 experience was that VaR-based capital reached its lowest just before the crisis and its highest during it, so the framework demanded least capital when it was most needed and most when raising it was impossible. Stressed calibration breaks that loop by anchoring the measure to a fixed historical period of significant stress relevant to the bank's portfolio. The cost is responsiveness — a stressed-period calibration will not react to a genuinely new risk — which is why it sits alongside a current-period backtest rather than replacing it. The same procyclicality argument drives the countercyclical capital buffer and the floors on margin models.
questions.technique: Procyclicality and stressed calibration
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires articulating the feedback loop, not just naming the calibration.

questions.prompt: Under FRTB, a risk factor has fewer than 24 real price observations a year. What follows, and why is the threshold defined in terms of real prices?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It becomes a non-modellable risk factor and is capitalised through a separate stressed-scenario add-on rather than inside the ES model. Real prices are required because a factor with no observable transactions cannot be modelled credibly, only interpolated.
questions.explanation: The modellability criteria require at least 24 real price observations a year with no 90-day gap, where a real price means an actual transaction, a committed quote, or a price from a third-party vendor backed by a transaction. The point of the definition is to stop banks from claiming modellability on the basis of their own marks or of interpolated curve points, which is precisely what made some pre-crisis models unfalsifiable. NMRF capital is punitive and non-diversifiable across factors, which has real business consequences: it has made some bespoke and long-dated products uneconomic to hold, which is arguably the framework working as intended.
questions.technique: Non-modellable risk factors
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the observability criterion and its intended behavioural effect.

questions.prompt: Under the previous regime, market risk capital included both VaR and stressed VaR. What was the effect of adding them together?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It roughly doubled market risk capital, because the two are summed with no diversification benefit — the framework assumed the current-period and stressed-period losses could occur together.
questions.explanation: The sum is deliberately conservative and was a direct response to 2008, when VaR calibrated on the preceding calm period proved far too low. The structure has an odd property worth understanding: because stressed VaR is fixed to a historical window, it does not fall when the bank reduces risk in ways that only recent data would reflect, so the marginal capital cost of a position depends on how it would have behaved in 2008 rather than how it behaves now. FRTB resolves this more cleanly by using a single stressed-calibrated ES rather than adding two numbers together.
questions.technique: VaR plus stressed VaR aggregation
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires seeing the no-diversification assumption in the addition and its consequence for marginal capital.

questions.prompt: A bank wants to move a position from the trading book to the banking book to reduce capital. Under FRTB, what stops it?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Reclassification requires supervisory approval, is expected to be rare, and — crucially — any capital benefit is disallowed: the bank must hold a permanent Pillar 1 capital add-on equal to the reduction. There is also a presumptive list assigning instruments to a book by type.
questions.explanation: Removing the incentive is the whole design. Under Basel II the boundary was defined by trading intent, which is unobservable and self-declared, so positions migrated to whichever book was cheaper — in 2008 illiquid credit sat in the trading book on the strength of a claimed intent to trade, attracting light capital for what was in substance a hold-to-maturity credit exposure. FRTB replaces intent with a presumptive assignment by instrument type, requires documented justification and approval to deviate, and neutralises the arbitrage by pinning the capital benefit at zero. The residual issue is internal risk transfers between the books, which FRTB regulates separately through prescribed hedging structures.
questions.technique: The trading book boundary and its anti-arbitrage design
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing the specific mechanism (the capital add-on) that removes the incentive, not just that approval is needed.

questions.prompt: What is the leverage ratio, and why does a risk-insensitive measure sit alongside a risk-weighted framework?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Tier 1 capital divided by total exposure, with no risk weighting — a minimum of 3% under Basel III. It exists as a backstop against risk weights being wrong or gamed, since a risk-weighted framework can be satisfied by a very large balance sheet of assets that models say are safe.
questions.explanation: Every risk-weighted requirement depends on the risk weights being right, and before 2008 they demonstrably were not: AAA-rated structured credit and sovereign exposures carried near-zero weights and produced enormous losses. A leverage ratio cannot be optimised by model choice because it ignores models entirely. The design tension is real and acknowledged: a binding leverage ratio penalises low-risk, low-margin business such as repo and government bond market-making, which is why the constraint is set as a backstop rather than as the primary requirement, and why several jurisdictions temporarily excluded central bank reserves from it in 2020.
questions.technique: The leverage ratio as a model-independent backstop
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires both the rationale and the acknowledged distortion it creates.

questions.prompt: Under the Basel traffic-light backtesting framework applied to 250 days at 99%, the red zone begins at:
options: 10 exceptions
5 exceptions
8 exceptions
15 exceptions
questions.explanation: Zero to four exceptions is green (multiplier stays at 3.00), five to nine is amber with an add-on rising from 0.40 to 0.85, and ten or more is red, where the multiplier goes to 4.00 and the supervisor will normally question the model's continued approval. The thresholds come from the binomial distribution: with an expected 2.5 exceptions, ten is far enough into the tail that chance is not a credible explanation, while five is ambiguous — hence a graduated penalty rather than a cliff.
questions.technique: Traffic-light zones
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of a threshold, with the statistical reasoning behind the graduation.

questions.prompt: What is the capital floor in the finalised Basel III package, and what problem does it address?
questions.canonicalAnswer: An output floor setting a bank's total risk-weighted assets at no less than 72.5% of what the standardised approaches would produce. It addresses the excessive variability in modelled RWAs across banks holding similar portfolios.
questions.explanation: Supervisory benchmarking exercises found that banks given identical hypothetical portfolios produced risk-weighted assets differing by a factor of two or more, which meant capital ratios were not comparable across institutions — undermining both market discipline and the level playing field. The floor caps how much benefit any internal model can deliver, regardless of how sophisticated it is. It is contentious for a defensible reason: it weakens the incentive to invest in better risk measurement, since beyond a point better models buy no capital relief. The counterargument is that comparability and a hard limit on model optimism are worth that cost.
questions.technique: The output floor and RWA variability
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the specific problem (RWA variability across banks) rather than a generic 'prudence' answer.

questions.prompt: Why is CVA capitalised separately under Basel III, and what did the crisis reveal about it?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because roughly two thirds of counterparty credit losses in 2008 came from CVA mark-to-market moves rather than from actual defaults, and the pre-crisis framework capitalised only default risk. Basel III added a CVA capital charge for the volatility of the adjustment itself.
questions.explanation: Before the crisis a bank held capital against a counterparty actually failing. What happened instead was that counterparty credit spreads widened enormously, CVA reserves had to be increased, and the resulting accounting losses were very large even where no counterparty defaulted at all — monoline insurers being the canonical case. The charge capitalises that spread volatility. It also created a live hedging problem: banks hedge CVA with credit default swaps, which reduces the accounting volatility but introduces its own basis and, under some frameworks, was not recognised as a hedge for capital purposes — a mismatch that itself became a source of risk-management distortion.
questions.technique: CVA risk capital
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the empirical finding about the composition of crisis losses, which is the whole justification.

questions.prompt: Distinguish the countercyclical capital buffer from the capital conservation buffer.
questions.canonicalAnswer: The capital conservation buffer is a fixed 2.5% of risk-weighted assets that banks must hold above the minimum and can draw down in stress, with restrictions on distributions as it depletes. The countercyclical buffer is variable, set by national authorities between 0% and 2.5% according to where the credit cycle stands.
questions.explanation: Both exist to make capital usable rather than merely present, but they answer different questions. The conservation buffer is always on and creates a graduated zone above the hard minimum, so a bank that dips into it faces automatic constraints on dividends and bonuses rather than a sudden breach. The countercyclical buffer is a macroprudential tool — raised when credit growth looks excessive, released in a downturn — and its purpose is to build capital in good times specifically so it can be released to support lending in bad ones. Whether banks will actually use buffers when permitted is the open empirical question; evidence from 2020 suggests reluctance, because markets read buffer usage as distress.
questions.technique: Basel III buffers
questions.difficultyRationale: Two similar-sounding buffers with genuinely different purposes and mechanics.

questions.prompt: Your bank's FRTB standardised capital is 1.8 times its internal model number. Give three legitimate reasons for a gap that large.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Prescribed supervisory correlations are more conservative than realised ones, so the standardised approach grants less diversification benefit; the residual risk add-on charges exotic positions on notional regardless of their actual risk; and curvature shocks are calibrated conservatively, penalising options books more than a simulated distribution would.
questions.explanation: A large gap is expected by design and is not by itself evidence of a problem in either calculation. The dominant driver is usually diversification: the standardised approach applies fixed correlations within and across risk classes and prescribes low or zero cross-class recognition, whereas an internal model uses estimated correlations that are typically higher. Second is any exotic book, where the residual add-on is a blunt notional charge. Third is optionality, since curvature is measured with prescribed shocks rather than a fitted distribution. What SHOULD prompt investigation is the reverse case or a ratio that moves sharply without a change in the book — and the ratio is itself a supervisory diagnostic for exactly that reason.
questions.technique: Reconciling standardised and modelled capital
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires identifying structural sources of divergence rather than assuming one number is wrong.

questions.prompt: What is the ICAAP, and how does it differ from the Pillar 1 calculation?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The Internal Capital Adequacy Assessment Process is the bank's own assessment of all material risks and the capital needed against them, reviewed by the supervisor under Pillar 2. Unlike Pillar 1 it is not formulaic — the bank must identify its own risks, quantify them with its own methods, and justify the result.
questions.explanation: Pillar 1 covers credit, market and operational risk by prescribed formula. The ICAAP covers everything else and everything Pillar 1 measures badly: interest rate risk in the banking book, concentration, pension risk, business and strategic risk, and the bank's own stress testing. The supervisor's review (the SREP in Europe) can impose an additional capital requirement on top of Pillar 1. The practical significance is that for many banks the binding constraint is a Pillar 2 add-on rather than the Pillar 1 minimum, so the quality of the ICAAP argument has a direct capital consequence — which makes it a genuinely important document rather than a compliance exercise.
questions.technique: Pillar 2 and the ICAAP
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires understanding what falls outside Pillar 1 and why the ICAAP is often the binding constraint.

questions.prompt: What is an internal risk transfer under FRTB, and why does the framework regulate it so tightly?
questions.canonicalAnswer: A transfer of risk between the banking book and the trading book, or between trading desks, executed internally rather than with an external counterparty. FRTB regulates it because without controls it is a route to shifting positions into whichever book carries lower capital.
questions.explanation: The economics are real — a bank genuinely may want to hedge banking-book credit or rate risk through its trading desk, which has the market access. The problem is that an internal trade moves capital treatment without moving any risk out of the firm. FRTB's answer is structural: internal risk transfers of interest rate risk must be executed through a dedicated notional trading desk, credit and equity risk transfers are recognised only if backed by an exactly offsetting external transaction, and the transfers must be documented and priced at market. The underlying principle is that capital relief requires risk to have actually left the institution.
questions.technique: Internal risk transfers and the book boundary
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires seeing why an internally offsetting trade is not risk reduction at firm level.

questions.prompt: In one sentence each, name the problem that Basel I, Basel II, Basel 2.5 and Basel III were each responding to.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Basel I: inconsistent and inadequate capital across international banks. Basel II: crude risk weights that ignored real differences in credit quality. Basel 2.5: trading book capital that proved far too low in 2008. Basel III: too little high-quality capital, excessive leverage, and no liquidity standard at all.
questions.explanation: Reading the sequence as a series of responses is more useful than memorising the contents. Basel I imposed a common standard but with four crude risk buckets that made a loan to a blue-chip corporate and one to a weak one identical. Basel II introduced risk sensitivity through ratings and internal models, and simultaneously created the model-arbitrage problem. Basel 2.5 was the emergency patch — stressed VaR and the incremental risk charge — bolted onto a trading book framework that had failed. Basel III addressed the capital stack itself (more common equity, deductions tightened), added the leverage ratio and the LCR and NSFR, and set in train the work that became FRTB. Each fix created the conditions for the next problem, which is the honest summary of financial regulation.
questions.technique: The Basel sequence as a chain of responses
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the causal thread through four regimes rather than a list of features.

questions.prompt: Why does a stress test result carry no probability, and how should that change the way it is used?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because the scenario is chosen, not sampled — nobody knows how likely a 300bp rate shock combined with a 30% equity fall is. So the result is used for capacity and contingency planning ('could we survive this, and what would we do') rather than for expected-loss or capital-allocation arithmetic.
questions.explanation: VaR answers 'how bad is a 1-in-100 day' and therefore carries a frequency you can backtest. A stress test answers 'what happens IF' and carries no frequency at all, which is a feature: it lets you examine events with no historical precedent, which is precisely where a probability estimate would be fiction anyway. The practical consequence is that stress results should drive limits, contingency funding plans and board discussion, and should not be blended with probabilistic measures into a single number — averaging a conditional loss with an unconditional one produces something that means nothing.
questions.technique: Conditional versus probabilistic risk measures
questions.difficultyRationale: Conceptual, but requires drawing the consequence for how the output is used.

questions.prompt: A stress scenario is described as "internally consistent". What does that mean?
options: The factor moves in it could plausibly occur together, given how markets behave
It uses the same risk factors as the VaR model
It produces a loss larger than VaR
It has been approved by the risk committee
questions.explanation: A scenario shocking equities down 40% while leaving credit spreads and implied volatility unchanged is not internally consistent — those things move together, and the scenario would materially understate the loss on a real book. Consistency is the main advantage of historical scenarios, since the combination actually happened. For hypothetical scenarios it has to be imposed deliberately, either by conditioning the other factors on the shocked one using estimated relationships, or by expert judgement, and the fact that the relationships used are themselves estimated from normal times is a known weakness.
questions.technique: Scenario consistency
questions.difficultyRationale: One definition, with the standard failure case as the illustration.

questions.prompt: How would you use conditional expectation to fill in the unshocked factors of a hypothetical scenario?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Treat the shocked factors as given and compute the conditional mean of the remaining factors under the estimated joint distribution: for jointly normal factors, E[Y | X = x] = mu_Y + Sigma_YX * Sigma_XX inverse * (x - mu_X).
questions.explanation: This is the standard way to make a partial scenario complete and consistent. You specify the few moves you care about — equities down 30% — and let the estimated covariance structure imply the rest. Two limitations that must be stated with the answer. The relationship is estimated from history, mostly from ordinary periods, so it will understate the co-movement that occurs in the very stress you are modelling; and it produces a conditional MEAN, not a stressed outcome, so the filled-in factors are central estimates rather than adverse ones. In practice the conditional expectation is a starting point that is then overridden by judgement where the analyst believes the relationship breaks.
questions.technique: Conditional expectation for scenario completion
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the conditional normal formula and the caveat that it is calibrated on the wrong regime.

questions.prompt: Describe how you would choose historical stress scenarios for a book that is mostly short-dated FX options.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Pick episodes where the relevant risk factors — spot FX and implied volatility — moved most violently together: the 2015 Swiss franc de-peg, the 1992 ERM crisis, August 2015 for the renminbi, March 2020. The selection should be driven by the book's own sensitivities, not by a generic list of famous crises.
questions.explanation: The mistake is to run the standard set of equity-crash scenarios against every book. A short-dated FX options book is dominated by gamma and vega on specific pairs, so the scenarios that matter are ones with a large spot gap and a volatility spike — and the de-peg is the sharpest example, since EURCHF moved roughly 30% in minutes and volatility markets stopped functioning. Two extensions worth mentioning: for a short-gamma book the LARGEST loss may come from a gap rather than a trend, so the scenario should be specified as an instantaneous move; and scenarios should include the liquidity dimension, because in that episode the book could not be rehedged at any quoted price.
questions.technique: Portfolio-driven scenario selection
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires mapping a specific book's sensitivities onto relevant historical episodes rather than reciting a standard list.

questions.prompt: What is a sensitivity ladder (or shock grid), and what does it show that a single stress scenario does not?
questions.canonicalAnswer: A table of P&L at a range of shock sizes — say spot at -30%, -20%, -10%, 0, +10%, +20% — often crossed with a second factor such as implied volatility. It shows the SHAPE of the exposure, revealing non-linearity, discontinuities and the worst point, which a single scenario cannot.
questions.explanation: A single scenario gives one number and implicitly suggests that risk grows monotonically with the size of the shock. For an options book that is often false: a short butterfly loses most at a moderate move and less at an extreme one, and a barrier option's P&L jumps at the barrier. The grid exposes those features directly, and the two-dimensional version (spot against vol) is standard on any options desk precisely because the worst cell is frequently not at a corner. It is also the natural tool for setting limits, since it shows where the exposure becomes unacceptable rather than only whether one chosen scenario is survivable.
questions.technique: Shock grids and non-monotone exposure
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing that the worst case need not be at the largest shock.

questions.prompt: How would you incorporate second-round effects into a stress test, and why do they matter more than the initial shock?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Model the feedback: the initial loss triggers margin calls, forced deleveraging, further price falls, funding withdrawal and further losses. It matters because in real crises the amplification through these channels typically exceeds the direct mark-to-market impact of the original shock.
questions.explanation: A standard stress test is a one-step revaluation and treats the firm as a price-taker facing an exogenous move. Real episodes are endogenous: LTCM, 2008 and the 2022 LDI crisis were all cases where the forced response to the first loss caused most of the damage. Modelling it requires stepping outside a single-firm framework — you need assumptions about who else holds correlated positions, how quickly they are forced to sell, and what market depth is available. Regulators approach this through system-wide exercises with common scenarios and, more recently, exploratory scenarios that model the reaction function of non-bank participants. The honest caveat is that these models are far less reliable than the first-round calculation, so their output is used directionally.
questions.technique: Feedback and amplification in stress testing
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires reasoning about endogenous system dynamics rather than a single-firm revaluation.

questions.prompt: Your stress test shows a £500m loss, well within capital. Name three ways that result could still be misleading.
questions.canonicalAnswer: The scenario may omit the risk factor that actually matters; the book may be assumed static when in reality positions cannot be exited at the assumed prices; and the calculation may rely on model prices that break down in the stressed conditions being modelled.
questions.explanation: Each failure is a different kind of blind spot. Omission is the commonest and the hardest to fix, because scenarios are chosen from imagination and history — this is what reverse stress testing is for. The static-book assumption cuts both ways: it ignores management action that would reduce the loss, and it ignores that liquidity may make even the intended actions impossible, which is usually the larger error. Model breakdown is subtle: the pricing models used to revalue the book are calibrated to normal markets, so a stressed revaluation of an exotic position may be using a correlation or volatility surface that would not exist in that scenario. A serious stress report states which of these apply.
questions.technique: Critiquing a stress result
questions.difficultyRationale: Open-ended; a good answer names structurally different failure modes rather than three versions of one.

questions.prompt: What is a liquidity stress test, and how does it differ from a solvency stress test?
