questions.canonicalAnswer: A liquidity stress test projects cash inflows and outflows under stress to see whether the firm can meet obligations as they fall due, over horizons from overnight to several months. A solvency stress test asks whether assets still exceed liabilities. A firm can pass one and fail the other.
questions.explanation: The two failure modes are genuinely different and firms usually die of the liquidity one first. A solvency test revalues the balance sheet; a liquidity test models behaviour — deposit run-off rates, drawdown of committed facilities, margin calls, loss of secured funding, and the haircuts applied to the assets you would monetise. Northern Rock was solvent on paper when it failed. The LCR is the standardised version of a 30-day liquidity stress test, with prescribed run-off assumptions, and the NSFR is its structural one-year counterpart. Internally, firms run their own with more granular and usually more severe assumptions.
questions.technique: Liquidity versus solvency stress testing
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires distinguishing two frameworks and knowing that behavioural assumptions dominate the liquidity one.

questions.prompt: In a reverse stress test you find the firm becomes non-viable if a single counterparty defaults while credit spreads widen 300bp. What do you do with that finding?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Assess whether the combination is remote enough to accept; if not, reduce the exposure, hedge the concentration, or hold capital and contingent funding against it. Either way the finding is escalated and the decision documented, because it is now a known vulnerability rather than an unknown one.
questions.explanation: The output of reverse stress testing is a decision, not a number. The value is that it converts an implicit vulnerability into an explicit one that someone has to accept or remove — and that acceptance is a governance act with a name attached to it. In this case the finding also identifies a concentration that ordinary stress testing missed, because a scenario-driven test would only have found it if someone had thought to combine those two shocks. It is common for reverse stress testing to surface exposures nobody was tracking, which is precisely why supervisors require it.
questions.technique: Acting on reverse stress test findings
questions.difficultyRationale: Tests whether the candidate treats the output as actionable governance rather than as a report.

questions.prompt: Why do supervisors run the same stress scenario across many banks simultaneously?
questions.canonicalAnswer: To get comparability — a common scenario makes results across banks meaningful — and to assess system-wide capital adequacy rather than each firm in isolation.
questions.explanation: If every bank chose its own scenarios, the results would be incomparable and each firm would naturally choose scenarios it survives. A common scenario removes both problems and lets supervisors rank vulnerability across the system. The system-wide view also catches something no individual test can: if every bank's plan under stress is to sell the same assets and cut the same lending, the aggregate response makes the scenario worse than any single firm assumed. The trade-off is that a single prescribed scenario invites banks to optimise against it, so supervisors vary scenarios year to year and increasingly add exploratory ones without capital consequences.
questions.technique: Concurrent supervisory stress testing
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the system-level rationale, not just comparability.

questions.prompt: What is scenario severity calibration, and how do you decide how severe a hypothetical scenario should be?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It is the choice of shock magnitudes. The usual anchors are historical extremes for each factor, a target return period (a 1-in-25-year move), or the point at which the firm's capacity is genuinely tested — severe enough to be informative, plausible enough to be taken seriously.
questions.explanation: Too mild and the exercise is theatre; too extreme and the business dismisses it and no action follows. Anchoring on history is the most defensible starting point — take the worst observed move for each factor over a long window — but it must be adjusted for factors whose history is short or whose regime has changed, and it cannot capture combinations that have never occurred. A useful discipline is to state the severity in comparable terms across factors, for instance calibrating every shock to the same estimated return period, so the scenario is not accidentally extreme in one dimension and mild in another. Regulatory scenarios typically target something in the region of a 1-in-25-year severity, which is deliberately less extreme than the 99.9% capital quantile.
questions.technique: Calibrating scenario severity
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires several calibration anchors and the practical point about consistency across factors.

questions.prompt: A risk manager proposes assigning probabilities to stress scenarios so they can be combined with VaR into a single number. Argue against it.
questions.canonicalAnswer: The probabilities would be invented — the whole reason scenarios are used is that these events are too rare or too unprecedented for their likelihood to be estimated. Blending an invented probability with an estimated one produces a number whose error is unknowable, and it destroys the conditional information the scenario carried.
questions.explanation: The value of a stress test is precisely that it says 'if X, then loss Y' without any claim about how likely X is — that statement is verifiable and useful to a decision-maker. Attaching a subjective probability makes the output look more rigorous while making it less reliable, and it invites the failure mode where a low assigned probability lets a large exposure be dismissed. There is a legitimate related practice worth acknowledging: scenario probabilities ARE used in some economic capital frameworks, and central banks do publish scenario likelihoods. The defensible version keeps the conditional loss as the headline and treats any probability as an explicitly subjective overlay, rather than aggregating the two into one figure that hides which is which.
questions.technique: Why conditional and unconditional measures should not be merged
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires arguing a position while fairly acknowledging the practices that cut the other way.

questions.prompt: A stress test assumes management takes no action. Is that conservative?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Not necessarily. It is conservative in ignoring hedges and de-risking that would reduce the loss, but optimistic in ignoring that forced actions — margin calls met by selling, funding withdrawn — can make things worse, and that the assumed exit prices may not exist.
questions.explanation: The static assumption is a modelling convenience, not a conservative choice, and treating it as automatically prudent is a common error. Two corrections pull in opposite directions. Realistic management action reduces the loss, and supervisors allow banks to model it provided the actions are documented, credible and actually available in the scenario — which rules out 'we would raise equity' in a system-wide crisis. Forced action increases the loss, through exactly the deleveraging spiral the static model omits. A well-constructed stress test states which actions are assumed and shows the result both with and without them.
questions.technique: Management actions in stress scenarios
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires recognising that the assumption errs in both directions, which most answers miss.

questions.prompt: How do you stress test a correlation assumption, given correlation is not a price?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Re-run the portfolio valuation with the correlation matrix replaced by a stressed one — typically all correlations pushed towards 1 for same-direction exposures, or towards the values observed in a historical crisis — and report the change in P&L or VaR.
questions.explanation: The most informative version is deliberately crude: set every pairwise correlation to 1 and see what the book loses. That is the 'no diversification' case, and for a portfolio whose risk framework depends heavily on offsetting positions it is often startling. More refined versions use a crisis-period correlation matrix, or shock the first eigenvalue upward to represent a market where everything loads on one factor. Two practical notes: the stressed matrix must still be positive semi-definite, so naive entry-by-entry edits need repairing; and for options books correlation is a priced input, so a correlation stress moves valuations directly rather than only the risk measure.
questions.technique: Stressing the dependence structure
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires a concrete procedure plus the PSD constraint that makes naive versions invalid.

questions.prompt: Which of these is the strongest evidence that a firm's stress testing programme is actually working?
options: Scenario results have changed a limit, a hedge or a business decision
The programme covers every risk factor in the firm's inventory
Scenarios are refreshed quarterly and approved by the board
The worst scenario loss is comfortably within available capital
questions.explanation: Everything else is process. Coverage, refresh frequency and board approval are necessary and easy to demonstrate, which is exactly why they are poor evidence of effectiveness — a programme can satisfy all three and change nothing. A loss comfortably within capital may simply mean the scenarios are too mild. The one observable that distinguishes a real programme is whether its output has ever led to a different decision, and it is the first thing a good supervisor asks for.
questions.technique: Evaluating a stress testing programme
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires distinguishing process compliance from effectiveness.

questions.prompt: What is a sensitivity stress test on volatility, and why is a vol shock specified differently from a spot shock?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It shocks implied volatility while holding spot fixed, to isolate vega. It is specified differently because volatility is quoted in absolute points and is bounded below at zero, so shocks are usually additive (plus 10 vol points) or relative with a floor, rather than a simple percentage.
questions.explanation: A 30% relative shock to a 10-vol asset is 3 points, and to an 80-vol asset is 24 points — the same relative move means completely different things, so vol scenarios are commonly specified in absolute points for that reason. The scenario should also respect the term structure and the skew: volatility spikes are concentrated in short maturities and in downside strikes, so a parallel shift of the whole surface understates the effect on a short-dated downside book and overstates it for long-dated. Serious vol stress tests shock the surface non-parallel, which is why the risk system needs the surface as a set of factors rather than a single number.
questions.technique: Specifying volatility shocks
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing why the shock convention differs and that a parallel surface shift is inadequate.

questions.prompt: Why is it a mistake to build a stress scenario purely by taking the worst historical move of each risk factor?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because the worst moves did not occur on the same day, and combining them produces a scenario far more extreme — and far less plausible — than anything that has happened. It also ignores that some factors move in offsetting directions in real crises.
questions.explanation: Taking each factor's worst observed move independently and applying them together implicitly assumes perfect correlation across every factor simultaneously, in whatever direction hurts most. That is not a 1-in-25-year scenario but something with no meaningful return period at all, and it will be dismissed by the business precisely because it is implausible. It also misrepresents real crises, where flight to quality means government bonds RALLY while credit and equities fall — a worst-case-everything scenario would shock rates upward and miss that offset. The disciplined alternative is to pick a coherent narrative and derive consistent factor moves from it.
questions.technique: Why worst-case-per-factor is not a scenario
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires recognising the implicit correlation assumption and that real crises contain offsets.

questions.prompt: Design a stress test for a book that is long credit, short equity index and long volatility. What is the scenario that hurts most?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Not a crash — the short equity and long volatility legs profit in a crash while the long credit leg loses, so the book is partly hedged. The worst scenario is a slow, grinding rally with falling volatility: credit gains little, the equity short bleeds, and the long volatility position loses to both a falling surface and time decay.
questions.explanation: The instructive part is that the intuitive scenario is the wrong one. Each leg has to be examined for what it loses on, and then you look for a state of the world in which several lose together. Here all three legs are, in different ways, positioned for trouble, so the scenario that hurts is the absence of trouble — a common profile for a book constructed defensively. Two extensions worth naming: a credit-specific idiosyncratic event that hits the long credit leg without moving the index would be painful and would not appear in any macro scenario, and the long volatility position's carry cost means the loss accumulates with TIME as well as with prices, so the scenario needs a duration attached, not just a set of moves.
questions.technique: Identifying the worst scenario from position structure
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires reasoning leg by leg to a counterintuitive answer, rather than applying a standard crash scenario.

questions.prompt: What role does stress testing play in setting risk limits, as opposed to monitoring them?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Stress results size the limits: a position limit should be set so that the loss under the firm's chosen severe scenarios remains within risk appetite. VaR and sensitivity limits then monitor day-to-day adherence.
questions.explanation: The distinction matters because the two measures answer different questions. A VaR limit controls normal-conditions variability and can be monitored daily, but it says nothing about capacity to absorb a severe event — a book can sit comfortably within VaR limits and still be unable to survive a scenario the firm regards as plausible. Working backwards from scenario loss to position size makes the limit framework connected to risk appetite rather than to a statistical artefact. In practice both are used together, with stress-based caps on concentrations and tail-sensitive exposures, and VaR or sensitivity limits for ongoing control.
questions.technique: Stress testing in limit setting
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires separating the sizing role from the monitoring role.

questions.prompt: Your firm ran a pandemic scenario in 2019 and it looked nothing like what happened in 2020. Does that mean the exercise was worthless?
questions.canonicalAnswer: No. The value of scenario work is largely in the preparation — knowing which exposures are sensitive to which factors, having the data and the process ready, and having rehearsed the decisions — and that transfers even when the specific scenario is wrong.
questions.explanation: Scenarios are almost never right in detail, and treating predictive accuracy as the success criterion misunderstands the exercise. What a 2019 pandemic scenario would have produced is a mapping from a shock to the firm's vulnerable exposures, a working set of models and data feeds, and a management team that had already had the argument about what it would do. In March 2020 that preparation is worth far more than a correct forecast, because the binding constraint in a real crisis is the speed of analysis and decision-making, not the availability of a matching scenario. The reasonable criticism is different and worth conceding: if the scenario had led to no action at all, then it really was theatre.
questions.technique: What stress testing is actually for
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires defending the exercise on the right grounds while conceding the legitimate criticism.

questions.prompt: How would you stress test a portfolio for a risk factor that has no history at all — say a newly listed instrument or a novel regulatory event?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Use judgement anchored on analogues: find the closest instrument or episode with history, apply its extreme moves with a conservative multiplier, and state the analogy explicitly as an assumption. Where no analogue exists, size the shock from first principles — what is the maximum economically possible move.
questions.explanation: The first-principles route is often more defensible than a forced analogy. A bond cannot lose more than its recovery-adjusted value; a currency peg can break by at most the distance to its free-float estimate; a position's loss is bounded by its notional plus any leverage. Anchoring on those bounds gives a scenario you can defend without pretending to have estimated a distribution. The essential discipline either way is to write down the assumption and its basis, because the number's credibility rests entirely on the reasoning rather than on data. FRTB's non-modellable risk factor regime is the regulatory version of the same problem, and its answer is likewise a judgement-based stressed scenario rather than a model.
questions.technique: Stressing factors without history
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires proposing a defensible method where the usual data-driven approach is unavailable.

questions.prompt: Daily volatility is 1.2%. What is the annualised volatility, assuming 252 trading days?
questions.explanation: Variance is additive over independent periods, so volatility scales with the square root of time: annual = daily * sqrt(252). The number worth memorising is sqrt(252) = 15.87, close enough to 16 for mental arithmetic — which gives the useful shortcut that 1% daily is about 16% annual. Going the other way, divide: 20% annual volatility is 20/16 = 1.25% a day. The assumption doing the work is that daily returns are independent; volatility clustering means they are not independent in magnitude, though the scaling remains approximately right for volatility itself.
questions.technique: Square-root-of-time annualisation
questions.difficultyRationale: One multiplication, with sqrt(252) as the fact to hold.

questions.prompt: In GARCH(1,1), sigma_n^2 = omega + alpha*r^2 + beta*sigma^2, what does a fitted alpha + beta very close to 1 tell you?
options: Volatility shocks are highly persistent and decay very slowly
The model has failed to converge
Volatility is close to constant
The long-run variance is close to zero
questions.explanation: Alpha plus beta is the persistence: the speed at which a volatility forecast reverts to its long-run level is governed by (alpha+beta)^k over k days, so a value of 0.99 means a shock's influence decays with a half-life of about 69 days. Typical equity estimates sit between 0.95 and 0.99, which is why volatility regimes persist for months. If the sum reaches or exceeds 1 the process is non-stationary — the long-run variance omega/(1-alpha-beta) is undefined — which is the IGARCH case and, not coincidentally, exactly what EWMA is.
questions.technique: Persistence in GARCH
questions.difficultyRationale: One parameter interpretation, with the boundary case connecting GARCH to EWMA.

questions.prompt: A GARCH(1,1) fit gives omega = 0.000004, alpha = 0.05, beta = 0.93. Today's volatility is 2%. What does the model forecast for volatility in 20 days' time?
questions.canonicalAnswer: About 1.83% a day. Long-run variance is 0.000004/0.02 = 0.0002, and the 20-day-ahead forecast is V_L + (alpha+beta)^20 * (current variance - V_L) = 0.0002 + 0.668(0.0002) = 0.000334, so sigma = 1.83%.
questions.explanation: The forecast formula is E[sigma_{n+k}^2] = V_L + (alpha+beta)^k (sigma_n^2 - V_L): today's variance decays geometrically towards the long-run level. Here V_L = omega/(1 - alpha - beta) = 0.000004/0.02 = 0.0002, so the long-run daily volatility is 1.41%. Today's variance is 0.0004, twice the long-run level. With alpha+beta = 0.98, the decay factor over 20 days is 0.98^20 = 0.668, so the forecast variance is 0.0002 + 0.668(0.0002) = 0.000334 and the volatility is 1.83%. Note the shape: variance mean-reverts, not volatility, and the reversion is slow — after 20 days two thirds of the excess remains. This is what produces the term structure of volatility, and it is why implied volatility curves slope downward when spot volatility is elevated.
questions.technique: Multi-day GARCH volatility forecasting
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the mean-reversion formula and care that it applies to variance rather than volatility.

questions.prompt: What is a leverage effect in volatility modelling, and which model family captures it?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Negative returns raise future volatility more than positive returns of the same size. Asymmetric GARCH models capture it — GJR-GARCH adds a term that only activates for negative returns, and EGARCH models log-variance with an asymmetric shock term.
questions.explanation: Plain GARCH uses the SQUARED return, so it cannot distinguish a 3% fall from a 3% rise, yet the asymmetry is one of the most robust features of equity data. GJR-GARCH adds gamma * r^2 * I(r < 0), so downside shocks get alpha + gamma while upside gets alpha alone. The name comes from one explanation — a price fall raises a firm's debt-to-equity ratio and hence the riskiness of the equity — though the effect is larger than leverage alone can account for, and a volatility-feedback story (higher expected volatility depresses prices) explains part of it. Either way it is the statistical counterpart of the equity volatility skew, and a model without it will misprice downside options.
questions.technique: Asymmetric volatility models
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires naming the model modification and connecting it to the options skew.

questions.prompt: What is realised volatility, and what advantage does it have over a GARCH estimate?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Realised volatility is computed by summing squared intraday returns over a day, giving a nearly model-free measurement of that day's volatility. Its advantage is that it uses intraday information, so it MEASURES volatility rather than inferring it from a model fitted to daily data.
questions.explanation: A daily GARCH estimate extracts one noisy observation per day — the squared return — and smooths it with a model. Realised volatility built from, say, five-minute returns uses roughly 78 observations a day and estimates that day's volatility far more precisely, turning an unobservable latent variable into something close to observable. That is what makes HAR and other realised-volatility models forecast better than daily GARCH. The complication is microstructure noise: as the sampling frequency rises, bid-ask bounce and discrete pricing bias the estimate upward, which is why five minutes rather than five seconds is the conventional compromise, and why realised kernels and two-scale estimators exist to correct it.
questions.technique: Realised volatility from intraday data
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the information argument plus awareness of the microstructure limit on sampling frequency.

questions.prompt: Why do we model volatility rather than returns, given both are unobservable in advance?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because volatility is predictable and returns are not. Return autocorrelations are near zero, but squared or absolute return autocorrelations are large and decay slowly, so there is genuine forecastable structure in volatility and almost none in direction.
questions.explanation: This asymmetry is the empirical foundation of the whole topic. If returns were forecastable to any useful degree the forecast would be arbitraged away, which is essentially the efficient markets argument; volatility forecastability survives because knowing that tomorrow will be turbulent does not tell you which way to trade. The practical consequences run through everything: option pricing needs a volatility forecast and not a direction forecast, risk management is a volatility-forecasting exercise, and the persistence of volatility means a single number estimated over five years is the wrong input for tomorrow.
questions.technique: Predictability of second moments
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the contrast between return and squared-return autocorrelation, and why the asymmetry survives arbitrage.

questions.prompt: Set up the maximum likelihood estimation of a GARCH(1,1) model on daily returns.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Assume r_t is conditionally normal with mean zero and variance sigma_t^2, recursively generated by the GARCH equation. The log-likelihood is the sum over t of -0.5*[ln(2*pi) + ln(sigma_t^2) + r_t^2/sigma_t^2], maximised numerically over omega, alpha and beta subject to positivity and alpha + beta < 1.
questions.explanation: The recursion is the key structural point: sigma_t^2 depends on sigma_{t-1}^2, so the likelihood must be built forward through the sample from a starting value — usually the unconditional sample variance — and every parameter change re-runs the whole recursion. Three practical notes. The constant term ln(2*pi) can be dropped since it does not affect the maximiser. Financial returns are fatter-tailed than the normal even after conditioning, so a Student-t conditional distribution usually fits better, though Gaussian quasi-maximum-likelihood remains consistent. And the likelihood surface is often flat in omega, so alpha and beta are estimated far more precisely than the implied long-run variance — which is why variance targeting, fixing V_L at the sample variance and estimating only alpha and beta, is common practice.
questions.technique: GARCH maximum likelihood
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the recursive likelihood construction plus the practical estimation issues.

questions.prompt: What does it mean for a time series to be stationary, and why does it matter for volatility modelling?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Weak stationarity means the mean, variance and autocovariances do not change over time. It matters because estimation and forecasting rely on the past being informative about the future — if the process drifts, sample statistics estimate nothing stable.
questions.explanation: Returns are usually treated as stationary; prices plainly are not, which is why every model in this area is built on returns. Within a GARCH model, stationarity of the variance process requires alpha + beta < 1, and that condition is exactly what gives a finite long-run variance for the forecast to revert to. When the estimate comes out at or above 1 you have an IGARCH process with no long-run level, and multi-day forecasts become a flat extrapolation of today. The practical warning is that apparent non-stationarity is often structural breaks in disguise — a regime change looks like a unit root to a test — and the two call for different responses.
questions.technique: Stationarity and its role in variance forecasting
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires connecting an abstract property to the concrete alpha+beta<1 condition.

questions.prompt: Implied volatility is 22% and your GARCH model forecasts 18% realised over the same horizon. Name three explanations before concluding the option is expensive.
questions.canonicalAnswer: A variance risk premium — implied systematically exceeds realised as compensation for bearing volatility risk; a horizon or measurement mismatch between the two figures; and the possibility that the market is pricing a known forthcoming event the historical model cannot see.
questions.explanation: The variance risk premium is the biggest and most systematic of the three: implied volatility exceeds subsequent realised volatility most of the time, by a few points on average, because option sellers demand compensation for a position that loses badly in crashes. So a 4-point gap is close to normal and is not by itself a signal. The mismatch problem is mundane but common — implied volatility is risk-neutral, forward-looking over the option's exact life, and quoted on a specific strike, while a GARCH forecast is real-world and horizon-averaged. The event explanation is the one a model can never supply: an earnings date, an election or a central bank meeting inside the option's life raises implied volatility legitimately. Only after clearing all three does 'expensive' become a defensible conclusion.
questions.technique: Comparing implied and forecast volatility
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing the variance risk premium is the default explanation rather than a mispricing.

questions.prompt: What is a volatility term structure, and what shape does it take when spot volatility is unusually high?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The curve of expected average volatility against horizon. When spot volatility is high the term structure slopes DOWNWARD, because mean reversion pulls the longer-horizon average back towards the long-run level.
questions.explanation: The mechanism is the GARCH forecast formula: each day's forecast decays geometrically towards V_L, so the AVERAGE over a longer window is closer to V_L than today's value is. With current daily volatility at 2% and a long-run level of 1.4%, the one-month average forecast might be 1.8% and the one-year average 1.5%. In calm markets the curve slopes upward for the same reason. The observable counterpart is the implied volatility term structure, which shows exactly this behaviour — inverting in crises and upward-sloping in quiet markets — and calendar spread trades are expressions of a view on its shape.
questions.technique: Term structure of volatility from mean reversion
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires deriving the shape from the mean-reversion property rather than memorising it.

questions.prompt: Why is a 60-day rolling window volatility estimate a poor input for a 1-day VaR, even though it is unbiased?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because it gives equal weight to a shock from 59 days ago and one from yesterday, so it responds slowly to regime changes and jumps twice per shock — once on entry, once on exit from the window.
questions.explanation: Unbiasedness is the wrong criterion here: you want the best estimate of TOMORROW'S volatility, which is a conditional forecasting problem, not an unbiased estimate of an average. Volatility clustering means recent observations are far more informative, so equal weighting discards the signal. The double-jump behaviour — the ghost feature — means the estimate moves for reasons unrelated to current conditions, which is unacceptable for a measure driving limits. EWMA fixes both by decaying the weights geometrically, and GARCH adds mean reversion on top. The 60-day window survives mainly because it is simple to explain and audit.
questions.technique: Why equal weighting is the wrong estimator
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires distinguishing unbiased estimation from conditional forecasting.

questions.prompt: Your GARCH model is fitted on daily closing prices for an asset that trades across time zones. What bias does that introduce, and how would you address it?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Close-to-close returns for a non-synchronous asset miss overnight moves and misattribute them to the next day, producing spurious autocorrelation and understated or misattributed volatility. Fix it by using synchronised snapshot times across assets, or by using range-based or realised estimators that use intraday data.
questions.explanation: The problem is worst in multi-asset work: if you correlate a European close with a US close, the European price reflects information from before the US session and the measured correlation is biased downward, since part of the co-movement shows up on different calendar days. That understates portfolio risk. The standard fixes are to snapshot all assets at a common time even if it is not any market's close, to use overlapping multi-day returns and adjust, or to move to intraday data. Range-based estimators such as Parkinson or Garman-Klass, which use the high and low, are also more efficient than close-to-close for a given sample and partly sidestep the issue.
questions.technique: Non-synchronous trading and measured volatility
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires identifying a data artefact and knowing it biases correlation as well as volatility.

questions.prompt: What is a range-based volatility estimator, and why is it more efficient than one built on closing prices?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It estimates volatility from the intraday high and low rather than from close-to-close returns — the Parkinson estimator uses (ln(H/L))^2 scaled by 1/(4 ln 2). It is more efficient because the range uses information about the whole path, not just its endpoints.
questions.explanation: A close-to-close return of zero is entirely consistent with a day that moved 5% in each direction, and a squared-return estimator records that day as having no volatility at all. The high and low capture what actually happened in between, which is why Parkinson's estimator has roughly five times the efficiency of the squared close-to-close return for the same sample. Garman-Klass adds the open and close for further gains. The limitations are practical: the theory assumes continuous observation, so a discretely observed high and low understate the true range, and the estimators handle overnight gaps badly since the range excludes the jump from previous close to open.
questions.technique: Parkinson and Garman-Klass estimators
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the efficiency argument and the assumptions that limit it in practice.

questions.prompt: How do you test whether a volatility model is adequate, once it is fitted?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Standardise the returns by the fitted conditional volatility and examine the residuals: they should have no remaining autocorrelation in their squares (Ljung-Box on squared standardised residuals), and their distribution should match the assumed conditional distribution.
questions.explanation: The logic is that a good volatility model removes all the predictable heteroskedasticity, so what is left should look like independent draws. If squared standardised residuals still show autocorrelation, the model has not captured all the clustering — perhaps it needs a longer lag structure or an asymmetric term. If the residuals are still fat-tailed relative to a normal, the conditional distribution assumption is wrong and a Student-t is indicated, though that does not invalidate the volatility dynamics themselves. A sign bias test on the residuals checks specifically for an uncaptured leverage effect. Comparing information criteria across specifications complements these but does not replace them, because a model can win on AIC while still leaving structure in the residuals.
questions.technique: Diagnostic testing of fitted volatility models
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the standardised-residual construction and knowing which diagnostic detects which deficiency.

questions.prompt: What is the VIX measuring, and why is it not simply the implied volatility of an at-the-money S&P option?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It measures the market's expected 30-day volatility implied by a whole strip of S&P 500 options weighted by 1/K^2, not a single option. That construction gives a model-free estimate of the risk-neutral expected VARIANCE, independent of any option pricing model.
questions.explanation: A single at-the-money implied volatility is a Black-Scholes inversion, so it inherits that model's assumptions and reflects one point on the smile. The variance-swap replication result says that expected variance under the risk-neutral measure equals an integral of option prices across all strikes weighted by 1/K^2, which is what the VIX formula approximates with the strikes actually listed. The practical consequences: the VIX is sensitive to the whole surface, so it rises when the skew steepens even with at-the-money volatility unchanged, and because out-of-the-money puts carry heavy weight it is particularly responsive to demand for crash protection. It is also a risk-neutral expectation, so it sits above expected realised volatility by the variance risk premium.
questions.technique: Model-free implied variance
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the variance-swap replication argument, not just a description of the index.

questions.prompt: A series of daily returns shows near-zero autocorrelation at all lags, but its ABSOLUTE values show autocorrelation of 0.2 that decays over months. What does this indicate?
options: Volatility clustering with long memory
A unit root in the return series
A data error, since the two cannot both be true
Predictable returns that the market has not arbitraged
questions.explanation: Unforecastable direction alongside strongly forecastable magnitude is the defining signature of financial return series, and the slow decay of the absolute-return autocorrelation — hyperbolic rather than exponential — is what is meant by long memory in volatility. It is entirely consistent with market efficiency, since knowing that tomorrow will be volatile does not tell you which way to trade. It also motivates models such as FIGARCH and HAR, which reproduce the slow decay better than a standard GARCH whose autocorrelation dies exponentially.
questions.technique: Long memory in volatility
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires recognising the joint pattern as a stylised fact rather than a contradiction.

questions.prompt: What are the three lines of defence, and where does model validation sit?
questions.canonicalAnswer: First line is the business that owns and takes the risk; second line is independent risk management and compliance, which challenges it; third line is internal audit, which checks that the first two work. Model validation sits in the second line.
questions.explanation: The point of the structure is independence. A model developed and validated by the same team is not validated, because the reviewer shares the developer's assumptions and has an interest in the outcome. Placing validation in the second line gives it a separate reporting line to the CRO, its own budget and the authority to restrict a model's use. Two practical qualifiers: validation must have the technical depth to actually challenge the model, otherwise independence buys nothing, and audit's role is deliberately narrow — it checks that validation happened properly, not whether the model is right.
questions.technique: Governance structure for model risk
questions.difficultyRationale: Recall of a standard structure, with the reason independence matters.

questions.prompt: A model is used far outside the range of data it was calibrated on. This is best described as:
options: A model use failure rather than a model specification failure
A calibration error
An implementation bug
Acceptable, provided the model is mathematically correct
questions.explanation: The model may be perfectly specified and correctly implemented and still produce nonsense outside its intended domain — the failure is in how it was applied, not in what it is. That is why a model inventory records each model's approved scope and limitations, and why a change of use requires re-approval just as a change of methodology does. The distinction matters because the remedies differ entirely: a specification problem is fixed by the quant team, a use problem is fixed by controls and governance.
questions.technique: Use failure versus specification failure
questions.difficultyRationale: One classification, with the remedy as the discriminating consequence.

questions.prompt: What belongs in a model inventory, and why do supervisors insist on one?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Every model in use, with its owner, purpose, approved scope, methodology, key assumptions and known limitations, validation status and date, materiality tier, and dependencies on other models. Supervisors insist because you cannot manage risk in models you have not enumerated.
questions.explanation: The unglamorous parts do the work. Recording approved SCOPE is what makes use-failure detectable. Recording DEPENDENCIES matters because models feed each other — a volatility surface model feeds pricing which feeds VaR which feeds capital — so a flaw propagates, and without the dependency map nobody knows how far. Materiality tiering is what makes the whole thing feasible: a large bank has thousands of models and cannot validate them all to the same depth, so effort is allocated by exposure and complexity. The recurring supervisory finding is not that inventories are missing but that they are incomplete — spreadsheets and end-user computing tools that make real decisions and were never registered as models.
questions.technique: Model inventory contents and purpose
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires identifying which inventory fields are load-bearing rather than listing everything.

questions.prompt: What is benchmarking in model validation, and what does it establish that backtesting does not?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Benchmarking prices or forecasts the same positions with an independent alternative model and compares. It establishes whether the model's output is defensible relative to reasonable alternatives, which backtesting cannot do when outcomes are rare, slow to arrive, or unobservable.
questions.explanation: Backtesting needs realised outcomes, and for many models they are unavailable in useful quantity — a 99.9% capital model, a long-dated exotic's price, a lifetime credit loss forecast. Benchmarking sidesteps that by asking a different question: does an independently built model agree? A large discrepancy does not tell you which is right, but it does tell you the output is not robust to modelling choices, and that is itself the quantity you want for a model reserve. The benchmark must be genuinely independent — a re-implementation of the same methodology tests the code, not the model — and the comparison should span the range of positions, since models typically agree at the money and diverge in the wings.
questions.technique: Benchmarking as a validation technique
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing when backtesting is unavailable and what benchmarking substitutes for it.

questions.prompt: What is a model reserve, and how would you size one for an exotic options book?
questions.canonicalAnswer: A deduction from reported value held against the uncertainty in the model used to price it. Size it by repricing the book across a range of defensible models and calibrations and taking a conservative point in the resulting distribution of values — typically the difference between the chosen model's price and a prudent percentile.
questions.explanation: The essential move is to convert model uncertainty into a spread of prices rather than a single alternative. Reprice with a local volatility model, a stochastic volatility model and a jump model, all calibrated to the same market quotes; the spread across them is the model uncertainty for that book, and it is often material for path-dependent and barrier products where the models agree on vanillas by construction and disagree on everything else. Two further points: the reserve should release as positions mature or as the market provides observable prices, and the calibration dimension matters as much as the model dimension, since the same model calibrated to different instrument sets can produce materially different exotic prices.
questions.technique: Sizing model uncertainty reserves
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires a concrete procedure that turns model choice into a price distribution.

questions.prompt: A desk's model is recalibrated daily and always fits market prices almost exactly. Is that reassuring?
questions.canonicalAnswer: No. A model that reprices the market perfectly every day may simply have enough free parameters to fit anything, in which case it has no predictive content and its hedge ratios are unreliable even though its prices look right.
questions.explanation: Fitting the market is necessary but nearly costless for a sufficiently flexible model — local volatility, for example, fits every vanilla by construction. What distinguishes a good model is the STABILITY of its calibrated parameters over time and the quality of the hedges it implies. If the calibrated parameters jump around daily, the model is absorbing market movement into parameters that are supposed to be structural, which is a warning sign: your delta comes from those parameters, so it is being computed from something that will be different tomorrow. The diagnostics that matter are parameter stability, out-of-sample pricing of instruments not used in calibration, and hedge performance measured as the P&L of a delta-hedged position.
questions.technique: Calibration fit versus model quality
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires recognising that fit and predictive validity are different, and naming the diagnostics that separate them.

questions.prompt: Two banks price the same exotic and differ by 8% of notional. Neither can be shown wrong. How should each treat that fact?
questions.canonicalAnswer: As a measurement of model uncertainty for that product. Each should hold a reserve reflecting the dispersion, review whether its own calibration and model choice are defensible, and treat the position as one whose value is a range rather than a number.
questions.explanation: The disagreement is information: it says the product's value is not determined by observable market prices plus no-arbitrage, but depends on modelling choices about which reasonable people differ. That is exactly what a model reserve exists for, and 8% of notional is large enough to be material to P&L and to any decision to trade. The secondary implications are practical. A position marked with that much uncertainty should not be used to book day-one profit without a reserve — recognising the full spread as revenue at inception is the classic failure, and IFRS 13's restriction on day-one gains for level 3 instruments addresses it. And if the two banks trade with each other on the strength of the disagreement, both are booking a profit from the same trade, which is only possible if at least one is wrong.
questions.technique: Interpreting price dispersion as model uncertainty
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires treating a disagreement as data rather than as a problem to resolve, plus the accounting consequence.

questions.prompt: How does model risk differ for a machine learning model compared with a parametric financial model?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The failure modes shift from wrong assumptions to opaque behaviour: overfitting is easier and harder to detect, the model may key on spurious features, its behaviour outside the training distribution is unpredictable, and its reasoning cannot be inspected the way a closed-form model's can.
questions.explanation: A Black-Scholes model has assumptions you can list and challenge one by one. A gradient-boosted model has no such list, so validation shifts to empirical technique: rigorous out-of-time and out-of-sample testing, stability analysis across periods, feature importance and partial dependence to see what it is actually keying on, and adversarial or edge-case testing. Two risks are specific to this class. Data leakage produces spectacular backtest performance from information unavailable at decision time, and it is common enough that a suspiciously good result should be assumed to be leakage until proven otherwise. And where the model touches customers, opaque features can encode protected characteristics indirectly, which is a regulatory exposure with no analogue in derivatives pricing.
questions.technique: Validating machine learning models
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires mapping familiar model-risk concepts onto a class where the usual assumption-based challenge does not apply.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between a model being conservative and a model being right, and why does the distinction matter for capital?
questions.canonicalAnswer: A conservative model deliberately errs in one direction; a right model is unbiased. The distinction matters because conservatism in a risk measure is not free — it distorts pricing, hedging and capital allocation, and it can be exploited.
questions.explanation: Conservatism is often treated as automatically prudent, and for a capital number it broadly is. But the same model usually feeds decisions where bias is harmful: an overstated risk figure makes a genuinely good trade look unattractive, misallocates limits, and produces hedge ratios that are wrong in a known direction. It also creates a perverse dynamic, since traders learn where the model is conservative and structure positions that look expensive to the model and cheap in reality, or vice versa. The disciplined approach is to keep the model unbiased and apply conservatism explicitly and visibly as a reserve or an add-on, so that everyone can see how much of the number is measurement and how much is prudence.
questions.technique: Where to put conservatism
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires arguing that a seemingly safe choice has costs, and proposing where the buffer belongs instead.

questions.prompt: What is model monitoring, and what would you monitor for a VaR model in production?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Ongoing checks that a model still performs as validated. For a VaR model: exception counts and their clustering, P&L attribution quality, input data completeness and staleness, the stability of calibrated parameters and correlations, coverage of the book by mapped risk factors, and the ratio of modelled to standardised capital.
questions.explanation: Validation is a point-in-time assessment; monitoring is what catches the model going stale as the book and the market change. The most valuable indicators are usually about INPUTS rather than outputs — a risk factor that stopped updating, a growing share of positions being proxied, a new product mapped to an approximate factor — because those degrade the model silently while the headline number continues to look reasonable. Exception clustering matters as much as the count, since three exceptions in one week and three spread over a year point at different problems. Thresholds should be defined in advance with an escalation path, otherwise monitoring produces a dashboard nobody acts on.
questions.technique: Ongoing model monitoring
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires naming input-side indicators, which are the ones that catch silent degradation.

questions.prompt: Give an example of a model whose widespread use changed the thing it was modelling.
questions.canonicalAnswer: Portfolio insurance in 1987: the model prescribed selling futures as the market fell, and because many participants ran it simultaneously, the selling itself drove the fall it was hedging against. Black-Scholes-implied hedging and the Gaussian copula in CDO markets are further examples.
questions.explanation: This is performativity — the model does not just describe the market, it participates in it. Portfolio insurance is the cleanest case, because the strategy's own execution supplied the liquidity shock that made it fail, and the effect only exists because the model was widely adopted. The general lesson for a risk manager is that a model calibrated on data from before its own adoption may not describe the world after, and that positions which are crowded carry a risk that no single-firm model can see — everyone's hedge is the same trade, and it will be attempted simultaneously. That is one of the strongest arguments for stress scenarios built around forced deleveraging rather than around price moves alone.
questions.technique: Performativity and crowded models
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires a concrete example plus the generalisation about crowded positions.

questions.prompt: Your firm buys a vendor model whose internals you cannot inspect. How do you validate it?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Validate what you can observe: test it on known cases with analytic answers, benchmark it against an independent model, sensitivity-test its behaviour across the input space for implausible outputs or discontinuities, review the vendor's own documentation and validation evidence, and confirm the vendor's change-management process.
questions.explanation: Black-box status reduces what you can do but does not remove the obligation — the firm using the model owns its risk regardless of who built it. Behavioural testing is the core of it: sweep each input across its plausible range and check monotonicity and smoothness where theory demands them, and test limiting cases where the answer is known analytically. Two governance points to add. Vendor change management matters because an update can change your numbers overnight, so you need notice and the ability to test before adoption. And concentration is a systemic issue in its own right: if most of the market uses the same vendor model, its flaws are correlated across firms and will not be discovered by anyone's independent check.
questions.technique: Validating third-party models
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires adapting validation technique to the case where the internals are unavailable.

questions.prompt: A pricing model and a risk model value the same position differently. Which is wrong, and what do you do?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Neither is necessarily wrong — they may legitimately differ in granularity, since risk models often use fewer factors deliberately. But the difference must be quantified, explained and bounded, because an unexplained gap means the risk model is measuring a different portfolio from the one the firm actually holds.
questions.explanation: The correct first move is decomposition: reprice with the risk model's factors under the pricing model to separate factor-coverage differences from methodology differences. A gap explained by the risk model omitting a factor is a known simplification to be documented, monitored, and capitalised if material. A gap that cannot be attributed is the dangerous case, and it usually means one implementation has a defect. This is precisely what FRTB's P&L attribution test institutionalises — it compares risk-theoretical and hypothetical P&L and penalises desks where they diverge — and it is worth noting the incentive that creates, since the cheapest way to pass is sometimes to simplify the front-office model rather than enrich the risk model.
questions.technique: Reconciling pricing and risk models
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires a decomposition procedure and the judgement that a difference is not automatically an error.

questions.prompt: Why is a model's data more often the source of failure than its mathematics?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because mathematics is checked once and stays checked, while data arrives every day and can be stale, missing, misaligned, revised, or drawn from a changed source — and the model will produce a plausible-looking number regardless.
questions.explanation: The asymmetry is about detectability. A wrong formula usually produces obviously wrong output and is caught in testing; a stale price feed produces a number that is merely slightly wrong, every day, and can persist for months. Common failure modes worth naming: a curve that stopped updating and holds its last value, timezone misalignment across regions, a corporate action not applied so a price series shows a spurious jump, survivorship bias in a backtest universe, and vendor methodology changes applied retroactively so history silently changes underneath a model. The controls are unglamorous — staleness checks, cross-source reconciliation, completeness monitoring, and versioned data snapshots so a calculation can be reproduced exactly.
questions.technique: Data quality as the dominant model risk
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the detectability argument plus concrete failure modes.

questions.prompt: What is the value of a model that is known to be wrong but is used consistently by everyone?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It is a common language. Black-Scholes implied volatility is the standard example: nobody believes the assumptions, but because everyone inverts the same formula, a quoted volatility is unambiguous and comparable across strikes, maturities and counterparties.
questions.explanation: The model is doing a translation job rather than a predictive one. Quoting an option at 22 vol conveys far more than quoting it at £3.40, because the volatility number is comparable across instruments in a way the price is not, and the mapping from price to volatility is one-to-one so no information is lost. The same applies to yield to maturity for bonds and to spread for credit. The danger is forgetting which job the model is doing: a quoting convention says nothing about hedging, so using Black-Scholes deltas because you use Black-Scholes quotes is exactly the mistake the volatility smile warns against.
questions.technique: Models as quoting conventions
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires separating a model's translation role from its predictive role.

questions.prompt: Which finding in a model validation report should trigger the most urgent action?
options: The model has been used for two years on a product type outside its approved scope
The model's documentation is out of date
The model's assumptions include constant volatility
The model has not been revalidated within its scheduled period
questions.explanation: Use outside approved scope means the firm has been taking decisions on numbers nobody has ever assessed for that purpose, and it has been doing so for two years — the positions, the P&L and any capital derived from them are all in question immediately. The others are real findings but bounded: stale documentation and an overdue revalidation are process failures with no immediate evidence that any number is wrong, and a constant-volatility assumption is a known limitation of many models that may be perfectly acceptable within scope. Ranking findings by what is already exposed, rather than by how bad they sound, is the substance of the question.
questions.technique: Triaging validation findings
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires ranking by realised exposure rather than by severity of description.

questions.prompt: What is parameter uncertainty, and how does it differ from the risk the model is measuring?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Parameter uncertainty is the error in the estimated inputs — volatilities, correlations, default probabilities — as distinct from the variability those parameters describe. It is second-order risk: uncertainty about the distribution rather than uncertainty within it.
questions.explanation: A VaR of £5m computed from an estimated volatility carries two distinct uncertainties: the loss may exceed £5m because that is what a 1% tail means, and the £5m may itself be wrong because the volatility was estimated from a finite sample. The second is routinely ignored, yet for correlations estimated from short samples it can dominate. Quantifying it means putting a distribution on the parameters — through the bootstrap, a Bayesian posterior, or simply repricing at the ends of a confidence interval — and reporting the resulting range. The general point is that a risk number without an error bar invites false precision, and the error bar is usually much wider than anyone expects.
questions.technique: Estimation error as second-order risk
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires distinguishing two levels of uncertainty that are easily conflated.

questions.prompt: A quant proposes replacing a simple model with a more sophisticated one that fits the data better. What questions should validation ask?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Does it fit better OUT of sample, not just in sample? How many additional parameters, and are they identifiable and stable? Are its hedge ratios better, not just its prices? Is anyone able to understand and challenge it? And what does it do at the edges where the simple model was at least predictable?
questions.explanation: Better in-sample fit is nearly guaranteed by extra flexibility and is therefore not evidence of anything. The questions that discriminate are about generalisation and robustness. Parameter identifiability matters because a model whose parameters are not pinned down by the calibration instruments will have unstable ones, and unstable parameters produce unstable hedges. Comprehensibility is a genuine criterion rather than a concession to weaker colleagues: a model nobody outside the developer can challenge has no effective validation, and the resulting concentration of knowledge is itself an operational risk. The honest framing is that sophistication has costs, and it must earn them.
questions.technique: Evaluating a proposed model upgrade
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires distinguishing in-sample fit from evidence of improvement, plus the non-technical criteria.

questions.prompt: A strategy has a Sharpe ratio of 2.5 in backtest. What is your first hypothesis, and how would you test it?
questions.canonicalAnswer: That the result is an artefact — lookahead bias, survivorship bias, unrealistic transaction costs, or selection from many tested variants. Test by re-running on strictly point-in-time data with realistic costs, and by asking how many strategies were tried before this one.
questions.explanation: A Sharpe of 2.5 is far above what liquid strategies sustain, so the prior strongly favours an artefact. Lookahead is the commonest and sneakiest: using a price, a fundamental figure or an index membership that was not knowable at the decision time — index constituents and restated financials are classic sources. Costs are routinely understated, and a strategy trading frequently can lose its entire edge to a realistic spread and impact model. The multiple-testing question is the one people resist: if 200 variants were tried, the best one's in-sample Sharpe tells you almost nothing, and the deflated Sharpe ratio adjusts for exactly that. The order of testing matters — check the data pipeline before admiring the result.
questions.technique: Diagnosing an implausible backtest
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires prioritising among several artefacts and knowing that the number of trials is part of the evidence.

questions.prompt: How would you tier a model inventory by materiality, and what changes between tiers?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Tier by the size of the exposure the model touches, the complexity and opacity of its methodology, and the consequence of it being wrong (regulatory capital, customer outcomes, financial reporting). Higher tiers get deeper validation, more frequent revalidation, more monitoring and stricter change control.
questions.explanation: Tiering exists because a large bank has thousands of models and uniform treatment would be both unaffordable and misallocated. A pricing model for a multi-billion exotic book and a spreadsheet estimating stationery costs do not merit the same scrutiny. What changes with tier is depth and cadence: a tier-1 model gets independent re-implementation, full benchmarking and annual revalidation, while a low-tier model may get a documentation review every three years. The failure mode to watch for is tiering by convenience rather than by exposure, and the classic gap is the low-tier model that quietly grew — a small tool that ended up feeding a material decision without anyone re-tiering it.
questions.technique: Materiality tiering
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the tiering criteria plus the specific way tiering goes wrong in practice.

questions.prompt: What is the difference between overfitting and look-ahead bias, and which is easier to detect?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Overfitting means the model has learned noise in the training data and will generalise poorly. Look-ahead bias means the model used information that was not available at the decision time, so its results are impossible rather than merely optimistic. Overfitting is easier to detect.
questions.explanation: Overfitting reveals itself in a properly constructed out-of-sample test — performance degrades and the gap is the diagnosis. Look-ahead bias survives out-of-sample testing, because the leaked information is present in every period including the test set, so the strategy performs beautifully everywhere and there is nothing to compare against. Detecting it requires auditing the data pipeline for timestamps: when was each field actually knowable, as opposed to what date it is stamped with. Restated financials, index membership applied retroactively, and any dataset assembled after the fact are the usual culprits. The practical rule is that unusually consistent performance across all periods is more suspicious than performance that varies.
questions.technique: Overfitting versus look-ahead bias
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires knowing that out-of-sample testing catches one and not the other.

questions.prompt: What does the Net Stable Funding Ratio require, and how does its horizon differ from the LCR's?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The NSFR requires available stable funding to be at least 100% of required stable funding over a ONE-YEAR horizon, addressing structural funding mismatch. The LCR covers a 30-day acute stress.
questions.explanation: The two are deliberately complementary. The LCR asks whether you survive a month-long run, and is satisfied by holding liquid assets. The NSFR asks whether your funding structure is sustainable — whether long-dated, illiquid assets are financed with stable, long-dated liabilities rather than rolled overnight in wholesale markets. A bank could pass the LCR with a large buffer while funding a mortgage book entirely in the overnight repo market, and the NSFR is what prevents that. Deposits from retail and small business count as more stable than wholesale funding, which is a direct lesson from Northern Rock.
questions.technique: NSFR versus LCR
questions.difficultyRationale: Two ratios with different horizons and different questions.

questions.prompt: A market's depth is best described as:
options: The volume available near the current price without moving it materially
The difference between the best bid and best offer
The number of trades per day
The time it takes to execute an order
questions.explanation: Liquidity has at least three separate dimensions and they are routinely conflated. Tightness is the bid-ask spread — the cost of a small trade. Depth is the size available before the price moves — the cost of a large one. Resiliency is how quickly the book refills after being hit. A market can be tight and shallow, which is the dangerous combination for a large position: the screen shows a one-basis-point spread and the position takes weeks to exit. Any liquidity measure built only on quoted spreads is measuring tightness and ignoring the dimension that matters for size.
questions.technique: Dimensions of market liquidity
questions.difficultyRationale: One definition, with the three-dimension framing as the substance.

questions.prompt: What is market impact, and how does it typically scale with trade size?
questions.canonicalAnswer: The adverse price move caused by your own trading. Empirically it scales roughly with the SQUARE ROOT of size relative to daily volume — impact is approximately proportional to volatility times sqrt(Q/V).
questions.explanation: The square-root law is one of the more robust empirical regularities in market microstructure, holding across asset classes and venues. Its practical implication is concave cost: doubling the size does not double the impact per share, so there is a genuine trade-off against the risk of executing slowly. That trade-off is exactly what optimal execution frameworks solve — trade fast and pay impact, trade slowly and bear price risk, with the balance set by your risk aversion and the asset's volatility. Note that permanent and temporary impact differ: temporary impact recovers after you stop, permanent impact reflects the information your trading revealed, and only the permanent part is a genuine transfer.
questions.technique: Market impact and the square-root law
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the scaling law plus its consequence for execution strategy.

questions.prompt: Explain the liquidity mismatch in an open-ended fund holding corporate bonds, and why it is a systemic concern.
questions.canonicalAnswer: The fund offers daily redemption while holding assets that may take weeks to sell. Redeeming investors are paid at today's NAV, funded by selling the most liquid holdings, leaving remaining investors with a less liquid portfolio — a first-mover advantage that can trigger a run.
questions.explanation: The mechanism is the key part. Selling the liquid assets first, called cash-first or vertical-slice-avoidance, means each redemption degrades the portfolio for those who stay, giving everyone an incentive to redeem early. That converts an ordinary outflow into a run without any change in fundamentals. The systemic dimension is that many funds hold similar assets and would sell simultaneously, which is what happened in March 2020 and required central bank intervention in corporate bond markets. Mitigants include swing pricing (making redeemers bear their own liquidation cost), redemption gates, notice periods, and vertical-slice liquidation — all of which work by removing the first-mover advantage rather than by holding more cash.
questions.technique: Liquidity transformation and run dynamics
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the first-mover mechanism, which is what makes it a run rather than an outflow.

questions.prompt: What is swing pricing, and what problem does it solve?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Adjusting a fund's NAV on days of large net flows so that transacting investors bear the associated trading costs rather than the remaining shareholders. It removes the first-mover advantage that makes redemption runs rational.
questions.explanation: Without it, a redeeming investor receives the unadjusted NAV while the fund incurs spread and impact costs to raise the cash, which are borne by everyone who stays — so redeeming early is strictly better, and a modest outflow can cascade. Swing pricing charges those costs to the flow that caused them by moving the NAV down on a net-redemption day and up on a net-subscription day, typically only past a threshold. The design questions are the swing factor's size and whether it reflects stressed rather than normal costs, since an under-calibrated factor leaves part of the advantage in place. It is standard in Europe and has been slower to adopt in the US, partly because it complicates same-day pricing operationally.
questions.technique: Swing pricing
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires linking the mechanism to the incentive it removes.

questions.prompt: Why do secured funding markets freeze in a crisis even though the lender holds collateral?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because the collateral's value and liquidity are themselves in question, and the lender does not want to own it — haircuts widen, eligible collateral narrows, and eventually lenders refuse regardless of price, since taking possession of an illiquid asset in a falling market is not an attractive outcome.
questions.explanation: Repo is often described as safe because it is collateralised, but the safety depends on being able to liquidate the collateral at close to the haircut-adjusted value, which is exactly what fails in a crisis. Haircuts on private-label structured credit went from a few percent to refusal in 2008, which withdrew funding entirely from firms whose business model assumed rollover. There is also an adverse selection dimension: a borrower posting a particular asset may know more about it than the lender, and in stressed conditions lenders assume the worst. The general lesson is that collateralisation converts credit risk into liquidity and market risk rather than removing risk, and the conversion is least favourable precisely when it matters.
questions.technique: Collateralised funding under stress
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires explaining why collateral fails to reassure, rather than restating that funding dries up.

questions.prompt: Describe the liquidity spiral in which market liquidity and funding liquidity reinforce each other.
questions.canonicalAnswer: A price fall raises margin requirements and erodes capital, forcing leveraged holders to sell; the selling pushes prices down further and widens spreads; wider spreads and higher volatility raise haircuts, tightening funding again. Each loop makes the next one worse.
questions.explanation: Brunnermeier and Pedersen's framing is the standard reference, and the two channels are worth naming separately. The loss spiral works through capital: falling prices reduce equity, so a leveraged investor must shrink the balance sheet to maintain leverage, which means selling into the fall. The margin spiral works through haircuts: volatility rises, lenders demand more collateral per unit borrowed, and the same position requires more capital than it did yesterday. Both are amplifiers rather than causes, which is why the size of a shock is a poor predictor of the size of a crisis — leverage and the procyclicality of margin determine the multiplier. The policy responses follow directly: countercyclical margin floors, central bank liquidity facilities that break the funding leg, and leverage limits.
questions.technique: Loss and margin spirals
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires both channels and the observation that they are amplifiers rather than causes.

questions.prompt: How does a liquidity gap analysis work, and what makes it different from simply listing contractual maturities?
questions.canonicalAnswer: It projects cash inflows and outflows into time buckets and shows the cumulative net position in each. It differs from contractual maturities because it applies BEHAVIOURAL assumptions: deposit run-off rates, loan prepayment, facility drawdowns, and the assumption that some maturing assets will be rolled rather than repaid.
questions.explanation: Contractual maturity is nearly useless on its own for a bank. Current accounts are contractually overnight but behaviourally multi-year; committed facilities are contractually undrawn but will be drawn in a stress precisely when the bank can least afford it; a mortgage's contractual life bears little relation to its expected one. The gap analysis is therefore only as good as the behavioural assumptions, and those assumptions are the model risk — they are calibrated on periods that did not include a run. Good practice runs the analysis under both normal and stressed assumptions and shows the cumulative gap, since a fund that is comfortable at every individual bucket can still be short on a cumulative basis.
questions.technique: Behavioural liquidity gap analysis
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires identifying the behavioural overlay as both the point and the weakness.

questions.prompt: What is a contingency funding plan, and what distinguishes a credible one?
questions.canonicalAnswer: A pre-agreed plan for meeting funding needs under stress: identified sources, the order in which they are used, triggers for activation, and named decision-makers. A credible one uses sources that will still be available in the stress, has been tested operationally, and has triggers that fire early enough to matter.
questions.explanation: The commonest weakness is relying on sources that vanish exactly when needed — uncommitted interbank lines, asset sales into a market where everyone is selling, or an equity raise during a systemic crisis. A credible plan therefore leans on pre-positioned collateral at the central bank, committed facilities, and assets that are liquid under stress rather than merely under normal conditions. Operational testing matters more than it sounds: firms have discovered in a crisis that collateral was not pre-positioned, that the legal agreements were unsigned, or that the operational path to pledge assets took days. And triggers must be leading indicators, since a plan activated once the firm is already in difficulty has lost most of its options.
questions.technique: Contingency funding planning
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires distinguishing a plan that exists from one that would work.

questions.prompt: Why is concentration a liquidity risk as well as a market risk?
questions.canonicalAnswer: Because a position large relative to normal traded volume cannot be exited at quoted prices — the unwind cost grows with size and the time to exit grows with it, so the effective risk is far greater than a mark-to-market measure suggests.
questions.explanation: Two positions with the same VaR are not equally risky if one is 2% of daily volume and the other 200%. The second faces market impact on exit, an extended unwind period during which market risk continues to accrue, and the near-certainty that other holders of the same position are trying to exit simultaneously. It also becomes visible: a position large enough to matter is known to the market and can be traded against, which is what happened to LTCM and to Amaranth. Practical controls are volume-based position limits — expressed as days of average daily volume rather than as notional — and liquidity-adjusted VaR that scales the horizon with the estimated unwind period.
questions.technique: Concentration as liquidity risk
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires seeing that identical market-risk numbers can carry very different liquidity profiles.

questions.prompt: What is a liquidity-adjusted VaR that accounts for an uncertain spread, and how is it constructed?
questions.canonicalAnswer: LVaR = ordinary VaR + 0.5 * (mean spread + z * spread standard deviation) * position value. The add-on charges the expected cost of crossing the spread plus an allowance for the spread being unusually wide when you need to trade.
questions.explanation: The construction treats the spread as a random variable rather than a constant, which matters because spreads are strongly correlated with the market moves that drive the VaR itself — you will be selling on exactly the days spreads are widest. Using the mean plus 2.326 standard deviations gives a 99% spread. Two refinements are worth mentioning: the add-on is usually added rather than combined in quadrature, since assuming independence between the market move and the spread is optimistic; and for a position large relative to volume, this measure still understates the cost because it ignores market impact entirely and assumes the whole size trades at the quoted spread.
questions.technique: Spread-based liquidity adjustment to VaR
questions.difficultyRationale: Requires the formula plus the reasons it remains conservative to add rather than combine.

questions.prompt: Distinguish the exogenous and endogenous components of liquidity risk.
